Iran lawmaker named in alleged illegal treasure excavation. A senior hardline Iranian lawmaker has been named in an allegation involving unauthorized excavation for antiquities and treasure, while parliament is also examining a reported excavation case involving an unnamed member of the legislature.

Family of executed January protester says Iran concealed burial site. The family of Alireza Raisi, executed this week over the January protests in Isfahan, still does not know where he was buried after security agents took his father blindfolded to the burial site, a source close to the family told Iran International.

Iran protester recounts torture, mock execution after January arrest. “Write your will.” Those were the words Iranian protester Erfan Nabian says he heard in solitary confinement before he was handed a sheet of paper and asked what he wanted for his final meal before his execution.

Parsian Exchange transferred millions of dollars for Iran despite sanctions. Iran’s Bank Parsian, under US sanctions, used its foreign-exchange arm to move millions of dollars abroad through a network of intermediaries, according to an Iran International investigation based on leaked internal correspondence and transaction records.

Rubio says Iran missed deal chances as Tehran digs in on enrichment. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that Iran had failed to take advantage of repeated opportunities to reach an agreement with Washington over its nuclear program, while also saying Tehran had “lost complete control” of the Strait of Hormuz.

Tehran divided over $2 billion plan to prop up rial. Iran’s central bank is offering as much as $2 billion in cash dollars to the public in an effort to slow the rial’s slide, triggering a fierce debate over whether the intervention can stabilize the currency or merely burn through increasingly scarce foreign reserves.

China shifts to Iraqi oil: is Iran using old workaround to beat US blockade?. China’s independent refiners are turning to Iraqi crude to replace dwindling Iranian supplies as a US blockade chokes Tehran’s exports, raising questions about whether Iran is using an old workaround to reach its buyers: disguising its own oil as Iraqi.

Kayhan attacks Ghalibaf’s role in talks. Didn’t Khamenei approve it?. An editorial questioning Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf’s role as Iran’s lead negotiator has raised an awkward question in Tehran: who exactly is Kayhan criticizing, given that senior officials have said the parliament speaker was given the job with the Supreme Leader’s approval?

‘$100k-a-month captains’: What it costs to move oil through Hormuz. Oil tanker captains are being paid as much as $100,000 a month and offered $50,000 bonuses for individual trips through the Strait of Hormuz, the latest sign of the extraordinary costs now required to keep crude moving through the waterway since the Iran war began.

Iran looks for escape routes as US sanctions close in. The widening reach of US sanctions across Iran’s transport and industrial networks has raised alarms in Tehran that Washington is seeking to close off the alternative trade routes the country has relied on to circumvent years of economic pressure.

From talks to war: Tehran sees the gap narrowing. Fears of renewed war with the United States, Israel or both are growing in Iran, as military officials talk openly about pre-emptive action and analysts warn that the distance between diplomacy and another round of fighting is becoming dangerously short.

Hezbollah recruitment network in Iran exposed, four safe houses identified. Hezbollah’s external operations unit has been recruiting foreign nationals in Iran and using safe houses in Qom and Tehran to train and shelter recruits, according to information obtained by Iran International.

Islamic Republic supporters take weapons home after training, citizens say. Some participants in military training programs for supporters of the Islamic Republic, including Basij militia members and seminary students, have been allowed to take weapons home, citizens told Iran International, as authorities expand firearms training to schools across Iran.

Police officer killed in armed attack near Zahedan as violence continues in southeast Iran. An Iranian police officer was killed on Thursday when gunmen attacked a patrol near Zahedan in Sistan-Baluchestan, the latest in a series of deadly attacks and clashes involving security forces in southeastern Iran.

Iran's reported $200 million Hezbollah aid angers cash-strapped citizens. Reports that the Islamic Republic sent $200 million to Lebanon's Hezbollah have drawn anger from Iranians struggling with rising living costs, low wages and medicine shortages, according to messages sent to Iran International.

Three years after October 7, Iran pays the price of miscalculation. Three years after Hamas's October 7 attack on Israel, the Islamic Republic faces a weakened network of regional allies, direct military confrontation and mounting economic pressure, upending its long-held strategy of deterring enemies while keeping war away from its territory.

US sanctions 17 ships in push to shut down Iran’s shadow fleet. The US Treasury sanctioned 17 vessels and their owners Thursday under Operation Economic Outcast, saying the action effectively neutralizes most of Iran’s remaining shadow fleet.

Saudi Aramco hires US firm to upgrade shared oil field as Iran lags behind. Saudi Aramco has hired a US engineering firm to upgrade an offshore oil field it shares with Iran, which has fallen far behind several neighbors in developing shared energy reserves.

Trump rules out Iran attack before midterms, Tehran says ready for prolonged war. US President Donald Trump said Thursday the United States would not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections and that "productive" talks were underway, after reports of US preparations for possible large-scale strikes.

US pressure hits Iranians harder than rulers, 68% in poll say. More than two-thirds of respondents to an Iran International Instagram poll said the Trump administration’s pressure on the Islamic Republic is hurting ordinary Iranians more than the authorities.

Taliban-run Afghanistan could get ‘land of its own’ on Iran’s coast, MP says. Iran has reached a preliminary understanding to allocate land at Chabahar to Taliban-run Afghanistan to build infrastructure for moving its goods to the sea, an Iranian lawmaker said.

Iraq creates PMF unit to take faction drones as arms plan advances - Erem News. Iraq has created a specialized unit within the Popular Mobilization Forces to take control of drones held by armed factions as part of Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi’s plan to bring weapons under state authority, Erem News reported on Friday, citing an Iraqi security source.

Iranian security forces face wave of deadly attacks in restive southeast. At least five Iranian military and police personnel were killed and several others wounded in four armed attacks across southeastern Iran within 24 hours, local rights group Haalvsh reported, as violence targeting security forces continued across the area.

Iran-origin campaign targeted Iran International, foreign media - OpenAI. An Iran-origin influence operation used fake Western journalist identities to place nearly 100 articles in online news outlets around the world and repeatedly generated hostile social media responses to Iran International, OpenAI said in a report released on Thursday.

Two men deny spying for Iran on Israeli embassy in London. Two men accused of carrying out surveillance on the Israeli Embassy, Britain’s oldest synagogue and other Jewish and Israeli-linked sites in London on behalf of Iran pleaded not guilty on Friday.

UK court hears how alleged Iran spy operation targeted Iran International. Men accused of spying for Iran exchanged information about Iran International’s offices and presenter Kambiz Hosseini, while one defendant discussed money transfers and his legal troubles with contacts in Iran, a London court heard.

Iran turns on Pakistan as Saudi defense pact takes effect. Iran has sharpened its criticism of a Saudi Arabia-Pakistan-Turkey defense pact after it became operational, warning against intervention in Yemen and questioning Pakistan’s role as a mediator between Tehran and Washington.

Teenage boy dies in custody after beating by Iran's Basij forces, source says. A 17-year-old boy died in custody in Iran’s Isfahan province after the IRGC’s paramilitary Basij forces beat him during his arrest and a judge refused his father’s plea for hospital treatment, a source familiar with the case told Iran International.

J’Accuse! Tehran defends French students, silences Iranian youth. Tehran has seized on protests by French high school students to accuse Paris of repression, seeking to obscure its own treatment of young Iranians by turning the language of human rights against one of its Western critics.

Iran executed over 2,000 people in past year, rights group says. Iran executed at least 2,003 people over the past year, a 29% increase from the previous period, rights group HRANA reported Friday, as UN experts warned that Tehran uses capital punishment to silence dissent and instill fear.

'Three golden weeks': Trump’s no-strike pledge fuels calls in Iran to act first. President Donald Trump’s pledge not to attack Iran before the November 3 US midterm elections has been greeted in Tehran as either a bluff or an opportunity, with some hardliners urging Iran to exploit the three-week window to strike first.

Iran-linked actors used US AI for fake journalism, military targeting. Iran-based and Iranian-linked actors have used two leading US artificial intelligence platforms to place articles under fake journalist identities and help develop targeting recommendations against US naval forces, according to separate investigations by OpenAI and Anthropic.

'Absolute isolation': US outlines plan to cut off Iran’s economic lifelines. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent this week outlined an expanding campaign of what he called “absolute isolation” against Iran, targeting its oil revenue, overseas financial access and transport routes as Washington seeks to strangle Tehran’s economy.

Iran turns to Turkey, Turkmenistan for power as war strains industry. Iran is seeking more electricity from Turkey and Turkmenistan as war damage and other outages leave thousands of megawatts of industrial and petrochemical power capacity offline, even as Washington presses neighboring countries to help restrict Tehran’s remaining economic routes.

Iran detains football coach over child sexual abuse allegations. Iranian judicial authorities have detained a football coach in the western city of Divandarreh after five people filed complaints alleging sexual abuse connected to a youth football club.

Jailed wife of executed Iran protester pressured to deny marriage. The jailed wife of an Iranian protester executed this week is being interrogated and pressured to deny that the couple married shortly before his execution, a source familiar with the case told Iran International.

Iran’s oil lifeline could run dry by mid-December, Kpler says. For the first time in Iran’s history, revenue from crude oil and condensate exports could dry up entirely by mid-December if the US blockade remains in place, according to the head of crude oil analysis at Kpler.

Iran may be restoring activity at nuclear-linked site struck by Israel. New construction and repairs at an Iranian compound previously targeted by Israel suggest Tehran may be moving beyond clearing war damage toward restoring operations at a site linked to nuclear weapons research, according to a Washington-based research institute.

War puts Iran’s nuclear ambiguity under scrutiny. A revisionist argument is emerging in Tehran over Iran’s nuclear strategy: that its longstanding policy of nuclear ambiguity failed its most important test when it did not deter the United States and Israel from attacking, and should now be reconsidered.

Zarif accused of aiding US, ‘suicidal attack’ on Iran’s security. Iran's hardline Kayhan newspaper accused former foreign minister Mohammad Javad Zarif of undermining national security and helping Washington by depicting the Revolutionary Guards as a threat.

Russia fears a pro-Western Iran more than an Iranian atomic bomb. Moscow would rather live with an Iranian nuclear weapon than with a change of regime in Tehran, senior Russia scholar Mark Katz told Iran International, arguing that a pro-Western Iran is the outcome Russia actually fears.

Freight costs from Turkey to Iran surge fivefold in two months. The cost of transporting goods from Turkish ports to Iran has surged over fivefold in less than two months to about $8,000, Iranian media reported, as Washington pressures Turkey to help cut off Iran's overland trade routes to further isolate Tehran economically.

US weighs strikes on Houthis and Iran after deadly Saudi airport attack. A deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh’s main airport drew a Saudi vow of retaliation on Saturday, as President Donald Trump raised the possibility of joining strikes on the group and resuming attacks on Iran.

US pressure threatens Iran’s political survival but may not bring concessions. The US blockade and tighter sanctions enforcement are cutting into Iran’s oil income and targeting financial networks that sustain the Islamic Republic, but may still fall short of forcing Tehran into concessions, experts said at an Iran International town hall in Washington.

World leaders condemn Houthi attack on Riyadh airport. An attack by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport drew condemnation from European leaders, the United Nations and regional governments on Sunday.

Machete-wielding men at IRGC-backed rally revive scrutiny of crackdowns. Footage and images showing men wielding machetes and swords at an IRGC-backed rally in the central Iranian city of Isfahan have renewed scrutiny of the Islamic Republic's history of using unofficial armed groups to suppress anti-government protests.

Iran-US diplomacy stalls as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia intensify. Efforts to end the war with Iran and restore normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remained deadlocked Sunday, as military pressure continued at sea and the Iran-backed Houthis carried out increasingly deadly attacks inside Saudi Arabia.

Can US sanctions derail Iran’s China trade route?. Washington’s new sanctions are unlikely to stop a China–Iran freight train at the border, but may make the route Tehran has turned to under pressure from the US naval blockade costlier and less reliable.

Iran warns of wider risks as regional attacks intensify. Two commercial vessels were attacked near Oman on Sunday, two Indian sailors were left missing, and a drone struck an Iranian Kurdish opposition camp in Iraq on Monday, as Iranian officials warned that a renewed war could put regional infrastructure at risk.

Tehran seizes on Rubio’s Xerxes remarks to champion a past it once disparaged. Marco Rubio’s invocation of ancient Persia in a speech championing Western power has given Tehran an opportunity to present itself as a defender of Iranian identity, even as critics recall the Islamic Republic’s own record of disparaging pride in the country’s pre-Islamic rulers.

Pétrole : les dessous de l’incursion manquée de Simon Tiemtoré dans l’aval africain. Le banquier américano-burkinabé s’était positionné, via Lilium Capital Group, pour l’acquisition d’un réseau de quelque 400 stations-service. Mais les discussions n’ont finalement pas abouti. Coulisses.

Prix Nobel de la paix : Navi Pillay, la juriste sud-africaine qui a dénoncé le génocide à Gaza. La juge de 85 ans a consacré sa carrière à qualifier juridiquement les crimes contre l’humanité et les génocides comme à Gaza, au Myanmar ou au Rwanda. Elle rejoint la prestigieuse liste de nobélisés sud-africains.

James Mwangi (Equity) : « L’Afrique doit ajouter de la valeur à ce qu’elle produit ». Expansion régionale, IA et projet de raffinerie à Lamu : le patron du groupe kényan Equity, leader en Afrique de l’Est, met en avant sa stratégie pour assurer l’essor et la diversification de ses activités. Tout en insistant sur la nécessité pour le continent de mieux maîtriser ses chaînes de valeur.

Détention d’Alain-Claude Bilie-By-Nze au Gabon : les coulisses d’un dossier sensible. L’ancien Premier ministre et opposant au président Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema est toujours incarcéré à la prison centrale de Libreville dans l’attente de son procès. Ses conseils fustigent une procédure judiciaire gelée et dénoncent une arrestation politique, ce que réfutent les autorités.

Maroc : avant le discours du roi, où en sont les négociations pour former une coalition ?. Les tractations conduites par Fatima-Ezzahra El Mansouri dessinent les contours possibles d’une majorité articulée autour du PAM et des trois partis historiques de la Koutla. Mais les consultations se poursuivent et d’autres options restent ouvertes.

Pénuries d’essence au Niger : le patron de la compagnie pétrolière nationale paye le prix de la crise. Le chef de la junte au Niger a démis de ses fonctions le patron de Sonidep. Ce limogeage sans explication intervient alors que le pays fait face à de vives tensions sur le carburant.

Les relations Algérie-Espagne à l’épreuve de l’affaire Ayoub Aissiou. Malgré le soutien de Madrid à la demande algérienne, la justice espagnole a refusé l’extradition de l’homme d’affaires, enrichi sous la présidence Bouteflika. Une décision qui pourrait peser sur les relations entre les deux pays.

FMI-Cemac : le Tchad, victime collatérale de la lenteur des réformes communautaires ?. Un an après la signature de son accord avec le FMI, N’Djamena n’a perçu aucun décaissement. L’institution financière conditionne ses versements à des engagements accrus de la part des membres de l’organisation régionale. Coulisses.

En Mauritanie, le gouvernement démissionne après la présentation d’un rapport d’enquête sur des incendies. En août dernier, deux incendies ont touché des infrastructures de la Somelec, privant Nouakchott de courant. Un rapport sévère a coûté sa survie au gouvernement de Mokhtar Ould Djiay.

Pétrole : comment Aliko Dangote est-il devenu le roi du raffinage africain ?. Alors que la crise géopolitique suit son cours au Moyen-Orient, la raffinerie du groupe Dangote à Lekki s’est hissée au rang de fournisseur majeur de carburants pour les marchés internationaux. Une réussite qui peut en appeler une autre, mais dans quelles conditions ?

Sénégal : Ousmane Sonko peut-il (vraiment) utiliser sa majorité à l’Assemblée contre Bassirou Diomaye Faye ?. Les lois votées par le groupe Pastef sont systématiquement bloquées par l’exécutif. Mais les députés de la majorité ont d’autres moyens d’utiliser leur tribune politique.

En Côte d’Ivoire, une affaire d’escroquerie impliquant des influenceurs révèle les failles du foncier. Une soixantaine de plaintes, plus de 320 millions de F CFA de préjudice provisoire et plusieurs célébrités citées : la vaste enquête visant la promotrice Rita Djédjé éclaire les risques qui continuent de peser sur les acquisitions immobilières. Décryptage.

RDC : Kabila règle ses comptes avec Tshisekedi et entretient le mystère sur ses intentions. L’ex-président congolais s’est une nouvelle fois exprimé, le 9 octobre, pour attaquer le bilan de son successeur tout en promettant, « dans les heures, les jours et les semaines à venir », d’annoncer des actions concrètes pour « sauver » le pays.

L’accès à la mer Rouge est-il le véritable enjeu de la guerre entre l’Éthiopie et l’Érythrée ?. Quatre ans après avoir combattu côte à côte lors de la guerre du Tigré, les armées d’Abiy Ahmed et d’Issayas Afewerki s’affrontent dans le nord de l’Éthiopie. Jusqu’où cette escalade pourrait-elle aller ? Décryptage.

Denise Dusauchoy au secret à Kinshasa, le Maroc face à la rupture Algérie-Émirats arabes unis, le calendrier serré de la dette du Sénégal… Les 5 infos qu’il ne fallait pas manquer. Cette semaine, le Brief de Jeune Afrique revient sur la chute de l’influenceuse congolaise Denise Dusauchoy, décrypte les ambitions sahéliennes de Saddam Haftar, s’intéresse aux avocats qui s’imposent dans les batailles politiques ivoiriennes, analyse les conséquences de la rupture entre l’Algérie et les Émirats arabes unis pour le Maroc et évalue la crédibilité du calendrier de restructuration de la dette sénégalaise.

Tramadol en Afrique : le filon des trafiquants, l’antidouleur des pauvres. 97 % des saisies mondiales de tramadol ont lieu en Afrique de l’Ouest et en Afrique centrale. Ce trafic prospère sur un terreau : une région où l’on manque de presque tout pour soulager la douleur. Décryptage en infographies.

Maroc : ces femmes qui font l’économie. Au Maroc, les femmes occupent désormais 29 % des sièges dans les conseils d’administration des sociétés cotées. Finance, banque, industrie pharmaceutique… Elles s’imposent au sommet des plus grands groupes marocains. Portraits de six dirigeantes qui façonnent l’économie du royaume.

Le 11 octobre 1996, la Mauritanie organise ses premières élections pluralistes. Si les habitants de la « Mauritanie française » ont obtenu le droit d’élire des députés en 1946, il a fallu attendre 1996 pour que le pays organise ses premières législatives pluralistes. Un essai non transformé, mais une date importante dans l’histoire mauritanienne.

Mali : qui sont les hommes de l’ombre d’Ismaël Wagué, le général chargé de la réconciliation ?. Pour tenter de renouer les fils du dialogue dans un pays en guerre, le ministre d’État, ancien porte-voix des putschistes qui ont renversé Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta (IBK) en 2020, s’appuie sur un réseau qui va des officiers aux chefs communautaires, en passant par les religieux et les influenceurs.

Face au chômage, l’exode des jeunes Ghanéens vers le Golfe s’accélère. De plus en plus de jeunes Ghanéens jettent leur dévolu sur l’Arabie saoudite, les Émirats arabes unis ou le Qatar. Des destinations plus accessibles que l’Europe mais souvent gérées par des trafiquants et des agences de recrutement douteuses.

Cameroun anglophone : dix ans après, la guerre refuse de s’éteindre. Privés d’une partie de leurs appuis dans la diaspora, les séparatistes anglophones n’en poursuivent pas moins leurs attaques sanglantes, une décennie après le début de la crise dans les régions du Nord-Ouest et du Sud-Ouest (Noso). Face à eux, Paul Biya, réélu il y a un an pour un huitième mandat, fait le pari de l’usure.

À Madagascar, un an après la chute d’Andry Rajoelina, la tentation présidentielle du colonel Michaël. Alors que la GEN Z, fragilisée par ses divisions internes, est marginalisée, le colonel Michaël Randrianirina doit organiser les scrutins qui mettront un terme, dans un an, à la transition qu’il préside. Et auxquels il pourrait bien participer.

Felipe VI à Ceuta et Melilla : la visite royale va-t-elle envenimer les relations Maroc-Espagne ?. Dix-neuf ans après la visite de Juan Carlos Ier, qui avait provoqué une crise diplomatique avec Rabat, c’est son successeur, le roi Felipe VI, qui se rendra les 13 et 14 octobre à Ceuta et Melilla, sur fond de crise migratoire et de tensions électorales en Espagne.

Sénégal, Gabon, croissance : les dossiers africains des assemblées du FMI et de la Banque mondiale. L’économie continentale résiste aux répercussions de la crise au Moyen-Orient. Un tournant stratégique se profile pour plusieurs pays africains dans leurs tractations financières avec le FMI.

Au moins 139 morts au large de Djibouti, l’UA appelle à « lutter contre le trafic de migrants ». L’embarcation surchargée a chaviré presque dès son départ, à quelques dizaines de mètres de la côte djiboutienne. Elle transportait 305 personnes, dont 80 ont pu être sauvées.

Gabon : Ali Bongo Ondimba à l’offensive pour récupérer ses comptes bancaires. Depuis le coup d’État qui l’a chassé du pouvoir en août 2023, l’ancien président gabonais, installé depuis plusieurs mois à Paris, n’a plus jamais eu accès à ses comptes locaux. Tandis que la banque BGFI lui oppose l’ordonnance d’un juge, lui y voit un règlement de comptes politique.

Un continent, deux modèles : comment Afreximbank défie Standard Bank sur le financement des grands projets. La banque multilatérale dispute au géant sud-africain la position de numéro un sur le terrain des mégaprojets. Un duel au sommet qui révèle surtout les failles du modèle bancaire commercial face aux besoins de l’Afrique.

La Sierra Leone sous l’emprise de la cocaïne, et de Jos Leijdekkers. La Sierra Leone serait devenue un quasi narco-État, sous l’emprise de Jos Leijdekkers, un trafiquant néerlandais qui fait désormais partie de la famille du président Julius Maada Bio.

Tchad-France : Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno attendu à l’Élysée par Emmanuel Macron. Le président tchadien atterrit à Paris en provenance de N’Djamena ce 12 octobre. Il doit rencontrer son homologue français, Emmanuel Macron, dès le lendemain. C’est déjà la troisième rencontre entre les deux hommes depuis le mois de janvier.

Côte d’Ivoire, Sénégal : le canadien Fortuna Mining peut-il réussir son pari africain ?. Après Séguéla en Côte d’Ivoire, Fortuna prépare le développement de Diamba Sud au Sénégal. Une nouvelle étape stratégique pour le groupe minier, qui cherche à étoffer ses actifs pour soutenir sa montée en puissance.

En Afrique du Sud, de nouvelles violences éclatent entre groupes antimigrants et ressortissants étrangers. Une circulaire ayant provoqué un afflux de demandeurs d’asile devant les bureaux de l’immigration aurait ravivé les tensions, trois mois après l’ultimatum lancé par des groupuscules xénophobes exigeant le départ des migrants en situation irrégulière.

Dans « Comme des hommes ? », Juliette Bour retrace l’itinéraire de 15 dirigeantes rwandaises activement impliquées dans le génocide. L’historienne détaille le parcours et les crimes de ces femmes, intégrées à des échelons plus ou moins élevés de l’administration rwandaise en 1994.

Le prix Nobel de la paix décerné à l’avocate sud-africaine Navanethem Pillay, à l’heure où la justice est « attaquée ». Agée de 85 ans, Navi Pillay a notamment été juge et haut-commissaire des Nations unies aux droits de l’homme et présidente du Tribunal pénal international pour le Rwanda.

Au Sénégal, Dakar, sous les eaux, se découvre très vulnérable en pleine saison des pluies hors norme. La capitale, touchée par un épisode climatique d’une intensité exceptionnelle, paie le prix de son urbanisation accélérée.

Où sont passés les milliards d’euros promis pour lutter contre le virus Ebola en RDC ?. La lutte contre l’épidémie de maladie à virus Ebola, officiellement déclarée à la mi-mai en République démocratique du Congo, attire les promesses de dons. Gaza: One year after ceasefire, killing and displacement of Palestinians persist Read More » “About four months after we returned to our home, her health began to deteriorate rapidly, and we had no idea what was wrong with her,” her husband, Sami al-Mabhouh, 62, told Middle East Eye. With none of Gaza’s 36 hospitals operating at full capacity and only around 20 functioning partially, tens of thousands of patients cannot access the examinations and treatment they urgently need. 'She survived the bombing, but not the blockade' - Sami al-Mabhouh, Palestinian husbend Dialysis unit availability deteriorated further over the same period, falling from 17 percent to 12 percent. “As we waited for her turn to travel, we contacted doctors in Italy and Egypt and shared her medical records with them. They included 505 cancer patients and 264 children, as evacuations remained far below pre-war levels. Between 10 October 2025 and mid-September 2026, around 3,423 patients were evacuated abroad for treatment, an average of around 10 patients a day, according to Physicians for Human Rights Israel. From uneasy partners to open distrust: Aoun and Hezbollah struggle to rebuild ties Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 10/12/2026 - 09:21 Restoring relations between Lebanon's president and Hezbollah will require much more than reopening channels of communication Lebanese President Joseph Aoun at the Presidential Palace in Baabda, Lebanon, 15 September 2026 (Joseph Eid/AFP) Off The relationship between Lebanese President Joseph Aoun and Hezbollah has deteriorated into a dispute over weapons, sovereignty and the future of Lebanon ’s security, with sources on both sides acknowledging that communication continues but trust has largely collapsed. When Aoun was elected president in January 2025, Hezbollah supported his election, helping end a prolonged presidential vacancy. But the political understanding that facilitated his election did not resolve the fundamental disagreement over Hezbollah’s independent military structure and the state’s authority to decide matters of war and peace. From the beginning of his presidency, Aoun made clear that he wanted weapons brought under state control. In his inaugural address, he pledged to affirm the state’s right to monopolise arms, linking the principle to strengthening the Lebanese Armed Forces, protecting the country’s borders and implementing international resolutions. His position became more explicit in a speech marking Army Day in July 2025, when he called for the army and security forces to have the exclusive right to bear arms, urging Hezbollah and its supporters to “place your bet solely on the Lebanese state”. The disagreement deepened in January 2026, when Aoun said the circumstances that had once justified weapons outside state control no longer existed, and that their continued presence had become a burden on Hezbollah’s own community and Lebanon as a whole. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Hezbollah criticised the remarks, expressing “disappointment” with Aoun’s position. Party spokesperson Youssef al-Zein argued that Hezbollah was exercising restraint in the face of Israeli attacks and that further disarmament should not be discussed before Israel withdrew from positions it continued to occupy in southern Lebanon. The dispute extended beyond disarmament. In late January, Hezbollah's leader Naim Qassem said the party was “not neutral” in a potential conflict involving the United States and Iran . The presidency reiterated that decisions on war and peace belonged to the Lebanese state, underscoring the tension between Hezbollah’s regional commitments and Aoun’s insistence that such decisions be made by state institutions. The decisive rupture came on 2 March, when Hezbollah launched rockets at Israel following the US-Israeli assassination of Iran's Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei . The government responded by banning Hezbollah’s military and security activities, calling on the group to surrender its weapons and directing the army to advance its plan to bring all weapons under state control north of the Litani River. Aoun condemned the rocket launch, further straining relations with the party that had supported his election. 'Aoun 1, Aoun 2' A source close to Hezbollah said trust in the presidency had been exhausted, citing what the source described as Aoun’s failure to honour previous understandings and his support for the government’s response. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); “The first step is to reverse the decision,” the source said, arguing that normal engagement was impossible while Hezbollah’s military and security activities remained banned. The source also accused Aoun of placing excessive faith in Washington, saying he appeared to believe that meeting US President Donald Trump had made the United States his ally. The source offered a pointed assessment of the president’s transformation: “You could say there is Joseph Aoun 1, the army commander, and a different Joseph Aoun 2, the president. The first is not like the second.” South Lebanon: 'It's torture, they are razing our lives before our eyes' Read More » The presidency disputes Hezbollah’s account of the relationship. A source close to Baabda said ties had not been severed, but remained below the level required given the sensitivity of the current period. Communication continued through an established channel, the source said, but there had been no return to high-level engagement. “Nothing” prevents direct communication from the presidency’s side, the source said, adding that Hezbollah’s demands were unrealistic under the current circumstances. The source also said that attempts to communicate with Hezbollah had been made on several occasions, but questioned who was making decisions within the organisation. “To be frank, we do not know who is leading the party today, or whether they themselves even know who actually makes the decisions within Hezbollah,” the source said. The competing accounts reveal a relationship in which both sides believe the other must make the first move. Hezbollah wants the government to reverse its March decision before trust can be restored, while the presidency maintains that state authority over weapons and decisions of war and peace cannot be negotiable. The deeper question is whether the two sides can agree on a security arrangement that places decisions firmly in the hands of the Lebanese state while addressing Hezbollah’s argument that its weapons remain necessary in the face of Israeli occupation and attacks. For now, neither side describes relations as formally severed. But the gap between their positions, and the distrust expressed by sources close to both, suggests that restoring ties will require more than reopening a channel of communication. It will require agreement on the limits of Hezbollah’s military role and the authority of the Lebanese state. Israeli elections: Grotesque court spectacle sets a chilling precedent Submitted by Orly Noy on Thu, 10/08/2026 - 20:05 Ruling to uphold the disqualification of Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh shows the true face of our 'democracy' Sami Abu Shehadeh, pictured at centre, and other Arab politicians attend a hearing at the Supreme Court in Jerusalem, on 1 October 2026 (Ilia Yefimovich/AFP) Off If Israel still had any masks left to conceal the depths of its anti-democratic descent, they were shattered in the Supreme Court last week, when an expanded panel of nine justices heard petitions seeking to disqualify all Arab lists from running for the Knesset, as well as two individual candidates : Hadash MK Ofer Cassif and Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh. It is a ritual repeated in every Israeli election: the Central Elections Committee, a political body dominated by the governing coalition, broadly disqualifies Arab parties and individual candidates. The Supreme Court then overturns those decisions in order to preserve Israel’s image as a democratic state. This time, in a profoundly dangerous precedent, the court did not overturn the committee’s decision regarding Abu Shehadeh , and upheld his disqualification from running for parliament. This was not the only red line crossed. Under Israeli law, an individual or a list can be disqualified from running for the Knesset on several grounds , including rejecting Israel’s character as a Jewish and democratic state, and supporting armed struggle against the state. Because the first could theoretically be used not only to disqualify Arab parties, but also non-Zionist ultra-Orthodox parties, the court has over the years found ways around this obstacle. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); As for supporting armed struggle, right-wing parties have long invested enormous resources in trying to pin this accusation on Arab parties and representatives. Every statement made by a Palestinian candidate over the years, every article they have written, every social-media post or event they have attended - all are examined under a magnifying glass, in hopes of somehow proving such support. This time, the “trophy” they found was an article by Abu Shehadeh published in Arabic on 8 October 2023, the day after the Hamas attack, offering an initial analysis of the event and the reality that had emerged. Broad support The petition to disqualify Abu Shehadeh on the basis of that article was filed by National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, the ideological descendant of Meir Kahane , whose own movement was declared a terrorist organisation and outlawed in 1994 after the Ibrahimi Mosque massacre, carried out by Kahanist Baruch Goldstein . The fact that the disqualification petition was filed by Ben Gvir - a man convicted of supporting a terrorist organisation, who had a framed photograph of the mass murderer Goldstein in his living room , and who celebrated his most recent birthday with a cake bearing a festive image of a noose , which has become his trademark - should alone have been enough for any decent party to reject it. Yet this is where the first dangerous precedent emerged. Not only was the disqualification petition supported by the Jewish right and centrist opposition parties; it was also backed by the Democrats, led by Yair Golan - the party supposedly representing the Zionist left, which speaks frequently of “ Jewish-Arab partnership ”. Like everything else in the only democracy in the universe, even the right to be morally outraged is a privilege reserved exclusively for Jews That partnership, it turns out, can easily be tossed into the garbage the moment the Zionist left seeks to prove its loyalty to the other Zionist parties with which it hopes to form the next government. For that purpose, they will not hesitate to throw under the bus a Palestinian leader engaged in a political struggle for justice and equality. The second precedent set in this case is far more serious and dangerous. For the first time, the Supreme Court did not overturn an entirely political decision by the Central Elections Committee, and instead upheld Abu Shehadeh’s disqualification from running for the Knesset. This was despite the objections of a long list of prominent legal scholars, including former Deputy Attorney General Dina Zilber, law professor Barak Medina, academic David Harel, and even attorney Moshe Cohen-Eliya, a law professor associated with the far right, whose own analysis concluded that there was no legal basis for the disqualification. But these proceedings had very little, if anything, to do with law. More than anything, the case resembled a Shin Bet interrogation. I sat in the courtroom, stunned, and watched this disgraceful hearing for more than three hours. The Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party was represented by Ben Gvir himself, and by attorney Ze’ev Wolf , previously convicted of murdering a Palestinian man in Jerusalem’s Old City in November 1992, two years after Rabbi Meir Kahane’s assassination. He was later pardoned. This is the Jewish and democratic state: two men convicted of terrorism-related offences seeking to silence a Palestinian leader who has devoted his life to a political struggle for equality and justice. They are backed by the entire Zionist spectrum, from right to left, as well as by the Supreme Court itself. Moral outrage In a country whose political and military leaders have called for the indiscriminate annihilation of a civilian population and the starvation of more than two million people in Gaza; a country facing proceedings over the commission of genocide , and whose prime minister is the subject of an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court; in this country, a Palestinian public leader is given a show trial over an article he wrote. This is Israeli democracy in all its glory. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); There is not enough space here to recount all the miserable absurdities that unfolded during the hearing. But one thing in particular caught my attention: the emotionally charged vocabulary used by the justices and the lawyers on the right. One expression, above all, kept recurring: “disgust”. Netanyahu won't stop until all Arab political parties are gone Read More » They felt disgust at the fairly elementary analysis in Abu Shehadeh’s article, in which he wrote that a pressure cooker eventually explodes, and that the struggle must be redirected towards political channels. They felt disgust at Cassif’s uncompromising solidarity with the oppressed. They felt disgust at Balad’s insistence on genuine equality and substantive democracy for everyone. Even I, a candidate ranked 15th on the Joint List for the Knesset, representing Balad, apparently managed to arouse a measure of their disgust because of an article in which I wrote about the obligation to distinguish between combatants and a civilian population. The genocide in Gaza , with its tens of thousands of victims and two million people starved and dehydrated, many of whom have been orphaned, maimed and displaced, needless to say, did not arouse their disgust. The Palestinians sitting in the courtroom, stone-faced as they watched this grotesque spectacle unfold, expressed no disgust. Perhaps their souls, crushed day after day beneath the wheels of Jewish supremacy, are simply too exhausted to feel disgust anymore. Or perhaps they know all too well that, like everything else in the only democracy in the universe, even the right to be morally outraged is a privilege reserved exclusively for Jews. Another strike on the airport on Sunday killed one more person. The Saudi -led coalition blamed Yemen 's Houthis and called the attack a war crime. In a statement on Sunday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had targeted the airport "in three stages" since Friday evening, closing it completely, and warned that Saudi airports were "unsafe", except those serving Mecca and Medina. The attack capped a summer of escalation. A UN-backed truce that had largely frozen Yemen's war since 2022 broke down in July after Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa airport, and the Houthis then declared a maritime blockade on the kingdom. In September, the Sanaa-based group seized the Red Sea port of Mokha and pushed towards the Bab al-Mandab strait . (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Saudi-backed government forces launched a counter-offensive in early October, and the UN special envoy has warned that Yemen has returned to full-scale war . Heavy clashes are continuing around the strategically important city of Taiz, which sits above the Red Sea coast. The renewed fighting has displaced 130,000 people . Who are the Houthis? Officially known as Ansar Allah, or "helpers of God", the movement emerged in Yemen's far north in the 1990s around the cleric Hussein al-Houthi. It is rooted in Zaydism, a branch of Shia Islam whose followers are a minority in Yemen but concentrated in the northern highlands. The group fought six rounds of war with the government of former president Ali Abdullah Saleh between 2004 and 2010. Hussein al-Houthi was killed in the first and leadership passed to his brother, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, who still heads the movement. Houthi fighters captured Sanaa in September 2014, and in March 2015, Saudi Arabia led a military coalition into Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government , which has mostly governed from Riyadh and the southern Yemeni city of Aden. By the time of the 2022 truce, the Houthis held about 30 percent of Yemen's territory but around 80 percent of its population. What do they want? At home, the Houthis have sought greater autonomy for the north and, increasingly, recognition as Yemen's governing authority. What would Houthi control of Bab al-Mandeb mean for the region? Read More » They have demanded an end to what they describe as a Saudi land, air and naval siege of Yemen, a characterisation Riyadh rejects. In his statement on Sunday, Saree said the group would keep escalating attacks deep inside Saudi Arabia under what he called an equation of "siege for siege, escalation for escalation", until the "aggression" stopped and the siege on Yemen was lifted. Their ambitions, however, extend beyond Yemen. The movement's frames its politics in opposition to US and Israeli power in the region. Since 2023, the group has attacked more than 100 commercial ships in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, saying it was acting in solidarity with Palestinians during Israel's genocide in Gaza . The strikes were temporarily halted in May 2025 in a ceasefire deal with Washington, brokered by Oman. In March, it began firing missiles at Israel in support of Tehran after the US and Israel launched their war on Iran. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); How close are they to Iran? Iran counts Ansar Allah as part of its "Axis of Resistance" alongside Hezbollah and Hamas, and has courted the group since at least the late 2000s. Much of the Houthi arsenal has been designed or supplied by Tehran. The Houthis deny being an Iranian proxy. After the Riyadh strikes, Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said on Monday that Tehran was "deeply concerned" by the escalation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, and offered to help facilitate dialogue between the two sides. How strong are they militarily? The Houthi fighting force grew from an estimated 30,000 in 2015 to around 350,000 by 2024, although counts vary. The group has no conventional navy and little air power, but it fields drones, explosive-laden drone boats and medium-range ballistic missiles that have reached targets about 2,000km away in Israel. Why does the Bab al-Mandab matter? The strait links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is the southern approach to the Suez Canal. Its importance has grown since the war on Iran disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, driving up oil prices and leaving the Red Sea as a key alternative route for Saudi exports. Emergency, governor's rule imposed in KP as president approves cabinet decision. Key developments: Emergency imposed under Article 232 , governor’s rule under Article 234 Cabinet recommended move due to KP govt’s ‘ deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism’ Technocratic council formed ; Fakhr Alam appointed as KP chief secretary PTI’s Gohar condemns decision as undemocratic, says peace cannot be established by weakening provincial autonomy Governor Kundi calls for unity for ‘new chapter’ in KP’s development ISLAMABAD: The federal government on Sunday imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa following the president’s approval of the recommendations by the federal cabinet. The measures have been approved under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution, the President House said in a statement. The two provisions pertain to the proclamation of emergency and governor’s rule. Following the imposition, internet disruptions were being reported from parts of Peshawar, with Dawn unable to contact its correspondents there. According to sources in the telecom sector, mobile network and data services have been slowed or shut down in selected areas of some cities. However, there is no province-wide shutdown of mobile data or internet. Internet watchdog NetBlocks said network data showed a major disruption to internet connectivity in parts of KP as emergency was imposed. The federal government also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in KP. On the ground, shipping containers were placed around the city of Peshawar to block several roads, with heavy police deployment. The decision to impose the emergency provisions came during an emergency meeting of the federal cabinet chaired by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, where he was briefed on the security situation in KP. A statement issued by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said cabinet members reviewed the situation and took note of the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”. The members proposed, given the “gravity” of the situation, that the PM advise the president to exercise “his constitutional authority and impose an emergency in the province under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution”. The emergency imposition comes a day after PM Shehbaz met President Zardari and discussed the country’s overall security situation. That meeting came amid heightened tensions between the PML-N-led federal government and the KP government led by the PTI — which is in opposition in the Centre. They have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their Oct 3 talks . The PTI has said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre has denied . It also calls for reviewing the counterterrorism policy and opposes military operations. On the other hand, the Centre has been criticising the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objects to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban. It may be recalled that in July 2024, when Afridi’s predecessor Ali Amin Gandapur was the chief minister, the KP Assembly passed a resolution urging the federal government to consult with it and the provincial government before launching a new military operation. The resolution, passed by a majority vote, cautioned that proceeding without provincial consent could hinder the offensive’s success and result in adverse consequences, for which the federal government would be responsible. In December that year, the assembly voted unanimously against a potential military operation in parts of Khyber and Bannu districts. About a year later, after Afridi became the KP CM, the provincial assembly convened a grand jirga with Governor Faisal Karim Kundi and other parties in attendance. The moot unanimously demanded that the Centre prioritise negotiations with Afghanistan and consult the KP government over Afghan policy. Constitutional provisions Emergency Article 232 of the Constitution provides for the proclamation of emergency in a province. It says, “If the president is satisfied that a grave emergency exists in which the security of Pakistan, or any part thereof, is threatened by war or external aggression, or by internal disturbance beyond the power of a provincial government to control, he may issue a Proclamation of Emergency.” However, invoking this article “due to internal disturbances beyond the powers of a provincial government to control” requires a resolution from the provincial assembly of that province. In case the president “acts on his own” — which is not currently the case — the Proclamation of Emergency is to be placed before both houses of Parliament for approval by each house within 10 days. According to this provision, parliament “shall have power to make laws for a province, or any part thereof, with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Federal Legislative List” during the time of the proclamation of an emergency. Nothing in this Article shall restrict the power of a provincial assembly to make any law which the Constitution empowers it to make, but if any provision of a provincial law is repugnant to any provision of an Act by Parliament, the latter would prevail and the provincial law would be void as long as the parliamentary Act is in effect. Governor’s rule On the other hand, Article 234 deals with the imposition of the governor’s rule “in case of failure of constitutional machinery in a province”. For imposition of the governor’s rule, the president simply requires a request from the provincial governor, it says. “A proclamation issued under this Article shall be laid before a joint sitting and shall cease to be in force at the expiration of two months, unless before the expiration of that period it has been approved by resolution of the joint sitting and may by like resolution be extended for a further period not exceeding two months at a time,” the Constitution reads. However, it adds that no such proclamation shall in any case remain in force for more than six months. Article 233, which provides powers to the president to suspend certain fundamental rights during the emergency period, was not mentioned in the summary signed by President Zardari. Where is Sohail Afridi? A couple of hours after the imposition of emergency was announced, KP Information Minister Shafi Jan, who had been accompanying now dysfunctional KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on the PTI’s long march , claimed that the he had been taken into custody. Dawn contacted police for a confirmation soon after Jan’s claim, but there was no response. Meanwhile, MNA Shahid Khattak also claimed Afridi’s “arrest”, as well as MNA Junaid Akbar and others from there party. He also said he would be leading the march now. Later, the PTI issued a statement, condemning the “arrest” of Afridi and other and describing it as an act of “political victimisation and an attempt to weaken the province’s elected leadership and democratic institutions”. It quoted PTI spokesperson Sheikh Waqas Akram as saying that Afridi’s “arrest” could not be viewed in isolation from the federal government’s decision to impose emergency and governor’s rule. “The developments reflect a broader effort to bypass elected institutions and undermine the constitutional authority of the province. “The arrest of Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and Junaid Akbar has exposed the political nature of the federal government’s actions. These measures are not directed at addressing security challenges; they are intended to weaken PTI, undermine the elected government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and disregard the democratic will of its people,” he said. Akram demanded the “immediate and unconditional release” Afridi, Akbar and “all other political detainees arrested in connection with the ongoing action against PTI”. He also demanded that the federal government publicly disclose the “legal grounds, specific charges and procedural basis for the arrests of the chief minister and the PTI provincial president”. However, he sounded less certain while speaking on Geo News programme ‘ Naya Pakistan ’. He said they had received reports of Afridi and Akbar’s arrest, and adding that they were unable to confirm whether Jan and Khattak, too, had been taken into custody. “We are unable to contact some people […] Because the internet has been suspended in several areas, we are unable to contact. You do not know the havoc they have created in KP. People are escaping and going into hiding,” he said. In a clip shared on PTI’s official X account, Salman Akram Raja, the party’s secretary general, said, “We do not know where Sohail Afridi is, in what condition he has been kept. Junaid Akbar is also missing.” When Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry was asked about reports of Afridi’s arrest during ‘ Naya Pakistan ’, he said some individuals had been detained in view of the law and order situation but did not confirm whether they included Afridi. He said those who did not have a criminal record or were not wanted would be released. Council, chief secretary appointed Following the imposition of emergency, the federal government formed an 11-member technocratic KP Advisory Council to assist the governor with running the province. Later, Governor Kundi also chaired the first meeting of the council, vowing to restore peace in the province. Earlier in the day, the federal government appointed Dr Muhammad Fakhr Alam Irfan as the chief secretary of KP, according to an official notification, a copy of which is available with Dawn. The appointment will take effect immediately and remain in place until further orders, it said. Dr Irfan, a Grade 22 officer of the Pakistan Administrative Service (PAS), was previously serving as secretary of the Power Division in the federal Ministry of Energy. He hails from Mardan. In a separate notification, the federal government also placed Muhammad Yahya Akhunzada at the disposal of the KP government with “immediate effect and until further orders”. Akhunzada, a Grade 20 PAS officer, was serving as an additional secretary at PMO. He hails from Charsadda and has also served as additional political agent for North and South Waziristan, secretary of health, information and education in KP, and commissioner of Dera Ismail Khan. ‘Peace cannot be established by weakening provincial autonomy’ PTI Chairman Gohar Ali Khan strongly condemned the imposition of emergency in KP and “completely rejected” it. “This is an extremely alarming and grave political mistake and an undemocratic measure — the people will never accept such actions against their rights,” Gohar wrote in a post on X. He stated: “There is still time; this decision can be withdrawn in a few days. Let the federation set aside its ego, understand the ground realities, accept legitimate demands, respect the sentiments and emotions of the people, and save the country from further political and economic damage and from pushing back the democratic process. “Revisiting political decisions is not a sign of weakness but of wisdom in the national interest — otherwise, great damage will be done.” Stressing that the mandate of the people of KP was their constitutional and legal right, the PTI chairman said: “Peace cannot be established, nor stability brought, by ignoring this mandate, weakening provincial autonomy, and creating conflict between the federation and the province.” He asserted that there was “no disagreement on eliminating terrorism, but the fight against terrorism cannot be used as a justification to suppress the people’s voice, achieve political objectives, or limit the province’s constitutional authority”. “Terrorism can only be combated through national unity and a joint strategy,” Gohar maintained. “The federation cannot be strengthened by weakening the provinces. The solution to problems lies not in force, confrontation, and extraordinary measures, but in political wisdom, supremacy of the Constitution, and meaningful negotiations and practical steps.” The PTI chairman said his party will raise the matter on “every constitutional, legal, and democratic forum for the protection of the people’s mandate, provincial autonomy, and constitutional and democratic rights”. Later in the day, Gohar said PTI would challenge governor’s rule through the courts, assemblies and public forums. The PTI parliamentary committee held a meeting and categorically rejected the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule in KP. In a statement issued afterwards, it termed the development “a direct assault on the public mandate and an unacceptable move”. “In a three-hour-long meeting of the PTI parliamentary party, the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule in KP was strongly condemned and unanimously rejected. The meeting declared this step contrary to facts, unconstitutional, undemocratic, and a blatant insult to the public mandate of the province,” the statement said. “The parliamentary party made it clear that measures to render the elected provincial government ineffective and usurp its constitutional powers could pose grave threats to the federal system and democratic traditions. Such decisions will increase political instability and public unrest in the province, while already existing tensions between the federation and the province will further intensify,” it added. The statement added that the solution to political differences should be found through constitutional and democratic procedures and mutual consultation, rather than through force and coercion. It also raised serious questions regarding the conduct of the federal government. “The parliamentary party took the stance that if terrorism and the deteriorating law and order situation are the primary justification for the imposition of emergency, then why is the situation in Balochistan being ignored?” the statement asked. The meeting also made it clear that Afridi was the elected chief minister and a member of the provincial assembly. “Measures regarding his arrest, detention, or the usurping of his constitutional and democratic powers were strongly condemned. The meeting termed such actions an insult to the public mandate and a dangerous precedent for democratic traditions,” it said. The Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP), of which PTI is a part, termed the move a violation of the Constitution. In a statement, the opposition alliance particularly assailed President Zardari’s PPP, claiming that the “most undemocratic actions and the imposition of governor’s rule” had been the hallmark of the party in the country’s history. “On the one hand, despite the extremely dire administrative and law and order situation in Balochistan, no such step has been taken, while on the other hand, this province — whose assembly and government stand on the true and real mandate of the people — has been targeted,” it contended. TTAP said it would convene a meeting on the matter and announce a joint course of action. Governor Kundi urges unity for ‘new chapter’ Meanwhile, Governor Kundi said the decision was made for “establishing peace in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the prosperity of its people, and the development of the province”. “I am your governor, but beyond that, I want to play my role as a servant of this soil and a protector of your rights. Let us come together to bring peace to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and begin a new chapter of our province’s development,” he said in a statement. Kundi assured the public that it was his responsibility to raise their issues on the relevant forums. Recalling the sacrifices made in the fight against terrorism, he said, “Now the time has come that we do not let these sacrifices go to waste and together establish lasting peace in our province.” The PPP leader urged the public to set aside their political differences and unite for the province’s peace, the protection of its people, and the future of the coming generations. “We must not let our differences become an obstacle in the path of our province’s common interests.” Cannot allow PTI to destabilise the economy: PM tells cabinet Addressing the cabinet meeting, the premier said the PTI-led KP government cannot be allowed to derail the stabilising economy amid tensions between the two sides. “I will not allow them (PTI) to destabilise the economy,” he said during the meeting. On terrorism in KP and Balochistan, the premier said, “The way common citizens are being martyred, the way police officials and security officials, children and mothers [..] there can be nothing more heart-wrenching.” He recalled that Pakistan has repeatedly urged neighbouring Afghanistan to rein in the terrorist elements; however, “they still do not understand it”. PM Shehbaz also reiterated his condemnation of the recent deadly Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia, noting the long-standing fraternal ties between Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. “Our only goal is that peace should be restored in the region,” he said. “Pakistan expresses solidarity with Saudi Arabia and stands with it. We will not tolerate any aggression against Saudi Arabia,” he said, adding that it was a “red line” for Pakistan. During his address, PM Shehbaz also spoke of the recent staff-level agreement reached with the International Monetary Fund (IMF). “It is hoped that we will unlock the $1.2 billion tranche within this year,” he said, recalling a meeting with the IMF’s Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva at the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) last month. He commended the political and military leadership for “working together day and night” in bringing fiscal discipline to Pakistan. The premier recalled his visit to London last month, where he had met with senior executives from leading global financial institutions. He also spoke of Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts in the international community, taking note of the appreciation Pakistan has received for mediation in the Middle East conflict. “Pakistan continues to play its role with hard work and sincerity,” he said, particularly lauding the role of the Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir. Textile makers warn of steep decline in exports from Oct to Dec. • Pakistan Textile Exporters Associ­ation cites weak Western demand, higher freight, rising production costs • Exporters seek 6-8pc Duty Drawback of Local Taxes and Levies support, clearance of outstanding refunds • Industry says announced 4.5pc Export Finance Scheme rate yet to be implemented ISLAMABAD: Textile exporters have warned the government of a steep decline in goods exports during the second quarter (October-December) of the current fiscal year, citing weakening demand in Wes­tern markets, rising freight charges and escalating production costs. In a statement issued on Sunday, Pakistan Textile Exporters Associ­ation (PTEA) Patron-in-Chief Khur­ram Mukhtar said the country’s export sector was facing mounting pressure from multiple directions, threatening its competitiveness and share in international markets. He said inflation in Western markets had weakened dem­and from international buyers, while sea freight charges had increased by 1.5 to 2.5 times, squeezing exporters’ already thin profit margins. Rising input and logistics costs were further undermining the competitiveness of Pakistani products, he added. “The decline in export trade volume is unprecedented,” Mr Mukhtar said, warning that only financially strong exporters would survive the prevailing conditions. He cautioned that regaining lost market share would be extremely difficult. He said declining exports were affecting the entire textile value chain, including ginning, spinning, weaving, processing and knitting. The situation had been compounded by weak domestic demand amid high inflation, putting several segments of the industry under severe financial pressure. Mr Mukhtar urged the government to provide temporary support thro­ugh the Duty Drawback of Local Taxes and Levies (DLTL) scheme at a rate of 6pc to 8pc to help exporters ret­ain their international market share. He also demanded immediate clearance of outstanding refunds under various heads to ease the liquidity crisis across the textile supply chain and called for the removal of cross-subsidies embedded in industrial energy tariffs to reduce production costs. Highlighting anomalies in the Export Finance Scheme (EFS), he said the government had announced a fixed financing rate of 4.5pc in the FY27 Finance Bill, but the decision had yet to be implemented. According to him, banks were charging exporters a minimum of 5.5pc, while some were charging as much as 8.5pc, contrary to the announced rate. Mr Mukhtar claimed that around Rs200 billion in financing had been extended under the EFS to yarn exporters despite yarn being on the scheme’s negative list. He also questioned the provision of financing to sugar exporters, describing sugar as a highly regulated sector. In contrast, he said, eligible textile exporters whose export performance exceeded the State Bank of Pakistan’s mandatory requirement by a substantial margin were being denied financing allocations. He said some exporters were achieving five to six times the requi­red export performance against the mandatory threshold of two times, yet were unable to obtain financing. Such allocations, he argued, discouraged value addition and penalised exporters contributing significantly to the country’s foreign exchange earnings. Mr Mukhtar welcomed the incre­ase in EFS financing allocations for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) but questioned whether the additional funds could be effectively utilised. He said an additional Rs300bn allocation for SMEs would require export performance of Rs600bn, which, according to him, did not currently exist. He pointed out that the Rs100bn allocation for SMEs in the previous fiscal year had lapsed without being utilised. He urged the government to review the distribution of EFS financing according to the export contribution of each segment, arguing that the top 100 exporters accounted for up to 60pc of total export volume and should receive proportionate financing. To strengthen the textile supply chain, Mr Mukhtar proposed a targeted financing pac­kage of Rs140bn for modernisation and technological upgrading of four major segments. The proposed package incl­udes Rs20bn each for ginning and sizing, and Rs50bn each for weaving and processing. He said these sectors required specially designed short- and long-term financing facilities for balancing, modernisation and replacement of machinery, improving productivity and introducing automation and sustainable production practices. Mr Mukhtar said the federal government and the State Bank should jointly develop the proposed financing programme in consultation with industry representatives. He also called for a 10-year strategic plan for textile exp­orts, focusing on Pakistan’s exis­ting industrial expertise, exportable surplus and structural reforms needed to impr­ove international competitiveness. “Historically, we have been reactive. The current situation demands a proactive appro­ach,” he said, warning that timely intervention would cost considerably less than efforts to recover lost export markets. Rs268bn power tariff burden on consumers opposed. • FPCCI urges Nepra to reject inflated, disputed claims; flags previously disallowed, unverified adjustments • Demands detailed written responses, participation in public hearings • Discos claim Rs2.64tr in revenue requirements for CY2027 ISLAMABAD: The Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FPCCI) has opposed an additional Rs268 billion burden on consumers sought by former Wapda distribution companies (Discos) through prior-year adjustments in power tariffs. In a comprehensive representation, the country’s top business body, representing large and small businesses, including manufacturing industries, asked the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) to reject the “inflated claims” previously disallowed by the regulator or disputed by third parties. The representation follows tariff petitions filed by 10 Discos seeking adjustments to the indexation of multiyear tariffs (2025-30) for calendar year 2027 and other consumer-end tariff adjustments. Collectively, the Discos have claimed Rs2.64 trillion in revenue requirements for CY2027 on account of distribution and supply of power. The FPCCI said it had constituted a special Energy Advisory Committee (EAC) to review tariff filings, including claims related to working capital, power purchase prices, prior-year adjustments (PYAs) and returns on revenue base. The committee found that Discos were seeking to pass hundreds of billions of rupees in prior-year adjustments on to consumers. It said a substantial portion of these claims was retrospective, contested by third parties or previously disallowed by Nepra. Some claims were inconsistently calculated against the Discos’ own formulas or lacked sufficient disclosure for independent verification. The EAC reviewed all 10 Discos’ CY2027 indexation and PYA petitions, including financial statements and annexures, on behalf of FPCCI’s constituent chambers, trade and industry associations. According to the FPCCI, Islamabad Electric Supply Company’s (Iesco) PYA claims exceeded 212 per cent of its proposed annual margin, while Sukkur Electric’s claims amounted to 113pc of its distribution margin. Faisalabad Electric’s PYA claims amounted to 91pc of its distribution and supply margin, followed by Multan at 68pc and Quetta at 60pc. The corresponding shares for Lahore, Peshawar and Gujranwala electric companies stood at 41pc, 40pc and 32pc, respectively. Tribal Electric did not disclose the figures. “These are not routine formula-based true-ups and ought not to be approved as such,” the FPCCI said. The representation included itemised objections for each Disco and a cross-company comparison, identifying disputed amounts, grounds for objections and proposed disallowances based on petitions, financial statements and annexures published by Nepra. The FPCCI demanded that its objections be made part of each Disco’s tariff-setting process, including public hearings, and that the companies respond in writing to specific objections before the hearings. It also urged Nepra to reject undifferentiated lump-sum PYA claims, require component-wise substantiation and allow trade and business bodies to participate in hearings. Faisalabad Electric has sought Rs535bn in revenue requirements for 2027, including Rs57bn in PYAs. The FPCCI called for rejecting Rs26bn in claims involving 11-year post-retirement benefits and previously disallowed supplementary charges. Gujranwala Electric sought Rs70.4bn, including Rs17bn in PYAs linked to 19-year-old Azad Jammu and Kashmir sovereign receivables. Sukkur Electric claimed Rs68bn, including Rs36bn in PYAs. Lahore Electric sought the highest revenue requirement, Rs759bn, including approximately Rs33bn in PYAs. The FPCCI said Rs27bn in claims were liable to be rejected because they had not been verified. Iesco submitted the largest PYA claim of Rs158bn within its Rs525bn revenue requirement. The FPCCI said 70pc of Iesco’s PYA claims were either disputed or involved noncash items, had been filed as a lump sum and should be rejected. Peshawar Electric sought Rs233bn in revenue requirements, including Rs35bn in PYAs. Of these, Rs33bn related to seven-year-old input tax claims that the FPCCI described as inadmissible.
