Pakistani national killed, 11 wounded as Riyadh airport hit by Houthi strike. A fresh Houthi strike hit Riyadh’s international airport on Sunday, killing one person — a Pakistani resident — and wounding 11 others, a day after another deadly attack claimed by the Yemeni group forced authorities to suspend operations there. Saturday’s attack, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, was a sharp escalation in the Yemen war, where Riyadh has long militarily supported the internationally recognised government against the Houthis. The group on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the last 24 hours, including on the airport, and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom’s transit hubs, calling them “a theatre of operations for our forces”. Hours later, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group reported that a projectile struck King Khalid International Airport, sparking a fire. Air defences also intercepted a missile nearby, it added. The fresh attack on the airport killed one person — a Pakistani resident — and wounded 11 others, Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said on X. Authorities have extended the closure of the airport by 24 hours until 2100 GMT (2am PKT) on Monday, the tracking site Flightradar24 said on the same platform. AFP journalists and locals reported hearing multiple blasts in the Saudi capital on Sunday. “The birds went into a frenzy after the sound. The whole house shook,” said one resident of the Al-Aarid neighbourhood in the north of the city. The civil aviation authority also reported another attack on Dammam airport in the east — which the Houthis also said they had targeted — a day after the Saudi coalition reported a projectile landing nearby. Shortly afterwards, the coalition reported shooting down a drone, also in the east. It said early on Monday that it had also “intercepted and destroyed” a Houthi ballistic missile heading for the southern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, home to a major military base. ‘Full-fledged war crime’ The Houthis have stepped up their attacks on the Riyadh airport — where three people were also killed on Thursday — as well as on other key targets in the world’s top crude oil exporter. And although Saudi Arabia has poured billions into its military, Houthi attacks continue to slip through. “Saudi air defences have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it’s simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves against Houthi attacks,” said Thomas Juneau, security analyst at Ottawa University. The anti-Houthi coalition called Saturday’s attack a “full-fledged war crime” and vowed to “respond decisively”. Houthi media reported two Saudi strikes in Yemen’s Houthi-controlled Sanaa governorate on Sunday. Saturday’s attack drew condemnation from the United Nations and leaders around the world, including US President Donald Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose country does not have diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia, also denounced the “horrific terrorist attack”. Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed, the civil aviation authority said, with 309 wounded. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia also said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded the day before. A Riyadh-based Western diplomat told AFP the official number of injured may not give a full picture, as it did not appear to include those with minor wounds. Operations suspended Authorities suspended operations at the airport into Sunday, a senior aviation source said, with air traffic monitor Flightradar24 saying the closure was extended until 21:00 GMT (2am PKT on Monday). A second aviation source confirmed the halt in operations “until further notice”, adding radar and communications equipment was damaged and runways needed to be assessed. Witnesses to Saturday’s strike described chaos in the aftermath. “People who were in Terminal 3 started running towards us,” a 32-year-old Riyadh resident told AFP . “Some had lost a hand or an arm. People were running while carrying injured people, covered in blood.” The attack prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors, a medical source said. The US, Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia have warned their citizens to avoid Riyadh airport, while Australia urged its citizens on Sunday to stay indoors altogether and “shelter in place”. The Houthis also claimed to have targeted the Dammam airport, whose official website on Sunday showed many flights — both departures and arrivals — were delayed. ‘Rewrite the rules’ Saturday’s airport strike, on the eve of Saudi Arabia’s high-profile convention and entertainment season, was the deadliest attack in the kingdom since a 2015 suicide bombing. With the summer heat subsiding, October also usually marks the beginning of the high season for Umrah pilgrims, with millions of Muslims from across the world flocking to Makkah. Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen’s government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa. Ottawa University’s Juneau said the Houthis now “want to rewrite the rules of the game”. “They want to do to Saudi Arabia what Saudi Arabia does to them,” he said. “So if their airport in Sanaa has to be closed because of the Saudi air embargo, they want to do the same thing to Saudi Arabia.” On the ground in Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing in their counter-offensive against the Houthis around the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key shipping route, military sources said on Saturday. The Houthis claimed to have repelled them. Claims by both sides have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

Citizens protest against what is being built ‘in secret’ at Karachi's Nehr-i-Khayam. KARACHI: Environmentalists and residents from across the city, including Clifton Block 5 Residents Association, Clifton Defence Com­munity (CDC) and Karachi Resi­dents’ Community (District South), gathered at the construction site of Nehr-i-Khayam on Sunday to protest the building of a commercial belt there. Standing firm against the backdrop of a big yellow digger machine hard at work and a reversing concrete mixer truck, the protesters held up placards with messages such as ‘Violation of Supreme Court orders’, ‘No food street on Nehr-i-Khayam’, ‘What are you building? Share the plan publicly’, ‘Don’t suffocate our waterways’, ‘Narrow drain equals massive flood’, ‘Boat Basin Se Gutter Basin’, etc. Founder and CEO of the Clifton Urban Forest, environmentalist Masood Lohar lamented people who call themselves architects, engineers and town planners but don’t really know what they are doing. “Nehr-i-Khayam is a natural link between the Obhayo Lagoon and the Gizri Creek. You can’t mess up with the marine ecosystem. If you do, you brace yourselves for floods, storms and tsunamis,” he pointed out. Quoting the late Dawn columnist and social activist Ardeshir Cowasjee from his column published on Sept 10, 2006, one of the protesters and members of the Karachi Residents’ Community (District South), Rasha Tarek, said that he had called Nehr-i-Khayam “one of the major lungs of the Clifton area”, intended “to carry rain and/or tidal water and not sewage into the open sea”. Environmentalists, activists gather at construction site; say protecting city’s drainage infrastructure, channels, open banks is everyone’s concern Reminding the gathering that Nehr-i-Khayam is an integral part of Boat Basin and Karachi’s drainage infrastructure and that its channel, open banks and surrounding landscape are shared public assets whose protection concerns the entire city, she demanded an immediate stop to the ongoing construction, which would narrow and alter the channel and its banks. Rumana Khan, another protester, said that the people of this country are bearing the brunt of wrong decisions made by the government in the past too. “For instance, building dams in all the wrong places while restricting the natural flow of rivers. Then you get flash floods that destroy villages and settlements,” she said. Hummaa Ahmad, who lives in the vicinity, wondered how come a seemingly big commercial project such as this has no public project information board installed anywhere. “We want to know exactly what is being constructed here. We want full disclosure of the approved designs, land boundaries, environmental assessments, Sepa decisions, contracts and expenditure regarding the project,” she demanded. “It is illegal commercialisation,” said another protester Sheeraz Qureshi, whose family has resided in Clifton Block 5 for the last 40 years. “You cannot build a dense commercial area in the middle of a dense residential area. That way you disturb all the residents,” he said. Echoing him, Dr Nadia Kiran, a resident of one of the apartments overlooking Nehr-i-Khayam, said, “We have heard that they are going to narrow the drain and build a food street over it. “The resulting traffic, rush and noise every day and night will dest­roy our peace of mind,” she added. “As it is, the authorities look the other way while allowing untreated waste to flow to the sea through drains such as Nehr-i-Khayam while overlooking the negative impacts of it on marine life,” said Humaira Khan of the Clifton Defence Commu­nity and Clifton Block 5 Residents Association. “Whatever way you see it, it is encroachment, plain and simple! Build­ing commercial belts is not the job of the Sindh government, which should be more concerned about saving the environment than contributing towards destroying it,” she said. CDC President Abdur Rehman pointed out that there have been previous attempts to encroach on Nehr-i-Khayam, too. “Basically, it seems that it is the government’s priority to make money one way or the other,” he said. “Water streams or flowing waterways anywhere should be seen as a gift of nature but sadly we love to encroach upon them or constrict the flow. We are constructing roads and big buildings but for some strange reason we don’t build a proper infrastructure for the flow of water, be it clean or sewage water. Lyari River and Malir River are sitting examples of the ill-will of our rulers. Then when the city drowns after a little bit of rain they say ‘more rain means more water’,” he shrugged. The protesters, who also included Elia Qazil­bash, Syed Tipu Sharif, Shumaila Daw­ood, also demanded full financial disclosure of the project, said to be announced at Rs500 million. They said that this must include the approved budget, funding sources, contract scope, contractors, payments and actual expenditure. Their further demands included protection of the channel’s storm-water cap­a­city and public open space, no shops, food street or other commercial encroachment on the cha­nnel land, proper sewage treatment before discha­rging wastewater into the sea and an independent scrutiny of drainage and environmental impa­cts and meaningful public con­sultation before any decision on further works. When contacted, a KMC spokesperson told Dawn that the project was being executed by the local government department and it had nothing to do with the KMC or Karachi mayor. Peshawar becomes city of containers. PESHAWAR: Despite being in throes of violence for the past many decades, Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, has most of the time enjoyed political stability. The violence came and went but political stability was always there despite the sabre-rattling with federal government and marches on Islamabad. A semblance of understanding between Islamabad and Peshawar, no matter how little, was still there. However, all this changed on Sunday after the imposition of governor’s rule and emergency in the province. The night before, skies of Peshawar poured buckets, flooding roads and drenching the city; however, the Sunday morning was warm and sunny. Yet it started with a sense of dread as uncertainty hung heavy over the city. The telltale signs of not everything is good dawned upon after reaching for telephone, the ritual everyone does upon waking up. The impending doom was there for all to see: no mobile signals. Routine journey in the city turns into hectic exercise as governor’s rule imposed The city had witnessed a nearly 48 hours long mobile service blackout just days ago owing to PTI protest march. Outside, the stations of Peshawar Bus Transit (BRT), whose buses come on road early in the morning, remained shut. The GT Road was closed at Firdous Chowk by placing shipping containers. A large number of police personnel was deputed at this spot. Only pedestrians were allowed to move ahead on GT Road and a large number of cops were sitting outside the shuttered shops on GT Road between Hospital Road and Firdous Chowk, also called the Malik Saad Shaheed Chowk. A bearded cop on the road stopped me and handed over a shopping bag containing fried peas. Perplexed, I looked at him and he turned his back toward me, asking me to put the peas into the back pocket of his bulletproof vest. The gates of Bala Hisar Fort, which houses the headquarters of Frontier Corps North, were shuttered and a contingent of policemen was resting on the footpath. A few steps from here just outside the KP Assembly is Surey Chowk, from where GT Road leads commuters to Khyber Road, which houses the city red zone. Police guard a road leading to the Red Zone, in Peshawar. — Reuters The road leading to Khyber Road was blocked with containers and the gate erected to control traffic was also closed. A large number of cops were milling around Surey Pul Square, which is the most favoured spot for protesters of all kinds and hues. At the end of Justice Rustam Kiyani Road near central jail , where the artery leads to Sher Shah Suri Road, an old armoured personnel carrier was parked and two cops there were telling walkers not to proceed further. A few of us ignored their warnings but just next to MPA Hostel, a large contingent of cops yelled at us to go back and take detour through Shoba Bazaar. The Jail Pul, which connects Sher Shah Suri Road with Khyber Bazaar, was also closed. I met an acquaintance there who offered to take me through Civil Secretariat and we entered the Police Road and secretariat without any hassle. Civil Secretariat, the beating heart of KP government, was completely deserted with a few cars parked outside the chief secretary office. On Sahibzada Abdul Qayyum Road, where houses of minister and governor are located, security was very tight and police personnel were checking everyone heading towards both the houses. From the distance, I saw a large number of vehicles parked outside the Governor’s Houses. Walking the road in the opposite direction towards Khyber Road, I saw an APC, a prison van and truck carrying riot police, heading in the direction of Chief Minister House. After a few minutes’ walk, a barricade was erected on Khyber Road near Army Stadium and when I approached the personnel standing there and explained that I needed to cross to the other side, a plainclothes youth holding a radio just sputtered a series of “no, no, no, no. You must go back. This road is closed and we cannot open this barrier.” I stood there in plain confusion thinking of what to do. No question of going back and with no telephone, I was unable to approach any official. Then as a last resort, I pleaded with paramilitary personnel to let me out and one of them signalled another guard to open the gate for me. But the plainclothes again jumped in front of me and said no. Then the other, standing behind laughed, perhaps, they were enjoying my confusion or saw fear on my face. “How rudimentary freedom is,” muses one of the characters in JM Coetzee. Waiting for the Barbarians. Little did we realise how important is the ability to move freely without any fear, without being stopped. Outside the stretch of Khyber Road, connecting University Road and Airport Road, Amn Chowk was open but there was little traffic. A large contingent of cops was present at Amn Chowk, previously called the Gora Qabristan Chowk. The University Road was blocked at Tehkal with containers, a biker told me. There were also containers on Stadium Chowk only letting cars in a single line on both sides. Saddar Bazaar was partially open oblivious to changing political fortunes and game of thrones which was currently under way just a stone’s throw away. A container was also placed on Arbab Road, connecting Mall Road to Saddar Road, with a few cops lazing under a tree outside the Presentation Convent School. For many years, marchers from Peshawar used to result into turning the federal capital into a fortress of containers but this time Islamabad instead sent containers to Peshawar. It is to be seen how long these containers are going to stay here. In the afternoon, the internet also died. Published in Dawn, October 12th, 2026

Unease among Punjab police personnel on reports of deployment in KP. LAHORE: The concerns of the Punjab Police personnel, already facing issues of bad food and missing facilities during deployment in Rawalpindi division to counter the PTI march, further deepened on Sunday on the ‘rumours’ that 25,000 of the total 40,000 would be moved from Attock (Punjab) to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa after declaration of an emergency and imposition of the governor’s rule. Disillusioned by fatigue, lack of sleep and poor living conditions, a Punjab Police officer said, the exhausted police personnel were viewing the expected movement from Attock to KP as a new challenge and a serious trouble for them amid reports of poor facilities. During the last few weeks, there was a barrage of allegations surfacing against the Rawalpindi division police administration of supplying rotten and stale food to the deployed personnel while reports confirmed death of five policemen during the last two weeks in line of duty at Attock and Wah Cantt in connection with the PTI protest march. Two died of heart attacks, one drowned in a canal, two others died of medical complications while a constable was fighting for life after a snakebite in the jungle. As per the emerging reports, the police personnel have been complaining about the foul-smelling food, bad catering, poor washroom facilities and risky living conditions during the deployment, particularly in district Attock. IGP rejects reports, says no decision taken yet; 40,000 cops deployed to counter PTI march face lack of facilities, getting bad food; five lose life in line of duty Some senior officers also came to the support of their force and held the Rawalpindi police authorities responsible for the mismanagement. A senior officer said the videos recorded by the police personnel regarding the stale food continued to appear on social media with every passing day while the local police administration dubbed them merely ‘a conspiracy by some individual employees’ instead of resolving the problems. Some recordings showed insects or worms in food served to the force with personnel raising the issue. Most complaints were related to the foul-smelling food, poor catering and washroom facilities. Quoting some internal reports, the officer said that the Rawalpindi police top brass exchanged arguments with some senior officers of Punjab Police who highlighted the issue. The senior officers had arrived from other regions of the province to command their respective police force in Attock and Wah Cantt. About the deployment in KP, Punjab Inspector General of Police Abdul Kareem clarified that no final decision had been taken or any directive was issued for the relocation of the police force from Punjab to KP. “Although no final decision has been made yet to send the force to KP, if it happens, we will make it public officially,” he told Dawn . Regarding bad quality of food, he said steps to provide quality food to the force at Attock and Wah Cantt were being taken on a priority basis. He rejected the allegations of supply of adulterated food ‘on a large scale,’ terming the reports incorrect. “When complaints were inquired into, one of the police employees was caught mixing water in the food deliberately,” said Mr Kareem. Even then, he added, the Punjab Food Authority (PFA) had been tasked with checking the food quality and it had fielded teams to ensure provision of hygienic food and drinking water. The IGP confirmed the deaths of five personnel, saying, “Five police employees have lost their lives during the last two-week security deployment at Attock and Wah Cantt”. He identified them as constables Zulfiqar Ahmed, Zain Ali, Muhammad Imran, Muhammad Shahzad and Usman Idrees. “Two of them were martyred due to heart attack while one of them – Zain Ali - accidentally drowned after slipping into Ghazi Canal. The two other police personnel died in the line of duty due to severe medical complications,” the IG says. He rejected the reports about the death of a police employee by a snakebite, saying he was under treatment. Published in Dawn, October 12th, 2026

Another slain seaman’s family seeks return of his remains. KARACHI: Just days after kidnapped sailors from MT Honour 25 were reunited with their families, another Pakistani seafarer’s family is seeking the return of his mortal remains, following his demise after his ship came under attack near the Strait of Hormuz last month. Muhammad Hammad Obaida, a third engineer and crew member aboard the Panama-flagged oil tanker MT El Gaia, was killed in an attack on the vessel on Sept 13, off the coast of Oman. Nearly a month on, however, the grieving family in Pakistan, including his three-year-old son and pregnant wife, is still waiting for his repatriation. Media reports provide conflicting accounts of the incident, which took place north of Oman’s Musandam peninsula. According to multiple accounts, the tanker came under attack on Sept 13, while Reuters reported that it was towed to an Omani port around five days later. Pregnant widow, toddler await Hammad Obaida’s body after he perished in attack off Oman coast last month While US and Iranian authorities traded blame over who was behind the strike, the bodies of two sailors — a Pakistani and an Indian — who had perished in an engine room fire were only discovered days after the incident, when the men were found to be missing during a headcount. According to Hammad’s family, they came to know about the incident through one of his colleagues on Sept 26. Hammad had left home only a few days earlier, on Sept 6. Just a day before the attack, he had spoken to his mother over a video call. “He was showing me around the ship… He was happy to be back at work,” his mother, Ather Pervaiz, told Dawn. Hammad, 34, was a qualified marine engineer who had graduated from Glasgow University in the UK. When his younger brother Fawwad took out his phone to show us a picture, Hammad’s three-year-old son, Musa, who had been busy playing with blocks on the floor, suddenly looked up and ran to take the phone from his uncle. “This is my Baba,” the toddler exclaimed, adding, “He is with Allah Mian [God Almighty] now.” He kissed the phone screen as both his elders struggled to hold back tears. “Hammad’s son needs to say a final goodbye to him. His young widow is expecting their second child. His father, brother, sisters and I have accepted what happened as God’s will. But please bring us his remains so that we can at least give him a respectful burial,” Ms Pervaiz said quietly. Fawwad explained that despite writing countless letters and rea­ching out to the Pakistan Embassy in Oman, the Foreign Office and the prime minister through social media, the family had received no clear official response. “We also approached the Sindh government… and were told that the matter was in the government’s knowledge,” he added. DNA sample Fawwad said the Pakistani embassy in Oman had confirmed that two bodies were awaiting DNA testing in the country, but no Pakistani authority had collected a DNA sample from the family to expedite identification. “I am also in touch with Vivek, the brother of Indian seafarer Sumit Kumar, whose body was found alongside my brother’s,” he stated. When contacted, the Foreign Office confirmed that the bodies of a Pakistani and an Indian seafarer were lying in a hospital mortuary in Oman, awaiting DNA testing for identification. Responding to Dawn’s query, the FO spokesperson said the bodies had been severely disfigured, making DNA testing necessary and delaying the repatriation of the remains to their families. Published in Dawn, October 12th, 2026

Pakistan looking to raise more than $1bn under govt push for privatisation, says finance minister. The government is looking to push for the privatisation of five to six entities that could raise upwards of $1 billion, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb told Reuters on Monday, stating that he expected the economy to grow by more than 4 per cent this fiscal year despite elevated oil prices. Pakistan’s economy is considered to be highly vulnerable to a prolonged Middle East conflict given its dependence on Gulf energy imports, remittances and financing support from the region, even as it remains reliant on external financing to bolster foreign exchange reserves and meet debt repayments. Pakistan has been able to procure adequate quantities of fuel, successfully avoiding any shortages, and critical sectors such as agriculture were holding up, Aurangzeb said. “So I’m still quite clear that we should clock north of 4pc ,” he said in an interview on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok. “And on the inflation side, obviously, we are keeping a very close eye because it does have a knock-on impact in terms of the commodity prices.” Following a period of severe economic turmoil exacerbated by the Covid-19 pandemic, the cash-strapped economy has recovered some of its footing, supported by a $7bn, 37-month IMF loan program known as the Extended Fund Facility signed in 2024 that includes some tough measures such as raising tax revenue on farm income. Following the privatisation of flag carrier Pakistan International Airlines last year, Aurangzeb said the government has around another dozen entities in the pipeline, including state-owned power distribution companies and the outsourcing of airport operations. “I expect about five or six of these to go through during this fiscal year,” he said, adding that they could raise more than $1bn. Privatisation has been seen as a key test of Pakistan’s reform credibility with the IMF, with officials previously underlining that failure to offload loss-making state firms risked renewed pressure on public finances. “We are quite clear that we want the private sector to lead the country,” said Aurangzeb. “So our role is to help support, assist any way we can in terms of the ecosystem.” Exchange stabilisation facility The US-Israeli-led war with Iran, now in its eighth month, and the inflation and hardship it has caused, will dominate the agenda and sideline conversations during the meetings that are being held outside Washington for the first time in three years. Pakistan, which reached a staff-level agreement with the IMF last week, potentially unlocking about $1.21bn in financing under the Extended Fund Facility and a climate program, is continuing discussions with the United States for a proposed $10bn exchange stabilisation facility, Aurangzeb said. But he declined to provide a time frame for the conclusion of negotiations. “If it comes through, this will be a great help for us,” he said, referring to the facility, which is in addition to ongoing talks with the Export-Import Bank of the United States and the US International Development Finance Corporation. “If it doesn’t come through, this does not, you know, create any problem for us in terms of access to market.”

DPM Dar defends emergency and governor's rule in KP, says measures not politically motivated. A day after the government imposed governor’s rule and emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar defended the move, saying it was not politically motivated but instead taken to curb terrorism. DPM Dar made the comments while addressing a seminar in Islamabad, a day after the federal government imposed emergency under Article 232 and the governor’s rule under Article 234 in KP. The Cabinet recommended the move, citing the PTI-led provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”. Referring to “recent developments” in the country, Dar said, “It is not a political move; it is surely against the menace of terrorism which that province (KP) has been hit with in the past decade and a half.” He asked if the Centre could “keep sleeping and looking towards one another because it may be deemed as a political move? “No, it is not. I can guarantee you.” Dar recalled that he negotiated with PTI in 2014 during a sit-in in Islamabad. Defending the move further, Dar held it was the federal government’s responsibility to take such steps “once it is totally determined that there is no solution other than what we have done yesterday”. He stressed that the ruling party PML-N bore a “heavy political cost” when the country was on the brink of default in 2022. Dar recalled that the government had to take difficult structural measures. “Political cost was paid, unpopularity was there, and we recovered a lot because we saved the country from the brink of default.” Dar said the government “had no choice but to take the measures we took yesterday, and we will implement it in totality”. He hoped the progress would show in the time ahead. “I am sure the province will be quite happy to see peace restored, their lives are safe and the radicalisation [will end]. Information Minister Attaullah Tarar also spoke at the seminar and defended the federal government’s actions. Following the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP, the federal government also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in the province. On the ground, shipping containers were placed around the city of Peshawar to block several roads, with heavy police deployment. On Sunday, federal ministers alleged that the PTI-led government in KP had a “nexus” with terrorist groups, as the Centre explained that the province’s security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there. The Centre and the PTI have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their October 3 talks . The previous night, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had posted on X along the same lines, saying that the decision was “neither a political decision nor an easy step”. He added, “It was a difficult CONSTITUTIONAL course made necessary by the circumstances on the ground. “When every avenue for cooperation has been exhausted, the Constitution and Pakistan should be the priority.” He reiterated that the government and its allies had “exhausted every avenue of parliamentary engagement, direct dialogue and back channel diplomacy”. “KP has borne a heavy burden of terrorism and our security forces and civilians have made immense sacrifices. In these circumstances, cooperation should have been the priority,” Naqvi said. Pakistan’s desire for peace must not be misconstrued as weakness: Tarar Tarar, in his address, spoke of counterterrorism, particularly the threat emanating from Afghan soil. He said that Pakistan wanted peaceful coexistence with Afghanistan, but went on to warn that the country’s desire for peace must not be “misconstrued as weakness”. Tarar said Pakistan had been at the forefront of the war against terrorism, paying a heavy price in terms of human lives and economic losses. “No other nation in the world can say that it has lost more than 90,000 lives in the war against terrorism,” he said, adding that Pakistan had suffered economic losses exceeding $100 billion. “When we represent Pakistan at conferences like this one, we stand before you as ambassadors of peace,” he said, describing Pakistan as a symbol of defiance against violent extremism and resilience against terrorism. He said Pakistan had acted as a shield between terrorists and the rest of the world, adding that the sacrifices made by Pakistanis in the fight against terrorism contributed to global peace. “When a Pakistani lays down his or her life fighting terrorism, it is not only to make Pakistan a safer place, but also to contribute to global peace,” he said. Tarar said Pakistan’s recent role in mediating between the United States and Iran had demonstrated its commitment to peace. He said Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, DPM Dar and Chief of Army Staff and Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir had made immense efforts to facilitate the mediation process, which had received international recognition. Given its strategic location and shared border with Afghanistan, Pakistan had always sought regional stability, he said, adding that a peaceful and stable Afghanistan would promote trade with Central Asia, attract foreign investment and strengthen regional cooperation and connectivity. He said Pakistan had participated in negotiations and engaged with the Afghan interim government to convey its desire for peace and prosperity in the region, particularly in Afghanistan. However, he added, Pakistan’s advice had “fallen on deaf ears”. Tarar said Pakistan had hosted more than four million Afghan refugees for over four decades and had paid a high price for its generosity. He regretted that Pakistan’s hospitality had not been reciprocated. He alleged that Afghanistan’s interim rulers believed in violence and extremism, adding that terrorist safe havens existed across the border. Citing United Nations and independent assessments, he said more than 6,000 Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) terrorists were estimated to be present in Afghanistan, with the total number of terrorists exceeding 20,000. Since the Afghan Taliban returned to power in 2021 , the TTP has continued to exploit Afghan territory for recruitment, training, facilitation and planning attacks against Pakistan, he said. Pakistan had responded to these attacks because it could not allow terrorists to use safe havens in Afghanistan to target the country, he added. Tarar also criticised the restrictions imposed on Afghan women, particularly the denial of their right to education and economic empowerment and their exclusion from the workforce. He said the regime’s interpretation of Islam had led to the denial of basic rights to women and minorities and promoted violent extremism. Referring to a recent visit to Kohat in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where a terrorist attack had taken place, he said he had met injured people at the Combined Military Hospital. Tarar also referred to the 38th report of the United Nations Monitoring Team, which he said had recorded the relocation of nearly 2,000 family members of TTP terrorists from border areas to locations deeper inside Afghanistan. “If Afghanistan continues to provide safe havens to these terrorists, how can peace be achieved?” he asked. He said Pakistan would achieve peace and eradicate terrorism not only within its borders but across the region. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP, that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded. According to a UN Security Council-mandated monitoring report — covering the period from Dec 16, 2025 to June 9, 2026 — Afg­han Taliban’s continued support for TTP has contributed to a rise in the frequency and lethality of terrorist attacks in Pakistan, even as Kabul has taken some initial steps to rein in the group.

LHC directs jail authorities to provide heart medication to Imran's sister Uzma. LAHORE: The Lahore High Court (LHC) on Monday directed jail authorities to provide heart medication to Dr Uzma Khan, sister of PTI founder and former premier Imran Khan. Imran’s three sisters, Aleema Khan, Noreen Niazi and Uzma, have been in detention for nearly three weeks under the Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance (MPO). Uzma and Noreen were detained for 30 days on September 21, ahead of the party’s Sept 27 protest call, later postponed to October 4. The development came a day after Aleema ’s detention on Sept 20. On Monday, Justice Abher Gul Khan took up a petition challenging the preventive detention of Imran’s sisters. Sakeena Niazi, daughter of Noreen, had filed the petition on Oct 6. During the hearing, Uzma’s husband, Ahad Khan, appeared before the court and stated that his wife had a heart condition and needed three medicines daily. He asked the court to direct the authorities to ensure that the medicines were delivered to her in jail daily. Petitioner’s counsel Rana Mudassar Umar requested the court to allow Noreen to receive clothes, medicines and spectacles in jail, saying these were basic necessities and her fundamental right. He also sought permission for family members and lawyers to meet the detained women. The counsel further requested the court to summon the Lahore Capital City Police Officer and the deputy commissioner in person, arguing that their appearance would help clarify the circumstances surrounding the detention notifications. After hearing the arguments, the judge ordered the jail authorities to provide medicines to Uzma and reserved decision on the request to summon the officials in person. In the previous hearing, the LHC sought a report on the provision of medicines, clothes and other basic facilities to the sisters and adjourned the hearing till October 12. On Sept 24, the LHC had turned down a request to immediately suspend the preventive detention notifications issued against Noreen and Dr Uzma. Earlier this month, Imran’s cousin, Qasim Zaman, was also taken into custody when he went to Adiala jail to meet the ex-prime minister. The detention had come amid reports of a crackdown on the PTI ahead of its countrywide protest and march to Islamabad, which the party had called to demand Imran’s release from jail and mobilise people for the supremacy of the Constitution.

'Wake-up call for the world' as UN global poverty index rises for first time since 2010. A United Nations global poverty index has risen for the first time since its creation in 2010, bringing the number of people affected to 1.2 billion, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) reported Monday. In the 2026 edition of their annual report, the UNDP and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative research center counted 51.5 million more people living in “acute” poverty compared to the previous year. UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo said the increase in poverty should be a “wake-up call for the world.” “Behind these figures are 1.2 billion people facing hardships that reinforce one another: hunger, missed schooling and a lack of clean water or electricity. This is unacceptable,” he said in a press release. More than half of those in acute poverty were children. ‘Mixed bag’ However, UNDP said a major factor in the recorded increase was population growth, and new data was only available for 13 of the 108 developing countries covered by the report. While the total number of people in poverty has increased, the report provides a mixed picture. Some 33 nations have halved the percentage of their people living in poverty as defined by the index in the past 15 years. Those included six countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Among the countries that have made the most rapid progress were countries in Asia — China and Vietnam — UNDP said. As in the previous year, the report found that the majority of the poorest people live in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, specifically the subcontinent, the most densely populated region on Earth. “In Egypt, Nepal, and Tajikistan, both the poverty rate and the number of people experiencing multidimensional poverty have decreased significantly,” the press release said. In Angola and Zambia, the poverty rate has also declined, but population growth has more than offset this decrease, resulting in an increase in the number of people living in poverty. The poverty index used in the report includes indicators such as the lack of adequate housing, sanitation, electricity, cooking fuel, food and education.

How startups are betting on AI to predict the future. Several startups are betting that they can leverage artificial intelligence (AI) to make better forecasts than even the most specialised experts when it comes to topics as varied as stock market movements, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, or how a Shakira song will perform on music charts. By 2030, “we’re going to feel that what we were doing for our decision-making was complete Stone Age thinking,” Dan Schwarz, cofounder of the forecasting company FutureSearch, said. AI forecasting models are already on par with the best “superforecasters” — gifted individuals whose estimates are markedly superior to those of ordinary people — thanks to troves of data acquired from both public and private sources. In early September, two AI models made history when they took the top spots in the Metaculus Cup, a competition among prediction champions, both human and nonhuman. FutureSearch’s in-house human wizard, superforecaster Tom Liptay, is aware that “he’s not secure in his job” in the medium term, Schwarz said. “He knows that these things are going to surpass him.” Theo Summer, who cofounded Preseen with Veniamin Veselovsky, used AI tools to turn $35 into $1.9 million in just seven months on the American prediction-making site Kalshi. The idea is not to guarantee a result but to define a probability of occurrence, with the ability to cross-check assumptions related to several interconnected events — for example, changes in the price of oil and the war in the Middle East. “Right now, the quickest buyers are normally the hedge funds, just because if they think they can make money off something, they can move pretty fast,” Veselovsky said. Algorithms have shaped Wall Street for more than a decade, but the rise of AI forecasting is likely to further increase the automation of financial markets. “I think it’s probably already having a small impact because we already have customers who use it when making trading decisions,” said Toby Shevlane, the cofounder of another forecasting startup called Mantic. Now-famous prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket, which are used by millions of Americans, are also becoming inundated by AI use. It might soon be too late for retail investors, who don’t have access to expensive AI tools, to profit on those types of consumer-oriented trading sites because “they will soon just be dominated by AI forecasting systems,” Veselovsky said. Risk Management The most advanced models no longer just predict events, either. They can also formulate their own questions about the future and then assign probabilities based on the different possible outcomes, Shevlane said. Their sphere of influence is beginning to extend beyond finance, as well, with potential applications in government policy, corporate decision-making, scientific research, and insurance risk assessments. Mantic provides a large American company with likely scenarios of regulatory developments in its sector and has also worked for the British government. Companies “are interested in risks and how to monitor them,” Shevlane said. Meanwhile, other customers might be more interested in medical research, particularly to help make decisions around which types of treatments would be best to fund, Schwarz said. Widespread access to these types of tools can come with costs, though. “I think that good can be derived from this,” Veselovsky said, but “I’m also a little bit scared because, you know, maybe Russia or China has better systems.”

Thousands march in India's capital to demand resignation of election chief over alleged misconduct. Thousands of protesters marched in New Delhi on Monday demanding the resignation of India’s election chief over alleged misconduct during a voter roll revision, in the latest showdown with authorities in the heavily fortified capital. The revision of voter rolls has resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to media reports. Critics say the measure has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims, but election authorities claim the move was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries. Opposition parties and supporters of the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party protest movement have taken to the streets in recent days, defying a strict security clampdown to demand a halt to the revision exercise and the resignation of the chief election commissioner. “You can see how big the crowd is already,” demonstrator Abhay Aryan, 28, told AFP as the crowd marched towards the Supreme Court, chanting slogans and waving placards. “The government has to listen to the voice of the people.” Critics say the large-scale revision of electoral lists could benefit Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party. The Election Commission of India, which oversees the voting process in the world’s most populous nation, has denied wrongdoing. A protester who gave his name as Mehvaish said he could no longer “tolerate the injustices” meted out by Modi’s government. “We want removal of this government (because) of all the injustices we have suffered in the past 12-13 years,” he said. “Now if they take away our right to vote, what is left with us?” Rights advocates and critics say Modi’s government has eroded democratic freedoms during more than a decade in power, citing pressure on journalists, civil society groups and political opponents — allegations the government rejects. Authorities deployed thousands of security personnel across central Delhi for a third straight day, erecting heavy metal barricades and closing key metro stations. “People are being stopped from reaching Delhi,” opposition leader Rahul Gandhi said at a news conference on Monday. “Delhi has been made into a fortress… there is police everywhere,” he added, accusing Modi of shielding the election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. Public attention has also shifted to the police response, after a chaotic weekend in which thousands of protesters including organisers were detained, according to local media reports. Most of those detained, including three top leaders of the “cockroach” movement, have since been released. Opposition figures have accused authorities of trying to suppress dissent through mass detentions. ‘Assault on democratic freedoms’ Parliamentarian John Brittas of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) alleged he was “manhandled, dragged, assaulted” by police during Sunday’s demonstrations. “This is not merely an assault on an MP. It is an assault on democratic freedoms and the rule of law,” Brittas said. Police did not respond to questions on detentions or their actions during a news conference on Sunday. Several journalists covering the protest said they were detained despite prominently displaying their press cards. Nitin Katiyar, a digital journalist, told The Times of India newspaper that a police official had punched him in the eye. AFP could not immediately verify his charge. Media rights group Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said at least 16 journalists were detained during the weekend protests, calling the police action “unacceptable”. Hundreds of yellow metal barricades were set up on roads leading to central Delhi, while six major metro stations remained shut. The protests have become a major political challenge for Modi, drawing together opposition parties, student groups and activists angered by the voter roll revision. The leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party, which has millions of social media followers, have pledged to continue their protests until Kumar steps down.

Islamabad court grants police 5-day remand of suspect in case of suicide over visa fraud. ISLAMABAD: A judicial magistrate on Monday handed over the main suspect to police on a five-day physical remand in a case related to the suicide of a young woman who was allegedly defrauded. The 20-year-old student, identified as Laiba Aijaz, allegedly died by suicide last week after a person defrauded her of Rs5 million, which she had paid to move to the United States for further studies, according to police. The case drew the government’s attention, with Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif directing the police to arrest the suspect. He and two of his female accomplices were later picked up during separate raids in the federal capital. Subsequently, on Monday, the main suspect was produced before Judicial Magistrate Zunaira Zafar with his face covered. Police sought a 10-day physical remand in the case registered at Ramna police station. Seeking the remand, the investigating officer told the court that a thorough examination of the facts and circumstances surrounding the incident was necessary. The officer said further investigation was required to determine the suspect’s alleged role in the incident and verify the available evidence. Items linked to him and other potential evidence also needed to be examined, the officer added. The allegations against the suspect remain subject to investigation. The main suspect had previously served in the Quetta Anti-Corruption Department, from where he was dismissed. Preliminary investigation showed that the main suspect, operating a gang with the two women and others, had also defrauded other people and minted millions of rupees. The case The deceased woman studied in the BS Physics programme at the International Islamic University Islamabad (IIUI) from 2019 to 2023. However, she was no longer enrolled at the university at the time of her death. According to the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA), the suspect allegedly obtained millions of rupees from Laiba’s family with the help of a female accomplice and by misrepresenting his identity and professional status. The money was allegedly taken on the pretext of securing employment for her brother and arranging her admission to Harvard University in the US. However, the suspect gave her fake travel documents, following which she committed suicide. Police registered a case under Sections 322 (punishment for qatl-bis-sabab) and 34 (acts done by several persons in furtherance of common intention) of the Pakistan Penal Code. A separate case was registered by the FIA on a complaint lodged by Laiba’s maternal uncle under provisions relating to cheating, abetment and immigration-related fraud. According to the FIR, Laiba’s father, Mohammad Aijaz, had agreed to pay Rs9.3 million to the suspect to arrange his daughter’s travel to the US. The family paid part of the amount through bank transfers and the remainder in cash. The suspect allegedly provided fake travel documents and a fraudulent transaction receipt. The FIA said the suspects had also provided fake scholarship award letters, admission offers and university fee payment receipts.

Closure of Riyadh airport extended after deadly Houthi strikes. Saudi authorities said on Monday they were extending the suspension of operations at the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, after deadly weekend attacks by Yemen’s Houthis. Operations at King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia’s second-busiest airport after Jeddah, were suspended to “allow for the completion of procedures to ensure the safety and operational readiness of the airport’s facilities”, the Saudi civil aviation authority said in a statement. The airport has been shut since an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. On Sunday, another attack killed one Pakistani and injured nearly a dozen others. The attacks marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi aviation in years, adding to pressures on an industry already grappling with conflict across the Middle East. The airport cancelled 99.7 per cent of all scheduled flights on Sunday, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium. An air traffic tracker from Flightradar24 showed no planes over the city. The disruption has forced airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services, while the Federal Aviation Administration advised US carriers on Sunday to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia. Lufthansa Group has cancelled all flights to Riyadh until October 16, while Air France-KLM has extended a previous suspension of services to and from the Saudi capital until the end of the month. Abu Dhabi’s Etihad Airways was among the airlines that further extended Saudi flight cancellations, affecting around 20 flights to Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam on Monday and Tuesday. The escalation with the Houthis has raised concerns over the broader economic impact. Saudi Arabia’s real gross domestic product is projected to contract by 3.6pc this year, reflecting a combination of factors including lower oil activity. The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh this month under pressure, including the kingdom’s flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the programme. Video released by Saudi authorities shows moment of Saturday blast Muslim pilgrims wrapped in white garments queued for a document check at Riyadh’s international airport, when a powerful explosion brought chunks of the ceiling down on their heads, footage released on Monday by Saudi authorities showed. Gate workers dived under their desks as passengers scrambled away from the direction of the blast, in dramatic security camera footage released by the Saudi media ministry showed the moment of the deadly strike on Saturday. Smoke and debris cloud the images, leaving only a sudden fire visible, while some blurry figures appear too shocked to flee. Many of the passengers in the video released by Saudi authorities appear to be pilgrims headed to Makkah on Umrah, the high season of which is just beginning as the intense summer heat starts to ease in Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities have warned of potential legal consequences against witnesses speaking out about strikes and have restricted media from accessing attack sites to independently report on them. The official release of footage from the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in a decade is a notable development after the government for weeks offered few public details on the extent of Houthi strikes on the kingdom. The Saudi Gazette said the footage underscored “the danger posed to innocent travellers whose journeys are dedicated to worship”, adding that the attack “raises serious questions about the Houthis’ claims to religious legitimacy”.

Islamabad ATC directs authorities to allow Imaan, Hadi to meet their legal team in jail. ISLAMABAD: An anti-terrorism court (ATC) on Monday directed jail authorities to allow lawyers representing human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari and her husband, Hadi Ali Chattha, to meet them in prison as the couple raised concerns over their access to their legal counsel and the fairness of proceedings in a case related to the removal of security barriers . The couple was indicted in the case on Oct 7. The case pertains to the alleged disruption of the security route of an international cricket team and incitement to public unrest. On Oct 10, the ATC had disposed of the couple’s plea seeking to drop the terrorism charges. ATC Judge Tahir Abbas Sipra, who presided over the hearing on Monday, ordered that Advocates Riasat Ali Azad, Zainab Janjua and Aimal Khan be allowed to meet the accused in jail. Imaan’s mother, former human rights minister Dr Shireen Mazari, appeared before the court along with Advocates Azad and Khan, while the couple attended the proceedings via video link. The defence sought an adjournment, informing the court that the Oct 10 order was also being challenged before the Islamabad High Court. “If your petition is accepted by the high court, the proceedings in this court will come to an end,” the judge remarked. Azad emphasised the need for a fair trial, saying the defence did not know what had happened or where the alleged incident had taken place. The judge also questioned the defence about whether proceedings conducted before the accused joined via video link should be treated as a trial. Azad replied in the affirmative. Justice Sipra recalled that at the previous hearing, Advocate Janjua had argued that proceedings could not be considered a trial because Imaan and Hadi had not been present via video link. During the hearing, the couple had complained about facing difficulty in communicating via video link, with Imaan and Hadi saying their voices were breaking up. “If we cannot meet then, how are we supposed to proceed with the case?” Advocate Azad asked. The judge observed that the anti-terrorism law required the trial to proceed on a daily basis and asked the prosecution how many witnesses remained to be examined. The prosecutor informed the court that nine witnesses had yet to be produced before the court. The judge then directed the prosecution to ensure that the accused were granted access to their lawyers. Meanwhile, Hadi objected to the manner in which the proceedings were being conducted and questioned why he and Imaan were not being presented before the court in person. “This goes against the principles of a fair trial,” he said, adding that they had been in jail for eight months and were struggling to pursue their case. He also raised concerns over the privacy of consultations with their lawyers, saying cameras had been installed in the designated meeting area at the jail, making confidential discussions difficult. “You are the ones who must decide our fate; please summon us to court,” Hadi told the judge, adding that the court had to determine whether he and Imaan were terrorists. The court adjourned further proceedings until Oct 14. In a related development, the court took exception to an apparent contradiction in reports submitted by Adiala jail authorities concerning Imaan’s production through a video link in separate cases. On Oct 10, the jail authorities produced Imaan before the ATC through a video link in the case pertaining to the removal of security barriers. However, in a report submitted in the case involving former MNA Ali Wazir, the same authorities stated that she could not be produced through a video link on that date because of a lack of internet connectivity. Judge Sipra expressed astonishment at the discrepancy and questioned the preparation of the reports. “Do you not read what you write in your reports? Do you just copy-paste?” the judge asked. The judge noted that Imaan had appeared through a video link in one case on Oct 10, while the jail authorities had cited the absence of internet service to explain her non-production in another case on the same day. The court issued a fresh show-cause notice to the jail authorities over the matter and directed them to produce Imaan through a video link in the case on Oct 19.

High-level Brazil delegation meets CDF Munir; both sides agree to bolster military collaboration. Pakistan and Brazil on Monday agreed to bolster their military-to-military cooperation as a high-level delegation from the Latin American country called on Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir. According to a statement from Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the delegation led by Brazil’s Admiral Renato Rodrigues De Aguiar Freire, chief of the Joint Chiefs of Staff of the Armed Forces, met the CDF at the General Headquarters in Rawalpindi. During the meeting, both military leaders discussed matters of mutual interest, the regional security landscape and avenues to bolster bilateral defence and security cooperation. “They expressed satisfaction with the longstanding cordial relations between Pakistan and Brazil and agreed to further strengthen military-to-military collaboration,” ISPR added. CDF Munir “emphasised Pakistan’s commitment to strengthening defence ties with Brazil”. Admiral Friere appreciated the military’s professionalism and operational preparedness and acknowledged their contributions to regional peace and stability, according to ISPR. “The visit reflects the shared resolve of Pakistan and Brazil to deepen defence cooperation and strengthen bilateral military ties,” the statement concluded. The visiting admiral was presented with a guard of honour by a smartly turned-out tri-services contingent upon his arrival at the GHQ. Brasilia has made efforts to boost ties with Islamabad as far back as 2018, when then-Brazilian ambassador Claudio Raja Gabaglia Lins visited the Sarhad Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Peshawar. The two sides had agreed on steps to increase bilateral trade and establish a joint chamber of commerce and industry to facilitate businesspeople and investors.

What’s the situation across KP on Day 1 of governor’s rule?. Scores of PTI workers have also been held in some districts, including Shangla and Charsadda. The order by the deputy commissioner (DC) also banned the display of weapons, and barred carrying spikes, ball bearings, laden batons, petrol bombs, or any instrument that could potentially be used for violence. Police personnel remain present on roads, with heavier deployment where the Cantonment limit begins Cops at some places seem alert, with batons in hands Road blockades All entry and exit points to Peshawar Cantt remain closed, with police deployed in the surrounding area. Railway Road leading to Shoba Bazar and Dabgari Garden is closed, as well as Sher Shah Suri Road. A rickshaw driver said he had to turn back midway after finding roads leading to Saddar from Warsak and Shami Road blocked with containers. This screengrab from Google Maps shows the M-1 (Islamabad-Peshawar Motorway) closed for traffic on the route leading from Peshawar to Swabi, as of 4pm on Oct 12, 2026. Routine activities Everyday activities continue as normal, with residents going about their daily routines. Markets in Wana, including Rustam Bazaar, remain open and traders continue their business activities. No major protests, significant disruptions to commercial activities or arrests have been reported. The situation remains generally calm despite the extraordinary administrative measures introduced at the provincial level. Traffic on the Wana Bypass Road near Wana Rustam Bazaar, indicating routine life continues. — AK Wazir Dera Ismail Khan Examinations DI Khan BISE has postponed SSC examinations in line with decisions taken by other educational boards in KP. The DPO has ordered strict legal action against those attempting to take the law into their own hands or disturb public order. Police have been directed to intensify patrolling along main roads and conduct strict snap-checking at all entry and exit points of the district.
