Patrick T. Fallon / AFP Commentary / United States 01 October 2026 20+ minutes Five Energy Market Factors That Could Tip the Scales in the Middle East War Oil, gas and fuel prices are central to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, with Washington striving to lower them and Tehran to keep them high. With both sides determined to prevail, five market-shaping developments in particular could affect whether fighting ramps up or de-escalates. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Global Order and Peacemaking United States Iran Israel/Palestine As Iran and the United States trade blows in the Gulf, they are both trying to sway at least one shared audience: global energy markets. The public and private companies that produce, refine, move and consume oil and gas around the world are listening rapt to what the belligerents say and watching every move they make in an attempt to understand where the war is headed. These commodities have many prices: for instance, what a barrel of crude oil is fetching today; how much customers are paying for derivative products like diesel or jet fuel in major markets like East Asia, the European Union or the U.S.; and what future delivery of such items is projected to cost. Together, these actual and estimated prices serve as a rough indicator of what the market thinks about the conflict’s likely trajectory. In turn, the price fluctuations are monitored in both Tehran and Washington, which factor them into strategy. U.S. President Donald Trump is plainly keeping one eye on the markets at all times. In June, when he signed a now defunct memorandum of understanding meant to end the war, he noted a market motivation, saying, “We run out of [oil] reserves at about four weeks”. On 13 August, with November’s midterm elections getting closer, Vice President JD Vance cited low fuel prices as Washington’s main war aim, saying “That’s goal number one – keep oil and gas cheap for Americans all over our country”. Preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons – Washington’s ostensible motive for launching its airstrikes in February – was apparently, at least for a time, goal number two. Iran, for its part, is trying to maintain the clout it obtained by asserting control of the Strait of Hormuz, for which it is willing to pay a big price. The Iranian economy is being hammered by intensifying sanctions and a resumed U.S. naval blockade that has halted exports from Iran’s southern coast. Washington has repeatedly hailed the impending death of Iran’s oil industry, due to lack of export and storage capacity. While these predictions were overblown, Iran is still reeling economically. As both the U.S. and Iran pin their hopes on being able to manage prices, the energy markets have proven unpredictable. Despite disruptions, the markets have displayed unexpected resilience, helping dilute the conflict’s economic consequences. Apocalyptic prophecies that oil would reach $200 a barrel have so far been incorrect. Instead, the price of the global benchmark, Brent crude, has risen from below $75 before the war to peaks that have not yet topped $130. These prices are high, but adjusted for inflation, they pale in comparison to previous spikes. Part of the explanation owes to buffers that have kept the markets from careening out of control. It helps that the world had an oil surplus when the war began, the U.S. had a few hundred million more barrels in its federal stores, Russia had more functional refineries and export terminals, China was building up rather than depleting its reserves and the Red Sea was largely open to tanker traffic. Since the war began, higher prices have pushed demand lower and raised production in some countries while new workarounds – in part orchestrated by the U.S. and Gulf states like the United Arab Emirates – and growing risk tolerance are sending a significant amount of oil through Hormuz despite Iran’s attacks. [T]he question remains whether the U.S. or Iran will outlast the other in what has become an endurance test. Still, the question remains whether the U.S. or Iran will outlast the other in what has become an endurance test. The feared tipping point at which a shortfall in oil supply causes a rapid price increase until demand falls has seemingly been forestalled by greater crude flow through Hormuz. But surging diesel and other fuel prices may now matter more than crude oil alone. U.S. retail diesel prices are soaring to record highs, generating support for a 90-day U.S. diesel export ban and even a measure of dissent from the war among members of Trump’s Republican Party (in many other parts of the world, rising fuel prices are already stoking significant public anger). Iran is cognisant of the correlation between fuel prices and the Republicans’ political fortunes; with the November midterm elections approaching and major Republican losses a significant possibility , Iran may think that such a result would produce new constraints on Trump’s war-making, in the form of more vigorous oversight from a Congress controlled by opposition Democrats. For this reason, many Iran watchers believe Tehran, along with its allies, will seek to prevent the U.S. from stabilising prices, even if it involves a mutually hurting re-escalation of the conflict. Indeed, in September, the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels advanced in Yemen, positioning themselves to more effectively threaten shipping in the Red Sea, a major energy corridor. But while Iran looks for ways to keep oil and gas bottled up in the Middle East, Washington and its partners continue to work on means of getting these items out, with the outflow of crude through the Strait of Hormuz reportedly hitting its pre-war baseline by the end of September, though refined products like fuel lagged far behind. Efforts are under way to keep raising this Hormuz outflow, and land routes add a few million more barrels. The U.S. conundrum now is that crude needs to reach refineries, and the resulting products to hit global markets, for the world to get out of its growing fuel crisis. As the U.S. increasingly looks to others to help manage the fallout of its war with Iran, it is also pursuing a number of costly mitigation measures, whose sustainability is questionable. This Crisis Group analysis examines the relationship between global energy markets and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. It looks at the cushions that have helped absorb war-related shocks to oil markets so far and the extent to which they are under pressure. It identifies five particular factors that could contribute to re-escalation or de-escalation of the conflict. U.S. concerns began with crude oil, but diesel may be the Trump administration’s undoing. Only Beijing knows how quickly and by how much China’s oil imports and fuel exports will recover. Ukraine’s strategic achievements threaten its patrons’ energy supplies. The Houthis have moved into Bab al-Mandab. The contest over the Strait of Hormuz has intensified. 1. U.S. concerns began with crude oil, but diesel may be the Trump administration’s undoing. The first factor to consider is U.S. energy security. The U.S. has developed several layers of protection from the worst market consequences of its own coercive action against major oil exporters like Russia (on which it has slapped Ukraine-related sanctions) and Iran (which it has both sanctioned and attacked). These include substantial increases in the efficiency with which oil is converted into economic output since the 1970s energy shocks and advancements like the shale revolution , which have made the U.S. itself the world’s top oil producer. Abundant natural gas production and Washington’s forcibly acquired control of Venezuelan oil export help, too. So does the U.S. strategic petroleum reserve. Yet these buffers are being put to the test. As part of a 400-million barrel release coordinated through the International Energy Agency to help keep a lid on oil prices, the U.S. is finishing up a drawdown of 172 million barrels from its strategic reserve. If completed, its holdings will drop to 243 million barrels. When the reserve draws down, private companies take the barrels as a loan, with repayment deadlines varying from early 2027 to mid-2029, and move the oil directly into markets. The releases to date have bolstered domestic refining, but they have also resulted in U.S. stores of oil falling to their lowest level since 1982 . The reserves are approaching what many analysts consider the minimum volume needed for the network of salt caverns and pipes the U.S. government uses for oil storage to stay functional. While the U.S. government has stated that the operational minimum of its reserves is 70 million barrels, a federal audit found that more than a quarter – implying an estimated 103 million barrels – likely cannot be withdrawn due to ageing storage facilities. Industry analysts have repeatedly put the operational minimum within a much higher range of 170-200 million barrels, with several experts warning of dangers to the salt caverns’ structural integrity below 300 million barrels, a threshold passed in early August. (The U.S. Energy Department disputes that any such problem exists.) U.S. strategic reserves could therefore be functionally empty in weeks to months, depending on the pace of withdrawals, with long-term risks to the viability of the entire system growing if they continue. Once this stockpile is depleted, U.S. concerns that need oil beyond that available from domestic production will need to look to commercial stockpiles and imports. Here uncertainty reigns. Aggregate estimates of a national operational minimum vary widely, and at least some analysts believe that a single U.S. figure is unknowable . Inventory at Cushing, Oklahoma – the storage and distribution hub for the U.S. domestic benchmark grade, West Texas Intermediate – has ebbed and flowed over the course of the war. Cushing storage rose in late September as refinery runs fell amid talk of a diesel export ban, after nearly hitting “ tank bottoms ” in June and July. Cushing does not represent the entire private U.S. oil or energy market, but its stock is an important signal alongside the status of strategic reserves, and it has shown real strain during the war. Nor is the demand side of the equation fully easing. U.S. crude exports, especially to East Asia and Europe, surged by some two million barrels a day or more through the first three months of the war, though in recent months they have started to fall, in part because of surging freight costs linked to the war. As to whether Venezuelan production can help soften the blow to global energy supplies or to U.S. stocks, it has likely done as much as it can already, at least for the short term. As to whether Venezuelan production can help soften the blow to global energy supplies or to U.S. stocks, it has likely done as much as it can already, at least for the short term. Following its January ouster of President Nicolás Maduro, the U.S. took control of Venezuela’s oil exports, and though the details of the arrangement remain unclear, Venezuela has consistently shipped 900,000 to over 1 million barrels per day in recent months. Its monthly crude exports peaked in May and declined through September as storage was drained, but they are still higher compared to the period just before the U.S. removed Maduro. The U.S. has been one of the largest destinations for Venezuela’s oil exports of late: its share rose to about two thirds in July, even as total exports fell slightly, before dropping to just under half by September. This flow from Venezuela is helpful to the U.S. at the margins but not by itself transformative. Average daily U.S. imports of Venezuelan oil in September were equivalent to under 3 per cent of the crude used daily by U.S. refineries (as of the week ending 18 September). In this way, Venezuela’s state oil company PDVSA has essentially become an unofficial if modest buffer alongside the dwindling U.S. strategic reserve. Over time, the U.S. government’s machinations could lead to greater output, though at a cost to Venezuela and its sovereignty. But significant short-term increases are unlikely, given years of reduced production and underinvestment. Trump has stated that he intends to fill U.S. strategic reserves with Venezuelan oil, but heavy Venezuelan crude is unsuitable for the reserve and would need to be swapped for lighter grades with the private sector. There are many hurdles to clear before that would be possible, suggesting that Trump’s statement is more intended to allay concerns about U.S. oil supply than to communicate real short-term solutions. Beyond inventory depletion and the limits of what Caracas can be compelled to do for Washington, the global market for fuels derived from crude oil is in much worse shape than when the war began and is now a more urgent issue for Washington than crude. As of August, global diesel exports had dipped by a third from mid-2025, while China’s fuel exports remain uncertain , Russian refineries are getting pummelled by Ukrainian aerial attacks and most other refiners around the world are already running at full capacity. Major maintenance work is looming for many. Russian and Gulf fuel exports were down over half from March to mid-August, spurring increased refinery production elsewhere such as in the U.S. and Europe; these heightened runs are far from making up the shortfall. Diesel supplies are especially tight, with U.S. prices up over 75 per cent from a year ago and still climbing. With national diesel inventory reaching a multi-decade seasonal low , the state of Texas declared an emergency over diesel prices, despite producing a third of U.S. diesel as of June. The squeeze has prompted one of the longest periods of running U.S. refineries near maximum capacity in a quarter-century – a “ super-refining ” spike that wears on equipment. Refineries will eventually need downtime for maintenance, or major breakdowns could occur. While the average U.S. consumer may not care about crude oil itself, rising fuel prices are felt intensely. Trump gathered executives from leading fuel refining and distribution companies at the White House on 1 September to ask them to lower fuel prices, but to little avail. Expensive diesel means higher costs for freight, such as the long-haul trucking and rail on which the U.S. economy depends, as well as for construction and agriculture . While the average U.S. consumer may not care about crude oil itself, rising fuel prices are felt intensely. Fuel accounts for up to 30 per cent of food costs in the U.S., for example. A barrel of crude is an abstraction; gasoline and food are survival. As noted, a 90-day diesel export ban is reportedly under consideration – one that may bring relief to some parts of the country at the considerable expense of others, as well as the global market, before refinery output falls. Previous warnings about being weeks away from domestic operational minimums helped persuade Trump to accept the memorandum of understanding with Iran back in June, but the recovery during the lull in hostilities that followed was not enough to push the timeline back significantly. Now energy markets – especially for fuels like diesel – are again showing major strain. 2. Only Beijing knows how quickly and by how much China’s oil imports and fuel exports will recover. The world’s largest oil importer, China, may have done more to stabilise the global market than the U.S. as the top producer. Surprising many, Beijing tamped down its oil imports by, at the peak, 5 million barrels per day, nearly half the pre-war volume, absorbing much of the initial shock of the U.S. attack and Iran’s retaliation in the Strait of Hormuz. By reducing its imports, Beijing kept global supplies from plunging further, protected itself from a price spike and burnished its image as a responsible actor. The world is now intently watching for signs that China will ratchet its imports up again and, if so, when and by how much. A modest increase in July crude imports, once thought to reflect an uptick from the brief June reopening of Hormuz, instead continued at a comparable level in August before dipping again through 24 September. Even in August, bullish estimates continued to project China returning to near 10 million barrels, or about 80 per cent of its pre-war imports, within months. Independent, or “teapot”, refiners, accounting for about one quarter of China’s refining capacity, were scouring crude markets for cargoes as fuel export restrictions eased, though the teapots are threatened by the most recent spike in oil prices and declining domestic inventory. China’s emergence as a swing consumer has ... drawn attention to its capacity to hold down imports. Historically, oil market observers focused on spare production capacity as an important indicator of stability, but China’s emergence as a swing consumer has instead drawn attention to its capacity to hold down imports. No one outside Beijing’s innermost councils knows how long China can continue to do so, but its restraint appears to have staying power. It was heavily stockpiling before the war, so no longer doing so accounts for some of the reduction in its demand. But the rest was achieved through a combination of commercial stockpile depletion, export controls and domestic demand reduction. Estimates vary, but China probably had something like 1.2 - 1.4 billion barrels in storage at the war’s start, giving it the world’s largest reserves. It drew down this inventory by some 100-200 million largely or entirely commercial barrels into August, still leaving the state with control of perhaps up to a billion more barrels than the U.S. Its estimated onshore crude stocks were far above the five-year average in August despite recent usage. Beyond the usual government and commercial holdings, China’s 2025 Energy Law requires commercial companies to maintain Corporate Social Responsibility Reserves, in effect a commercial extension of China’s strategic reserves. Fuel export restrictions beginning in mid-March also helped conserve stocks, which Beijing relaxed on a month-by-month basis starting in July. China’s development of the world’s largest coal-to-chemicals sector and heavy investment in electrification , particularly electric vehicles and renewable energy, has also helped keep oil demand much lower than it may otherwise have been. An additional, though rapidly diminishing buffer has been Iran’s oil. Beijing invoked its 2021 blocking law for the first time in May, instructing five refineries to ignore U.S. sanctions barring them from purchasing Iranian oil, while Trump reported that President Xi Jinping told him that China would continue buying oil from Iran at their May summit in Beijing. China has indeed continued these purchases throughout the war. By late September, Iran still had full tankers beyond the U.S. blockade line, carrying a volume of oil equal to maybe a few weeks’ worth of its recent daily deliveries to China. While the U.S. is blockading Iran’s coast and has chased down its tankers in the Indian Ocean, it has not touched the floating stockpile spread across the western Pacific from near Malaysia to the Yellow Sea, presumably to avoid a standoff with China. Hence, China has been able to keep buying oil and Iran to keep selling it despite all but halting loadings since the U.S. blockade was reimposed. These continued Chinese purchases of Iranian crude also loom over any deal that the U.S. may cut with Iran. Besides the blockade, U.S. sanctions are depressing Iranian oil sales. The June memorandum of understanding briefly eased these measures, allowing Iran to resume exports. It quickly hawked its oil to a range of potential customers, but few were willing to bite because a sanctions waiver is inherently temporary (and, as events subsequently proved, quickly reversible) and many had already contracted for alternative supplies. For now, the lack of other buyers means that China in effect controls the market for Iran’s oil. For now, the lack of other buyers means that China in effect controls the market for Iran’s oil, whether shipments already on the water outside the U.S. blockade line or others awaiting export. Beijing’s decisions about whether to increase its oil imports, how much of these imports will be Iranian and, absent credible, durable sanctions relief, what price it will demand as Iran’s only buyer will continue to largely set the value of renewed Iranian oil sales. Enticing other buyers would probably take even greater discounts – before the U.S. blockade, China had been buying at $7-12 per barrel below global benchmarks. At the moment, the lack of alternative buyers also means that Beijing can just let Iran’s remaining oil outside the blockade float at sea for as long as it needs to, comfortable that others are unlikely to snap it up. All these realities leave the U.S. in an uncomfortable spot: its ability to maintain its current course could well be linked to whether China maintains its massive import reduction while not reimposing deep fuel controls. While August fuel exports were up year-on-year, Beijing is rumoured to be considering new restrictions. But whichever way China goes, the U.S. is unlikely to push it too hard on its choice. Both because of Beijing’s influence over the energy markets, and because of its proven ability to retaliate for U.S. economic coercion by withholding rare earths, Washington has not gone beyond symbolic action in trying to stop Chinese purchases of Iranian oil, just as it has not reached for comparable tools regarding China’s purchase of sanctioned Russian oil. When asked why the U.S. was not imposing secondary sanctions on those still trading with Iran, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned of the consequences if the effort moved too quickly: “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” China’s interests would seem to be best served by riding out the energy shock without rapidly and substantially raising its oil imports as long as it can comfortably do so, letting the U.S. fritter away its own oil reserves, munitions stockpiles and international reputation. Like any consumer, China does not want expensive oil and fuel, and it might be able to hold out for months, but probably not indefinitely. Beijing’s evergreen concerns about its “ Malacca dilemma ”, a vulnerability stemming from reliance on another maritime chokepoint, the Strait of Malacca, mean that it is unlikely to burn through its strategic reserves as the U.S. has done without a more urgent threat like a direct attack on its supply lines. There are already signs that China’s import recovery has begun – the question is how quickly it will progress and how far it will go. The same goes for its fuel exports, which may yet be restricted again. 3. Ukraine’s strategic achievements threaten its patrons’ energy supplies. “Diesel, diesel…diesel” was how a Ukrainian official described the subject of a late September call between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The Russia-Ukraine war is one of the places where Trump is seeking solutions for a growing fuel crisis, though Kyiv shows no sign of letting up in its drone and missile strikes on the Russian energy sector. As of early August, “ the most dangerous commercial shipping environment in the world ” was in the view of some in the shipping industry neither the Strait of Hormuz nor the Red Sea, but the Black Sea. As it strives to fend off Russia’s all-out invasion for the fifth consecutive year, increase the costs of war for Russia and encourage de-escalation before winter, Ukraine has broadened its aerial campaign to the maritime theatre, attacking hundreds of ships in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov to paralyse Russian exports as well as Crimea’s supply lines and, in effect, lock Russia out of these water bodies. This wave of attacks is part of an effort to disrupt Russia’s energy sector and thereby cut off government revenue while raising the war’s costs for the average Russian. Meanwhile, Russia has stepped up its own air war, ordering more strikes on ships linked to Ukraine as well as export facilities like ports and grain terminals, as it did earlier in the conflict. The Black Sea campaign has severely restricted both countries’ grain exports, which together typically account for more than a quarter of annual global wheat exports, as well as Russian oil shipments. Thus, as the belligerents square off, global food and energy markets are taking collateral damage. Kyiv has been increasingly successful in its maritime disruption effort as its missile and drone capabilities improve. Kyiv has been increasingly successful in its maritime disruption effort as its missile and drone capabilities improve. Meantime, while Russia’s air defences are spread ever thinner, its strikes on Ukraine are becoming more effective as Ukraine exhausts its own air defence munitions. Russia’s refinery capacity was down nearly a third by the end of July, and almost half by the end of August, as Ukraine’s attacks became more precise, hitting critical equipment that is difficult to repair. As a conservation measure, Moscow banned diesel exports in July, adding to existing restrictions on gasoline and jet fuel exports, later extending its restrictions on fuel exports and beginning to import fuel itself. These measures took more than 10 per cent of global seaborne diesel off the water, contributing to surging global prices (though Gulf diesel export losses remain much higher than Russia’s in recent months). Despite the impact its attacks are having, Russia spurned a Ukrainian offer of a Black Sea ceasefire in mid-August. Ukraine’s attacks included at least five at or near the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) terminal on the Black Sea coast, through which about a million barrels of Kazakhstan’s oil pass a day – 80 per cent of its oil exports – alongside a small volume of Russian oil. That terminal is near the Russian port of Novorossiysk, which handles a share of Russian oil exports and a larger one of its grain exports, and became the main home for the remnants of Russia’s Black Sea fleet after it was mauled by Ukraine. It is not entirely clear why Kyiv would repeatedly target the CPC terminal, given that the main consumers of Kazakh crude are European refineries , little Russian crude typically passes through the terminal – though more might be diverted this way – and the transit fees earned by Russia are modest. Whether through miscalculation or intention, the attacks certainly got Washington’s attention. Not only did the forced suspensions involve typical exports equal to about 2 per cent of global daily oil demand, but U.S. oil majors Exxon Mobil and Chevron own almost a quarter of the pipeline, and both have sizeable stakes in large oil fields in Kazakhstan. Chevron’s investment in Kazakhstan production accounts for about 12 per cent of the company’s global output, and its CEO quickly complained about Ukrainian strikes on CPC to the White House in late July. Washington soon called on Kyiv to stop firing at the CPC terminal and non-Russian ships, though the wider aerial campaign continued. The impact of Ukraine’s missile and drone strikes has been blunted by, among other things, Russia’s ability to continue routing some of its exports through other ports, such as those on the Baltic Sea. Ukraine’s focus on refineries has freed up additional Russian crude for export, with July seaborne crude exports up 26 per cent year-on-year and total crude exports remained up 12 per cent in August despite further attacks on Black Sea terminals, though the increase means little for the availability of fuel if the crude does not reach refineries with spare capacity. Yet Ukraine’s attacks still raise energy costs, and Washington connected Ukraine’s aerial campaign to energy prices in early September, suggesting that the latest U.S. push to get Russia and Ukraine to the negotiating table may be partly motivated by the growing economic fallout of Kyiv’s war effort. As fuel prices continue to surge, Washington may lean harder on Kyiv to lay off the Russian energy sector. As fuel prices continue to surge, Washington may lean harder on Kyiv to lay off the Russian energy sector, an action that would help the movement of oil and give a psychological boost to traders looking for evidence of an easing crisis. In mid-September, Trump unilaterally announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, though it was not immediately clear that Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to the arrangement and strikes on energy infrastructure continued in the following days. Trump pressed Zelenskyy again at the UN General Assembly in late September, and the Ukrainian president (with the blessing of Kyiv’s European backers) again committed to a moratorium on attacking energy and grain facilities if Russia could credibly reciprocate. Even if such a truce came to pass, however, which is in doubt, refinery repair would take time. Washington’s most potent leverage over Kyiv is probably the missile interceptors Ukraine desperately needs to shield itself from Russian attack, especially as winter approaches. Trump previously said Ukraine could produce them domestically before reneging on the offer on the same day Vance asked Ukraine to back off the CPC. Ukraine hit a Greek-run tanker that reportedly loaded Russian oil at the CPC terminal on 16 August as well as a ship engaged in CPC terminal repairs in early September. Strictly speaking, these attacks did not violate its commitment to the U.S., even if they disrupted CPC operations. In the near term, Kyiv will likely keep firing at Russian refineries and export terminals, and keep the CPC terminal in its sights as well, unless the U.S. presses Ukraine harder or a Ukraine-Russia ceasefire is reached. 4. The Houthis have moved into Bab al-Mandab. The first weeks of September brought a flurry of news from the Arabian Peninsula that roiled global energy markets. The Houthis – an Iran-backed rebel force that has been fighting a civil war with Yemen’s internationally recognised government for more than a decade – were advancing rapidly down the Red Sea coast after breaking through their Saudi-backed opponents’ lines. At the same time, drones reportedly from Iraq struck several pumping stations along Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, forcing the pipeline’s suspension ; following repairs, a partial resumption began less than two weeks later, though complete restoration could take another six weeks. That pipeline ends at the Red Sea port of Yanbu. Prior to the war, it typically accounted for less than a million barrels per day of Saudi Arabia’s oil exports. From the war’s onset through July, it was carrying 3.3-4.3 million barrels per day of Red Sea crude exports. Those numbers began dropping once the Houthis shifted their attention to Saudi Arabia in late July, before the full suspension after the pipeline was hit. Any disruption to this flow is damaging to Riyadh and alarming to the global energy market, given the possibility of large drops in Saudi oil production if repairs are not fast or alternatives are not found. Earlier in the conflict, Iran briefly knocked out a pumping station on the pipeline, but otherwise operations had been smooth until the Houthis issued a 20 July warning to shipping companies not to load or discharge cargo at Saudi Arabian ports – in effect announcing a blockade. The Houthis then stepped up their attacks on Saudi Arabia and government-aligned Yemeni forces. Like Iran in Hormuz, the Houthis appear to want to act as gatekeepers, allowing transits linked to friendly or at least non-hostile states. Strictly enforced, the Houthi blockade would end Red Sea exports, which have allowed Riyadh to reroute millions of barrels per day that would have gone through the Strait of Hormuz. Within weeks of the blockade’s announcement, Saudi Arabia’s oil exports nearly halved from late July to late August as tanker arrivals at Yanbu dropped by more than a third . The kingdom’s oil shipments through Bab al-Mandab, the narrow strait connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, fell from more than 3.5 million barrels per day in early July to near-zero in August. In response, Riyadh began sending shipments of oil through Hormuz on “shuttle runs” (see below). Yet a number of ships still appear able to safely pass by Houthi-controlled territory, like those connected with Russia and China, even when the China-affiliated tankers are carrying Saudi crude. The group also reportedly told Washington that it had no intention of attacking U.S. shipping and had previously informed the EU that it would refrain from targeting European ships. Like Iran in Hormuz, the Houthis appear to want to act as gatekeepers, allowing transits linked to friendly or at least non-hostile states, rather than ending all trade through the Red Sea. The Houthis demonstrated their ability to threaten shipping in their previous Red Sea campaign , launched after Israel began its Gaza offensive in response to the 7 October 2023 attacks by Hamas in southern Israel. Houthi fire at Israel and later Red Sea shipping prompted two spates of U.S. bombardment in 2024 and 2025, alongside airstrikes by Israel. These efforts did considerable damage in Yemen, but they neither crippled the Houthis nor forced them to cut a deal with Saudi Arabia or the Yemeni government. The rebels agreed to a ceasefire with the U.S. in May 2025, though the deal applied only to U.S. naval forces and U.S.-affiliated merchant vessels. Their Red Sea attacks in that phase of hostilities ended in September 2025. Nevertheless, their actions left a mark that has endured into the present conflict. When the Houthis again began firing at Saudi-affiliated tankers on 23 July, traffic through the Red Sea was down some 60 per cent from before 7 October 2023. A number of things have changed, however, since the 2023-2025 campaign. Then, the Houthis included much of the world’s commercial fleet on their ever-expanding target list. This time around, when they were late entrants into the conflict, they have hit comparatively few ships. Instead, they have focused on their domestic adversaries and infrastructure inside Saudi Arabia, such as with repeated strikes on the Jizan refinery, one of the kingdom’s largest. That refinery showed no shipments in August. As with Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refining, these attacks may prompt Saudi Arabia to export more crude oil because it is unable to refine the latter given the reduction in capacity. At the same time, the new escalation has expanded the battlefield. On 10 September, the Houthis reportedly seized Mokha , the government’s only major Red Sea port, and several Red Sea islands, followed the next day by the remainder of the coast, including Perim, a key island in Bab al-Mandab. Mokha was previously a launchpad for the government’s efforts to interdict Houthi supply chains that now criss-cross the Red Sea. Perim may be an even greater prize, because it enables tighter control of Bab al-Mandab and Red Sea traffic than could be achieved from Houthi-administered territory farther north. That said, taking these areas is one thing; effectively weaponising them under fire is another. To exert greater influence in these waters, the Houthis would need to deploy the right capabilities throughout their new coastal and island territory. The Houthis’ southward blitz suggests that their maritime interests lie in controlling Bab al-Mandab and much of the Red Sea rather than sealing off the Saudi Arabian coastline. If the group can hold the islands, cities and flat, hard-to-defend plains of the western coast – likely by taking territory within the Kahboub mountains further inland – then they will have stolen a march on not only Yemen’s government, but also Saudi Arabia and the U.S. They will have enhanced their ability to project power in the strait and the Red Sea overall at a critical juncture in the U.S. war with Iran. The Houthis may have gained greater leverage over the kingdom’s Red Sea exports, but by doing so against the backdrop of the East-West Pipeline attack, the group has helped force those exports back east. In particular, the suspension of the pipeline immediately compelled Riyadh to either curtail production exceeding domestic consumption once storage was filled or to heavily increase the volume of oil it sends through the Strait of Hormuz under threat of attack by Iran. It quickly chose the latter, and its oil exports through Hormuz rose by over 2 million barrels per day by mid-September, or around half of the lost exports through Yanbu, and appeared to keep climbing thereafter. Though the pipeline is being quickly repaired, with roughly half its flow reportedly restored as of mid-September, using Hormuz to send oil to the Gulf region’s typical Asian customers is a much more efficient route than going through Yanbu and around the Cape of Good Hope to avoid the Houthis’ missiles and drones. There are few options for quickly reopening the Red Sea, anyway. Washington previously failed to restore freedom of navigation there through serial bombardment of Houthi positions, and its sanctions against the group and its supply chains are already severe. It has reportedly met with Houthi representatives in Oman to lower tensions, and it is reluctant to more deeply involve itself in Yemen as its war with Iran proceeds. So far, the only U.S. response to the Houthis’ latest territorial gains and salvoes against Saudi Arabia ... has been to increase intelligence and targeting support. So far, the only U.S. response to the Houthis’ latest territorial gains and salvoes against Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh itself, has been to increase intelligence and targeting support . Despite having elevated Riyadh to the status of a major non-NATO ally in 2025, Trump has reportedly rebuffed Saudi requests to strike the Houthis. Diverting naval and air assets from protecting shipping in the Strait of Hormuz or maintaining the blockade on Iran would benefit Tehran, with no promise of success against the Houthis. Trump could change his mind, but for the time being Saudi Arabia has been looking elsewhere for aid. It has yet to receive concrete assistance, however, whether from regional states like Egypt, the other parties in the newly formed Mecca Joint Defence Agreement alliance (Pakistan and Türkiye) or the new, thirteen-state Red Sea coalition . Several European countries either were already supporting Saudi Arabia – such as Greece, with its air defence deployment in the vicinity of Yanbu since 2021 – or have pledged other help, like the UK’s offer of what it characterises as “defensive” air-to-air refuelling. With no obvious options for finding barrels of oil and fuels elsewhere, the Houthis’ disruption of Saudi Red Sea oil exports is likely to continue forcing more exports through Hormuz via the “shuttle runs” discussed below, with all the risk that entails, for the foreseeable future. 5. The contest over the Strait of Hormuz has intensified. A top concern for global markets is if Gulf oil can find ways out of the Middle East despite Iran’s attacks on shipping and its neighbours. Two major pipelines bypass the strait, the damaged East-West pipeline and the UAE’s Habshan-Fujaira line that ends just east of the Strait of Hormuz. That UAE line is both operating and expanding , with work on a parallel line that will raise capacity from 1.8 to 3 million barrels per day more than halfway complete under the country’s “ Zero Hormuz ” strategy. “Shuttle runs” through Hormuz, despite Iran’s attacks, have increasingly succeeded in getting oil out through a lane along Oman’s coast in the southern half of the strait – though the risks and costs are significant. These runs account for most of the oil moving out of the strait. The battle over the southern corridor is a critical test of Iran’s capacity for preventing or raising the costs of shipping as well as the resolve of the U.S. and its Gulf allies, particularly the UAE. Finding a Way Out From the beginning of March into early May, the flow of non-Iranian crude fell to an average of 500,000 barrels per day – a far cry from the nearly 14 million barrels of non-Iranian crude and condensate just before the war, but not quite zero. Iran’s early attacks were enough to bring shipping to a near standstill as insurers, shipowners, charterers and seafarers were all wary of transiting the strait. Over time, as the financial and strategic costs have mounted and diplomacy has faltered, risk tolerance has grown, at least for oil (and double-hulled oil tankers that can weather a measure of damage). Scarcely a month into the war, oil tankers began transiting the strait seemingly without Iran’s permission. Those willing to risk Iranian attack are making short back-and-forth runs across the strait using the southern corridor, which, unlike its northern counterpart, is outside Iran’s territorial waters. A senior Gulf official suggested to Crisis Group that, in effect, the strait was open for those with sufficient nerve. These vessels are travelling with their location broadcasting turned off – or sailing “dark” – typically at night (though daylight slots were recently added) and often during periods when satellites are not capturing images of traffic on the route. The “shuttle runs” take place under U.S. protection that may involve a mix of aircraft and drones, though not escort by manned ships. There are also at least some U.S. military personnel operating within the strait. Oil is then transferred to more risk-averse ships waiting east of the strait in the Gulf of Oman. This model amounts to several oil producers – and a handful of shipping companies – assuming most of the hazards of transiting Hormuz. They charge a premium for doing so. The U.S. claimed that by early August oil flows were approaching pre-war volumes through the shuttle runs and bypass pipelines, with almost 9 million barrels per day going through Hormuz. Leading energy and freight analysts were dismissive of the U.S. government figure at that time. (U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright later clarified that the number was from all “waterborne routes”, suggesting a more expansive definition than some other Hormuz-specific tallies.) The true figure was probably closer to 6 million barrels per day for crude as of mid-August, though estimates vary, and a number of oil traders claimed it was between 6 and 8 million by the end of the month. To be sure, counting outbound barrels is as much art as science. It is complicated by ships going dark, even though industry estimates also draw on other signs of export activity like changes in Gulf oil storage, ship-to-ship transfers outside Hormuz and import data from oil buyers. It often takes days to weeks to get this information, meaning that early estimates are often later revised. There are a variety of reasons for such discrepancies (like double-counting ships or barrels, not discounting very small ships or not differentiating between crude and products). Aside from disagreement on the overall number of barrels, most observers concurred by early September that the volume was trending upward prior to the latest escalation, which may have briefly held outflow below 7 million barrels per day. The mid-September addition of more Saudi barrels reportedly brought crude exports through Hormuz near or back to the volume seen before the war, which has already helped lower global crude prices because of diminishing fears of further Saudi production cuts. Saudi Arabia has committed to maintaining its increased use of the strait, having sold almost 100 million barrels for delivery to Asian buyers in October and November, reportedly all via Hormuz. The growing volume of crude and products on shuttle runs is nearing the operational limits of regional capacity to service the ship-to-ship transfers that enable the runs. Combined with bypass pipelines, the gap between pre-war crude exports through Hormuz and outbound crude by late September may have been down to around one fifth or less . At the same time, the growing volume of crude and products on shuttle runs is nearing the operational limits of regional capacity to service the ship-to-ship transfers that enable the runs. Recent outflow may reflect a ceiling, or even have surpassed the ceiling, of what can then be moved beyond the U.S. blockade line by more risk-averse shipping, contributing to a growing bottleneck in the Gulf of Oman. Getting even more oil and fuel out of the southern corridor has already started to require longer distance shuttle runs, farther into the Indian Ocean, that increase costs or may otherwise force more crude back to the Red Sea. Yet with energy concerns increasingly shifting to fuels, even a few more million barrels of oil per day may not be enough to lessen Washington’s energy woes – or bring down spiking costs – unless Gulf Arab refineries are repaired or return to full capacity and are thus in a position to export. Some of those refineries are still under direct attack, and refined product exports remain down by around half to three quarters compared to pre-war figures because of refinery damage and a lack of means of export. These products are not moving on shuttle runs at scale, with movement through Hormuz still down around 80 per cent compared to before the war. Risky Business Shuttle runs are first and foremost about strategic concerns. The U.S. and the Gulf states feel compelled to find ways to move oil because they need to contest Iran’s claims to the strait and these exports are (in the case of the Gulf states) essential for national revenue. There is also a collective desire to protect oil infrastructure from damage due to prolonged shutdowns. Every convoy that makes it through the southern corridor weakens Iran’s hand, and so, to an extent, the cost of the transit is a secondary concern. Private companies tend to be motivated by skyrocketing tanker rates – the highest in the history of the supertanker market and at times surpassing $1 million per day for Hormuz transits, about double a month ago – alongside huge pay increases for seafarers and heightened oil prices. The players in shuttle runs and other dark oil transits have ranged from national oil companies like the UAE’s ADNOC to trading houses like Mercuria . ADNOC became a driving force behind the shuttle runs, even moving the exports of other Gulf producers , alongside the Korean-Italian owned shipping company Sinokor and a handful of others. ADNOC’s leading role is a demonstration of the varying risk tolerances among the Gulf states and Iraq. Other Gulf state companies like Saudi Arabia’s Bahri have also gotten involved , though at least one Gulf official has suggested that more states need to participate to further undermine Iranian claims and raise the costs if they continue attacks. Specialised crews commanding substantial wage premiums are also increasingly used for these runs, with rotations occurring after the vessel passes through the strait. The transits are expensive but not yet cost-prohibitive, though more successful Iranian attacks could change that. The transits are expensive but not yet cost-prohibitive, though more successful Iranian attacks could change that. Sinokor was at one point offering six months of extra pay to sailors to make a single shuttle run, while war-risk insurance was around 10 per cent of a ship’s value in early August – up from 0.25 per cent before the war – and rates specific to shuttle runs could be higher. It is also possible that the UAE (which was exporting more oil than pre-war in recent months ) and other shuttle operators will begin struggling to find tankers and crews for them as Iran damages those used for shuttling. Vortexa reported in August that only a few dozen tankers were making most of the shuttle runs. The largest, two-million-barrel tankers were handling about 60 per cent of shuttle activity. Every tanker that Iran disables thus makes a sizeable dent in the collective capacity for these runs, given the difficulty of rapidly replacing tankers that can cost hundreds of millions apiece. The costs of making these shuttle runs under duress are high enough, and the war has so distorted the global tanker market, that rising shipping costs are affecting routes far away from the Middle East. Indeed, U.S. crude exports have dipped recently in part because the cost of export is becoming prohibitive . A sustained increase of Saudi export of oil through the southern corridor via shuttle runs would, by one estimate , require a nearly 50 per cent increase in participating supertankers under certain conditions. Meanwhile, Iran is still trying to stop transit through Hormuz, with fresh ship attacks toward the end of September. On 24 August, Iran’s recently created Persian Gulf Strait Authority published a (largely ignored ) list of 45 ships it claimed had violated its protocols for the strait, with most of the listed ships involved in shuttle runs. That list grew in September to 77 ships as Iran stepped up tanker attacks, while the U.S. launched its own “ tanker-for-tanker ” policy by pledging to hit one or more tankers for each one struck by Iran, beginning with strikes on two vessels linked to Iran’s state tanker company. Eight tankers – five of them laden, a major shift by the U.S. – were hit from 5 through 8 September. These U.S. strikes were followed by Iranian attacks on U.S. warships and other military assets in the region. U.S. officials have told Crisis Group that the shuttle runs prove Tehran cannot control the strait, in part because it often does not know when they are taking place. But while there are clearly limits to Iran’s capacity, they should not be overstated. Given how narrow the strait is and the slowing pace of tanker transits and ship-to-ship transfers (among other things), it seems unlikely that Iran has ever been wholly ignorant of the shuttle runs. It may not spot every ship, but it surely knows the southern corridor is handling a greater volume of traffic – whether from open-source satellite imagery showing the increasing number of ship-to-ship transfers east of the strait or the dhows and other small craft (including Iran-flagged fishing and other vessels) regularly moving in the strait, as the U.S. itself acknowledged in mid-August. Iran also continues to curtail other shipping, even as it loses its grip on the passage of oil and other tankers. The southern corridor is a risky oil route, not a functioning all-commodity trade route. Even as oil moves through it, cargo shipping has not returned to the strait to the same extent, including other products like liquefied natural gas (LNG). Container ship traffic was down 94 per cent as of September. Exports of other critical commodities like sulfur and nitrogenous fertiliser were still down about 90 per cent and 70 per cent, respectively, from January to August. This overall lack of maritime trade continues to strain the Gulf economies even as they steadily increase oil exports. Still on the Escalation Ladder? The risk of a new round of escalation centred on the Strait of Hormuz remains. Forcing the suspension of the East-West Pipeline was an achievement for Iran and its allies, but it is not a clear strategic win on its own – even setting aside the speed with which it is being repaired. Instead, the suspension set up a new test of capabilities and wills in Hormuz, as Saudi Arabia shifts millions of barrels back to the strait. If Iran does not counter increased flow through Hormuz, the temporary blocking of Saudi Arabia’s alternative export route will have achieved only a considerable expansion in southern corridor throughput. This gambit puts more of Saudi Arabia’s crude exports back into Iran’s field of fire, but it also raises the costs for Iran of failing to bar passage through the southern corridor because it would further demonstrate that Tehran can no longer enforce its claims upon the strait. If instead Iran is willing and able to suppress southern corridor transit and strand even more Gulf oil, potentially forcing a large reduction in Saudi production, then it will have notched a major, if not necessarily permanent, strategic achievement. In this way, good news for energy markets today – more tankers through Hormuz – may herald new risks of Iranian escalation tomorrow. Indeed, further escalation by Tehran now would fit a familiar pattern. Past spikes in Iran’s attacks on shipping have typically followed efforts to decisively shift traffic from Iran’s northern corridor to the southern corridor. For example, Iranian attacks jumped following the 3 May U.S. announcement of Project Freedom (an effort to guide ships through the southern corridor). They also increased after the 18 June declaration by a naval coalition under U.S. leadership that Hormuz was open and the southern corridor mine-free. They went up again in early July as traffic in the southern corridor surged, diminishing transits through Iran’s corridor. These July attacks caused a short, sharp dip in the volume of crude oil passing through the strait, though they did not stop shuttle runs from proceeding. If U.S. protection proves too effective within the corridor even as more oil moves through it, then Iran may decide to widen the scope of its targeting beyond the corridor itself. If U.S. protection proves too effective within the corridor even as more oil moves through it, then Iran may decide to widen the scope of its targeting beyond the corridor itself. It may strike more ships at or near regional ports, as it apparently did with a laden tanker in Iraq’s territorial waters on 9 September, or hit those engaged in ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, which it has not done to date. Its announcement of a planned “restricted zone” stretching from within the Gulf to the U.S. blockade line and its growing list of “sanctioned” ships point to these risks. Such measures could force ship-to-ship transfers farther from Iran’s shores, raising costs and transit times. Costly U.S. overwatch is presently concentrated on the southern corridor itself, but ensuring blanket protection of tankers from Iraq’s coast out to the Arabian Sea could strain the capacity of the stretched U.S. forces, particularly since Iranian attacks have largely pushed U.S. troops out of the nearest military bases. In early September, as Iran intensified its fire at shuttle runs, the U.S. had already reduced its air defence coverage to a few daily time slots, down from a longer overnight period, in an effort to make its protection more sustainable and because, according to the U.S. military, “darkness has not proven to be the most secure time of day”. Yet it is not a foregone conclusion that Iran will escalate. It could show restraint for several, overlapping reasons: it may be satisfied with where prices of crude and especially fuels are hovering, observing the headaches afflicting the Trump administration as the November elections approach; it may want to calibrate rather than maximise – for now – the pressure on Saudi Arabia and other neighbours, leaving room for negotiations; and it may be under Chinese pressure to not escalate too far, including because of the risks to China’s own energy supply. Indeed, China reportedly requested that Tehran lean on the Houthis to de-escalate, following an entreaty from Riyadh to Beijing. Iran has consistently sought control of movement, and not a prolonged end to transits – now likely only achievable through comprehensive, hard-to-reverse mining of the entire strait, not only the original central corridor – which would leave Tehran with less room to negotiate. Tehran has at times shown more pragmatism than would be expected if its public statements about closure were literal policy – with some similarity to Washington’s exaggerated claims of the strait's openness or U.S. control. Instead, Iran has selectively permitted ships, crews and cargo to pass, depending on its immediate goals, making its efforts more akin to the checkpoints ubiquitous in conflicts around the world than a blockade. Its approach to Qatari LNG shipments is illustrative – it has at times permitted , attacked or otherwise blocked these transits depending on its objectives at that moment and Qatar’s engagement with Iranian unilateral arrangements for the strait, despite Doha’s role as a mediator. Arguably, the heavier toll is not financial, but strategic, as its adversaries chafe at accepting a newly imposed maritime order. If Iran manages to curtail shuttle runs, including by incapacitating a large number of tankers, it could reclaim greater leverage over time. The battle for Hormuz is not the Battle of the Atlantic during World War II, when the U.S. government and its allies along with their private sectors were willing to absorb huge losses of merchant ships. The private sector generally has little interest in a direct role in an attritional maritime campaign. Even state oil companies like ADNOC will have their limits. Conversely, for the U.S. and its partners to achieve their goals via shuttle runs, the latter would have to become so effective that – together with intense pressure on Iran’s economy – they lead Tehran to agree to lower its demands to reach a deal, at which point regular traffic would resume and a durable revival of Gulf refining would proceed. At a minimum, that appears far off. A Crude Compromise? Iran may still be willing to find a modus vivendi with its neighbours concerning Hormuz, especially if it is unable to deter traffic through the strait absent significant escalation. From Iran’s perspective, negotiations should be focused on the conditions under which movement takes place. A short-term compromise on the strait – such as the option under discussion in which the original central corridor is in effect divided between Iran and Oman, ensuring movement through the territorial waters of each – would help move crude and other commodities without the constant threat of attack, as the memorandum of understanding fleetingly did in June. But Iran’s initial asking price for Hormuz stability – recognition of its expansive maritime claims – is too high for other littoral states, even if the alternative is that oil exports remain under threat and other seaborne trade stays near rock bottom. (The Gulf states are engaging with the Oman-Iran track on Hormuz, though a 14 September meeting was postponed and has yet to be rescheduled.) There are further considerations that could shape efforts to reach a working arrangement. One is that any new agreement would be politically meaningless and likely short-lived in the absence of a wider deal involving the U.S. Another is that any arrangement for the strait that contravenes international legal protections for freedom of navigation, as Iran’s actions are widely seen to do, both implicates the rights of third-party states and could set a precedent that risks undermining global commerce. It is therefore likely to face high levels of international pushback. A related dilemma is that an arrangement intended to be temporary could remain indefinitely if negotiations on a new, permanent mechanism stall. Until a Hormuz-specific or a wider agreement is reached, the U.S. and Gulf producers have little choice but to continue the shuttle runs, which are as much freedom of navigation operations as economic activity. At the same time, Iran continues to occasionally crash drones and missiles into the bridges, engine rooms and hulls of ships – even at the cost of retaliatory U.S. strikes on its own tanker fleet and military installations. Oil is moving, but its price is still elevated. Diesel prices continue to reach new highs, especially in the U.S. The status quo is painful, and while both sides have incentives to find a way out – whether through inflicting more pain or through another attempt at negotiation, each may keep waiting for the other to blink. Diplomacy is the Best Bet for Restoring Affordability So, what will settle the energy markets? None of the first four factors listed above is likely to break in the direction of durable stability. Venezuela probably cannot quickly deliver major relief for a U.S. running short of strategic reserves and facing unprecedented diesel prices. China’s oil imports have begun rising (which puts upward pressure on crude prices), and its fuel export controls easing (which puts downward pressure on fuel prices), though these mixed trends both face headwinds. Russia’s refinery output and fuel exports continue to suffer under Ukraine’s aerial onslaught, which has also disrupted oil loadings at Russia’s Black Sea terminals. The Houthis are in Bab al-Mandab and pushing into the mountain range needed to secure their new coastal territory. Considerable uncertainty hangs over all these theatres, but events there mostly bode ill for fuel prices. One bright spot from the U.S. perspective is the shuttle runs through the Strait of Hormuz, where more oil has been moving over the last two months. That is an achievement, but for the increased flow to have a large impact on fuel prices, the crude oil needs to find its way to refineries with spare capacity and then that refinery output needs to be exported. There are few such destinations outside the Middle East. China is chief among them – and it will look to its own declining fuel inventories first. The status quo may also be unsustainable, as Washington runs the risk of a major Iranian escalation or a politically intolerable fuel crisis. On the other hand, Iran may be overestimating its leverage over the strait (and, by extension, the U.S.), leading it to overplay its hand in negotiations. In late September, Iran offered to reopen Hormuz as part of a phased deal. But an unblocked strait is not the incentive it was in June, because of the southern corridor’s success to date. Trump rejected the proposal, letting it be known that he expected U.S. military action to escalate after midterm elections. The export ban Trump is entertaining may temporarily drive down consumer prices in parts of the U.S., but it will cause prices to spike elsewhere. Nor would an unblocked strait – on its own – be the solution for rising diesel prices and other refined products that are eating away at paychecks in the U.S. and elsewhere. Here the problem can only be addressed by bringing capacity back online – and Washington has few levers within its reach to achieve this end. Most directly, it could lean harder into efforts to negotiate an end to the war; more indirectly, it could make a more serious investment in diplomacy to temper or halt the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. Such options would not bring instantaneous relief, either, given the time it will take for damaged or shuttered refineries to resume operations and for their output to reach destinations with high prices. The export ban Trump is entertaining may temporarily drive down consumer prices in parts of the U.S., but it will cause prices to spike elsewhere – especially in Latin America and Europe. Its domestic effects also may well prove disappointing because, faced with a sudden drop in demand once cut off from the global market, U.S. refineries will produce less fuel. The bottom line is that neither side has a whip hand when it comes to bending the markets to their will, not least because neither has control or complete influence over key outside actors – including China, the Houthis, the Gulf states, Russia and Ukraine – when it comes to affecting the world’s refining capacity. As U.S. reserves dwindle and prices rise, the status quo leaves Iran and the U.S. under mounting pressure, with the Trump administration feeling political pain and Tehran groaning under mounting economic stress. Yet it is not clear if either has fully committed to reaching a near-term diplomatic off-ramp. Absent such a deal, the road ahead will be rocky. A prolonged standoff between the U.S. and Iran promises to bring economic hardship to both even if it does not trigger a resumption of all-out war. But there is also a chance that it brings both – with an extended period of uncertainty simply the prelude to another major escalation. The UN described the attack as one of the deadliest in the state since the 2021 coup. The Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine group, vowed on Tuesday to take “retaliatory measures” against those responsible. The strikes came amid a military counter-offensive launched in early September on several fronts in and around Rakhine to retake territory from the Arakan Army. It has made little headway, says Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean. The market raid was likely intended to punish civilians and disrupt trade and governance in Arakan Army-held areas of Rakhine. U.S. - IRAN U.S. and Iranian negotiators held indirect talks on the UN General Assembly’s sidelines to end a conflict now in its eighth month. On 26 September, U.S. President Donald Trump said he had rejected an Iranian ceasefire proposal but continued to make counteroffers. On Wednesday, Trump warned of further military action, saying: “We blow them up or make a deal”. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says prospects for a breakthrough appear slim: Tehran proposes reopening the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the U.S. lifting its blockade of Iranian ports and releasing Iranian assets. Washington believes it has overcome Iran’s efforts to restrict shipping while continuing to weaken the Iranian economy. Tehran also wants to defer nuclear issues to subsequent talks; Washington seeks concessions up front. Fear of escalation could keep the door to engagement open, but significant gaps over substance and sequencing remain. YEMEN Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and their allies intensified this week, including around Taiz, a city in the middle of the country, where the rebels have been seeking to cut the road link with Aden on the southern coast. Taiz is home to more than 2 million people, many of whom have been displaced from other parts of Yemen. Meanwhile, the World Health Organization warned that Yemen’s health system was nearing “breaking point” amid mounting casualties. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says Houthi success around Taiz could help consolidate the group’s gains along the Red Sea coast. Diplomacy faces substantial obstacles: the Houthis are unlikely to accept de-escalation without tangible concessions from Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government, while Riyadh may seek limited battlefield gains before mediation. 25 September 2026 SOUTH SUDAN President Salva Kiir dissolved South Sudan’s transitional unity government Tuesday, three months before elections scheduled for 22 December, dismantling key power-sharing institutions established under the 2018 peace agreement. Following a hurriedly passed amendment to the National Elections Act, Kiir dismissed all five vice presidents, including his long-time rival First Vice President Riek Machar, and installed a caretaker government composed entirely of loyalists. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the changes allow Kiir to concentrate authority in his hands. Greater control of state institutions could help him retain power, through either a stage-managed election or a delay that prolongs his administration. The resulting political exclusion risks provoking greater conflict in an already deeply fractured country. UNITED NATIONS World leaders met this week in New York for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. Crisis Group expert Daniel Forti says the week’s events proved that states still value the UN as a forum for discussing global concerns, even if common ground between them remains elusive. Some countries expect the next Secretary-General to single-handedly get the UN back on track and provide solutions for crises around the world. That attitude is short-sighted. The UN needs the conviction of its members to tackle global risks from deadly conflict to artificial intelligence. Whether states choose to work together – or continue down the path of international fragmentation – will determine whether the next decade at the UN is defined by diplomacy or disorder. U.S. - CHINA President Donald Trump hosted Chinese leader Xi Jinping for a state visit in Washington this week. Xi touted their personal rapport, called for “healthy” bilateral competition “within bounds” and argued that U.S.-China cooperation is needed to address most global challenges. Crisis Group expert Ali Wyne says the summit’s outcome was modest: the two leaders agreed to extend by two months the trade truce that they blessed in Busan, South Korea last October; it was due to expire on 10 November. They do not appear to have made a breakthrough on managing cross-strait ties, spurring diplomacy to end the U.S.-Iran war or erecting guardrails around artificial intelligence. China’s readout called on the U.S. to “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’”, incorrectly but provocatively implying that the U.S. had changed its longstanding position (that it “does not support” that outcome). 18 September 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Protesters streamed into the streets of Kinshasa Tuesday to decry the government’s proposals to change the constitution by popular referendum. One person was killed in clashes with police who intervened to stop the marchers from reaching parliament. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says the government’s main aim in trying to alter the constitution is to revise the clause imposing a two-term limit on presidents, thereby allowing the incumbent Félix Tshisekedi to stand for a third term. Tshisekedi is keen to hold the referendum soon, despite the opposition, because he senses that the country’s political balance has tilted in his favour. Going ahead with this vote may prove unwise, however, even if it comes off fairly smoothly. It may produce an illusion of political stability that, in turn, deflects attention from urgent tasks like reducing poverty among ordinary Congolese and taming the interlinked wars raging in the eastern provinces. MALI Algerian Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb visited Bamako Monday in the latest sign of rapprochement between Algeria and Mali, whose relations had deteriorated badly in recent years. Crisis Group expert Jean-Hervé Jezequel says the thaw is welcome news for the Malian authorities. Bamako has been struggling to contain an insurgency linked to al-Qaeda, Jamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), which killed 50 Malian soldiers in its latest attack on an army base last week. JNIM has lately allied with northern separatists who have also been fighting the Malian army. Historically, Algiers has been an important mediator between Bamako and northern armed groups. The warming of Algeria-Mali relations raises hopes that it might again play such a role, though maybe a more limited one given the Malian authorities’ increasingly sovereignist mindset. It could nevertheless help mitigate the conflict that has torn at Mali since 2012. PHILIPPINES Regional parliamentary elections took place on Monday in the Bangsamoro, the swathe of the southern Philippines that won autonomy in 2019 as part of a 2014 peace agreement between Manila and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). At least five people were killed and twenty injured during the vote, though violence was less widespread than feared, with incidents concentrated in a few locations. No party secured an absolute majority, meaning that politicians will likely need to form a coalition. The elections were a big step forward for the Bangsamoro peace process, with all eyes now on a crucial meeting between national government and MILF delegations to discuss gaps in fulfilling the 2014 accord’s terms. 11 September 2026 IRAN The International Atomic Energy Agency referred Iran to the UN Security Council Wednesday for breaching its nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first time in twenty years the organisation has taken such a step. LEBANON Israel stepped up its attacks in southern Lebanon over the weekend with strikes that killed nearly 30 people and wounded dozens more. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Israel’s lethal escalation could continue, unless it faces strong pressure from the U.S., its most important ally, to desist.
