Regarding the exorbitant amount of the fine, al-Jamri said: “It would be difficult for anyone in Bahrain to pay, whether they had a case against them or not. A salary in Bahrain might be 350 dinars [a month], yet you’re asking me to pay installments of 375 dinars [every month] for two years.” As of October 5, Bahraini authorities have continued to pursue arrests for others from the 33 people convicted in 2016 and released in 2024, based on reports from some of those who authorities have contacted. “Bahrain’s government is going after former political prisoners released by royal pardon, giving them a difficult choice: pay huge fines or go back to prison,” said Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei, advocacy director at the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy. “The EU, UK, and US rushed to applaud Bahrain for releasing political prisoners. They should now speak out and call on Bahrain to cease targeting those who were released.”

Blogger Jailed for Four Years in Uzbekistan. Blogger Sirojiddin Adilov’s October 5 conviction on dubious extortion and fraud charges raises serious questions about fair trial standards in Uzbekistan, as well as the government’s commitment to upholding freedom of expression. Click to expand Image Sirojiddin Adilov, September 2026. © 2026 Abdurakhmon Tashanov A criminal court sentenced Adilov—who ran “Sirojiddin Media,” a YouTube channel with over 915,000 subscribers—to four years in a prison colony for committing extortion in the case of one individual and fraud in the case of two others. The court also ordered that he pay a total of 75 million Som in damages (approximately US $6370). The court explicitly noted that Adilov was not prosecuted in connection with his social media activities. Yet, Adilov’s arrest in March 2026 came just several months after he reported on a case of abuse of power in law enforcement, raising concerns that he may have been targeted for his critical reporting. The human rights organization Ezgulik reported on multiple procedural violations in Adilov’s case, including authorities’ refusal to allow Adilov to choose his own lawyer in pretrial detention proceedings and a warrantless police search of Adilov’s apartment and vehicle. The head of Ezgulik, Abdurakhman Tashanov, who monitored Adilov’s trial, informed Human Rights Watch that none of the individuals who filed complaints against Adilov provided substantiating evidence to support their claims. Tashanov also pointed out that from the time of the alleged incidents of fraud and extortion, it took the complainants over three years to file a complaint. Adilov’s “Sirojiddin Media” reported in 2025 on the efforts of a school principal from the Fergana region, Gulirano Kosimova, to hold accountable police officers who had beat her and made her strip naked on camera as part of an apparent set up to frame another official. In late November 2025, Kosimova won her case and a Fergana district criminal court convicted a district police chief and his deputy, sentencing them to four years in a prison colony. Adilov’s sentencing comes amidst increasing restrictions on freedom of expression in Uzbekistan. Authorities should stop prosecuting bloggers and others on dubious extortion charges and for non-violent offenses such as “insulting the president online.” Sirojiddin Adilov was entitled to a fair trial and should get a fair and impartial appeals hearing that respects due process and is capable of reviewing both the procedural aspects and evidence base of his conviction.

US: Deportations to African Countries Not Their Own. Click to expand Image “An ICE agent told me to sign for deportation to Chad. I refused . . . The ICE agent said, ‘I don’t care, I’m going to sign it myself.’ . . . I said, ‘I’m going to talk to my lawyer,’ but he said, ‘It’s too late.’ . . . I don’t know what happened, maybe later they changed their minds, because we ended up in Cameroon. . . . Even before we got on the plane, we asked where we were going, and they told us, ‘You’ll find out when you arrive.’” – Tesfay T., 35, an Ethiopian man deported to Cameroon. © 2026 John Holmes for Human Rights Watch The United States has sent more than 500 people whom it cannot deport to their own countries, because of the danger they would face there, to various countries in Africa where they have no connections, without giving them a meaningful chance to contest their removals to these countries.Some of the people have been detained upon arrival. Many, if not most, have been left with no practical option but to return to their home countries regardless of the harm they face there.The United States should stop deporting asylum seekers and refugees to third countries that lack the capacity to provide full and fair asylum procedures, and these countries should refuse to receive people under these conditions. (Washington, DC) – The Trump administration is sending hundreds of people who can’t be deported to their own countries, because of the danger they would face, to African countries where they have no connections, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today. Many have been left with no practical option but to return to their home countries regardless of the harm they face there. October 8, 2026 “To Scare People” US Expulsions of Third-Country Nationals to Countries in Africa Download the full report in English Appendix I: Third-Country Deportations by the Numbers Appendix II: Response Letters from IOM The 125-page report, “‘To Scare People’: US Expulsions of Third-Country Nationals to Countries in Africa,” documents that US authorities denied the more than 500 people transferred to third countries a meaningful chance to contest their removals or to articulate their fears of being removed to these countries. Some countries arbitrarily detained people they had accepted, and some have sent people onward to the risk of persecution or torture in their home countries, violating the international law principle of nonrefoulement. “Deporting people to countries where they have never set foot is part of a US policy designed to cause human suffering as a means to deter migration,” said Michael Garcia Bochenek, interim US program director at Human Rights Watch. “Because the US government uses these agreements to shirk its responsibilities and to deprive people of their due process rights, the African governments that have entered into these agreements should terminate or suspend them.” Human Rights Watch researchers conducted remote and in some cases in-person interviews between February and July 2026 with 24 third-country nationals transferred from the United States to 6 countries in Africa: Cameroon, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini, and South Sudan. Some of the people sent to these countries face the prospect of persecution and other serious harm in the receiving countries. The United States sent at least a dozen people who identified as lesbian, gay, bisexual, or transgender (LGBT) to African states that criminalize same-sex relations or public same-sex romantic conduct. These included refugees who had been granted protection in the United States based on the likelihood they would be persecuted in their home countries because of their sexual orientation or gender identity. Their deportation trapped them in situations in which it was neither safe to return home nor possible to obtain effective protection in the third country. Click to expand Image Graphic © 2026 Human Rights Watch The people interviewed consistently described abusive treatment during their flights from the United States, during which they were shackled, sometimes for 18 hours or more, and received little or no information about their destination. How the third-country nationals deported from the United States are treated upon arrival varies from country to country. In some cases, people being deported have not had access to needed medications or treatments for ongoing serious medical conditions. A 35-year-old man from Ethiopia who had fled to the United States after being imprisoned and tortured in his home country had been denied asylum because he had crossed the border irregularly, but a US immigration judge granted him “withholding of removal,” a bar on returning him to Ethiopia because of the likelihood he would again be tortured there. He said that when he refused to sign a voluntary departure form to send him to Chad, an ICE agent signed it himself. “We were chained and handcuffed, legs, hands, stomach” on the flight, he said. “We could not stand up. When I had to use the bathroom, they didn’t even take off the chains.” After arriving in Cameroon, he had repeated visits from representatives of the International Organization for Migration. “Every time they come, they ask the same thing: ‘Do you want to go back to your home?’ But every time I tell them, ‘I’m not going. Stop asking me that. I don’t want to die,’” he told Human Rights Watch in March. The threat of removal to a third country is part of the Trump administration’s policy of mass deportations. In practice, third-country removals have been used to frighten people into leaving before being thrown into the downward spiral of detention and deportation to unknown destinations. An unnamed US official told the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations that in fact, the purpose of third-country national transfers was to terrorize: “With countries like Palau or Eswatini, the point is that the Administration can threaten people that they will literally be dropped in the middle of nowhere,” the official said. “The point is to scare people.” The US government violates its domestic and international nonrefoulement obligations by sending people to places where they would face persecution, torture, or certain other serious threats to their lives or safety, or where they would likely be subjected to onward deportations to face such threats, Human Rights Watch said. It also deprives people of a meaningful opportunity to contest their removals to these countries and articulate any risk of abuse they may face if removed there. In December, the US Supreme Court will hear arguments about whether the third-country removal policy violates the Due Process clause of the US constitution or otherwise violates statutory bars against removing people to the risk of being tortured. The court has allowed the government to continue third-country deportations for now. The United States should stop deporting asylum seekers and refugees to third countries that lack the capacity to provide full and fair asylum procedures and in the absence of formal, transparent agreements that ensure they will have access to such procedures. These governments should also respect the principle of nonrefoulement and ensure the dignity, security, and fundamental rights of all persons under their jurisdiction, including third-country nationals whose removal they have accepted. “Several of these African governments are not only complicit in US abuses but have violated the human rights of these deported people themselves, including with arbitrary detention and in some cases sending them back to countries where they fled danger,” Bochenek said. “These countries should not detain people without a clear legal basis, and they should not coerce or send anyone to their home country or another country where they would face a risk of persecution, torture, or other serious harm.”

UN Child Rights Committee Calls for Free Pre-Primary Education in Uganda. Click to expand Image A teacher conducting a lesson at the private Parents' Hope Nursery and Primary School in Namayingo district. © 2022 ISER The United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child has called on Uganda to significantly expand government support for early childhood education and provide free, state-run pre-primary education to all children. In its latest review of Uganda’s record on children’s rights, issued October 1, the Committee expressed concern about high numbers of children out of school due to financial barriers, and highlighted “very limited access to early childhood education,” especially for children in rural areas and for children with disabilities. The Ugandan government provides free primary and secondary education, but under Uganda’s education law, pre-primary education is left to private providers, with parents responsible for the cost. The Committee’s findings echo 2024 research by Human Rights Watch and the Initiative for Social and Economic Rights (ISER), which found that the lack of government-funded pre-primary education in Uganda leaves most young children without access to this critical stage of learning. Fewer than 1 in 10 Ugandan children ages 3 to 5 were enrolled in a registered and licensed pre-primary school, while 60 percent attended no school before entering primary school. Human Rights Watch and ISER found that private preschool fees create an insurmountable barrier for many families,particularly those with low incomes and in rural areas. A mother of eight told me that selling coal didn’t earn enough to cover her children’s school fees. She had gone into debt to keep them in school and had no idea how she would ever repay it. Uganda adopted an Early Childhood Care and Education Policy in 2025. Recognizing the importance of pre-primary education, the policy commits the government to increasing equitable access to quality, inclusive early childhood education. However, it takes a piecemeal approach, that ultimately leaves early childhood education primarily in private providers’ hands. As a result, many families nationwide will continue to face financial barriers to pre-primary education, and many children will continue to miss out. Rather than subsidizing private pre-primary schools, Uganda should use or progressively expand current Universal Primary Education (UPE) infrastructure to introduce publicly funded pre-primary education for all children. Parliament should also amend Uganda’s Education Act to specify that universal pre-primary is a government responsibility. The Committee’s recommendation offers a clear path forward: make pre-primary education free and accessible to every child.

Louisiana Activists Draw Links Between Petrochemical, Climate Harm to Maternal Health. Click to expand Image Kaitlyn Joshua with her daughter, Lauryn, age 5, outside their home in Geismar, Ascension Parish, in Louisiana’s Cancer Alley. Joshua, a chronic asthma sufferer since childhood, said her physician told her, “Kaitlyn, it’s where you live. It’s the air quality. You’re going to have to move out of there.” October 20, 2023. © 2023 Eli Reed for Human Rights Watch Louisiana feminist activists came together on October 2 at the annual Black Birth Matters conference to demand that policy makers consider how toxic air pollution and other environmental damage negatively impact reproductive health. As part of a day-long examination of human rights in Louisiana, Kaitlyn Joshua, an environmental and reproductive rights expert, Shamell Lavigne from RISE St James, a key community-based environmental rights organization, and Tyra Gross, an academic with an interest in climate intersections with Black reproductive justice, led a panel on environmental justice. Joshua and Lavigne explained why industrial regulation is important for human and, specifically, maternal health, and Gross discussed ways communities can make sure pregnant people and new parents are better prepared for climate disaster. Louisiana is an especially pertinent place for this conversation. The state has the second biggest (after Texas) petrochemistry industry in the US with significant reproductive and other health consequences for fenceline communities. Public health in Louisiana is especially at risk from climate change impacts. Louisiana also has a maternal health crisis with worsening prenatal care access, large maternal care “deserts”, a premature birth rate that recently rose and devastating cuts to safe abortion and other lifesaving reproductive health care. There is evidence that petrochemical pollution can lead to an increased risk of reproductive harm. Local authorities should make sure impacted communities have the most up to date information on how emissions from extracting and burning fossil fuels, climate change, and the petrochemical industry might damage the health of pregnant women and other people. The collective work of Black Birth Matters’ participants shines a light on how communities sometimes face multiple and interlocked injustices. It’s time for the state government to take action to protect the environment and reproductive rights for the people of Louisiana and nationwide.

Niger’s Junta Tightens Its Grip on Free Expression. Click to expand Image Nigerien journalist Moussa Kaka, former correspondent for Radio France Internationale, February 12, 2007. © 2007 Seyllou/AFP via Getty Images A lawyer in Niger faces prosecution over comments about the army on social media while a prominent journalist and critic of the country’s military junta is being held in secret, with authorities refusing to identify his alleged offense. These cases together highlight a broadening crackdown in Niger, where the space for free expression is shrinking by the day. On September 21, police summoned Abrourahamane Lirwana, a well-known lawyer. A prosecutor in Niger’s capital, Niamey, charged him with “spreading data likely to disturb public order” under a broad cybercrime law and ordered him detained. Authorities have not explained the basis for the charge, though it appears linked to a September 12 Facebook post in which Lirwana described Niger’s army as divided, with some officers backing former President Mahamadou Issoufou and others former President Mohamed Bazoum. At an October 6 court hearing, prosecutors sought a five-year prison sentence for Lirwana. Meanwhile, Moussa Kaka, a journalist, went missing in Niamey on August 31, raising fears he had been forcibly disappeared. His family and colleagues received no information about his whereabouts until September 25, when Justice Minister Alio Daouda said during Niger’s Universal Periodic Review at the United Nations in Geneva that Kaka had been detained for an alleged “offense” and would “answer before the courts.” A Nigerien journalist told Human Rights Watch that Kaka “should never have been arrested, and authorities must now reveal where he is.” Lirwana and Kaka are hardly alone. The junta continues to arbitrarily detain former President Bazoum, his wife, the former Interior Minister Hama Amadou Souley, and Moussa Tiangari, a leading human rights defender. Since taking power in 2023, Niger’s military junta has entrenched authoritarian rule and curtailed fundamental rights and freedoms. The authorities have dissolved all political parties and several independent unions, suspended civil society groups, detained journalists under the cybercrime law, and stripped exiled opposition figures of their nationality. Niger’s authorities should drop the politically motivated charges against Lirwana and release him. They should immediately disclose where Kaka is being held and release him or promptly charge him with a recognizable criminal offense. Niger’s authorities should respect fundamental freedoms and ensure political opponents, journalists, and civil society activists can operate safely and freely.

Airstrike Damages Hospital in Central Ukraine. Click to expand Image A shattered window at the Consultative and Diagnostic Centre in the Podilskyi district of Kyiv, Ukraine, on September 24, 2026. © 2026 Ukrinform/NurPhoto via AP Photo A Russian airstrike damaged a hospital in the Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih on October 6, according to reports from local officials and media outlets. The attack injured several people, including at least two hospital workers, and also damaged residential and administrative buildings and an art school in the city center. The strike is the latest in a long string of Russian attacks in Ukraine that impact health care workers and facilities and seriously threaten the right to health. In some cases, these attacks may constitute war crimes. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recorded more than 3,300 attacks impacting health care since the full scale February 2022 invasion, resulting in the deaths of 248 health workers with 1,095 injured. In September, a Russian strike damaged a maternity hospital in Kyiv and killed one person in its car park. It was one of a series of drone and missile attacks across Ukraine that day that killed eight people, most of them in Kharkiv and two in Kyiv and the Kyiv region, Ukrainian authorities said. Attacks impacting health care can have devastating effects beyond the immediate casualties. A survey of civilians conducted by Médecins Sans Frontières’ (Doctors Without Borders) showed that, since the invasion, the percentage of respondents who reported being able to access health care “always” or “most of the time” dropped from 77 percent to 35 percent, in part due to these attacks. Those who can “rarely” or “never” access care rose from 7 percent to 35 percent. After years of hostilities, the WHO estimated the cost of rebuilding Ukraine’s healthcare sector at more than US$23 billion. International humanitarian law grants special protections for medical facilities, healthcare personnel, and medical transportation units, such as ambulances. Attacks on health care can also violate international human rights law, in particular the right to health, but also the rights to life and security. Russian authorities and state media have alleged that Ukrainian strikes have also damaged medical facilities in Russia's border regions and Russian-occupied territories. All parties to the conflict should immediately cease all attacks on health care and ensure their conduct is in line with international law.

War’s Hidden Mental Health Toll on Children with Disabilities. Click to expand Image Ibrahim, a 5-year-old boy with autism, is held by his father in Idlib, Syria, June 2022. © © 2022 Human Rights Watch. As armed conflicts proliferate around the globe, World Mental Health Day is a reminder that the psychological toll stemming from hostilities result in mental health harms that have lasting effects on people’s lives. Insecurity, trauma, anxiety, and confusion are the norm for many who have endured armed conflict. Access to services is frequently inadequate—even though over a fifth of conflict-affected populations are estimated to experience mental health conditions such as post-traumatic stress, depression or anxiety. For people, including children, with intellectual disabilities, these harms can be compounded by social, attitudinal, and environmental barriers, which interact with their disability and can heighten their exposure to violence and exclusion. The father of a boy with an intellectual disability in Syria, described in 2020 the effects that the war there had had on his son. The boy, who was 13 at the time, had become increasingly withdrawn and isolated. “He sits alone, doesn’t want to interact with any other kids,” said his father, who also described the psychological distress affecting his other children. “You can see the fear in their eyes. They have no hopes for the future.” Because of communication barriers, a lack of accessible information, and inadequate communication support, people with intellectual and other disabilities are frequently excluded from humanitarian assistance and mental health services, even when such services are available to others affected by the conflict. Human Rights Watch has documented lack of inclusive psychological support for people with disabilities in other armed conflicts, including Gaza and Sudan. Governments should address these gaps by integrating disability-inclusive mental health support during conflict and recovery, in line with their international obligations. Humanitarian agencies providing such services should also take steps to ensure that their programs are disability-inclusive and do not exclude people with disabilities. This could include providing accessible communication methods, such as pictograms and play therapy for children, training staff to provide disability-inclusive support, and equipping them with tactile regulation tools—like weighted lap pads, squeeze balls, and noise-canceling headphones—to help manage sensory overload. Accessible, inclusive mental health care and support are policies that cannot undo the trauma of war, but they can help create the conditions for recovery, inclusion, and hope for the future.

US Sanctions on ICC Put Global Justice at Risk. Click to expand Image Permanent premises of the International Criminal Court in The Hague, the Netherlands. © 2019 Peter Dejong/AP (New York) – The Trump administration’s decision to sanction the International Criminal Court (ICC) is an unprecedented assault on global justice and the rule of law, Human Rights Watch said today. On October 9, 2026, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the imposition of sanctions on the ICC. “The Trump administration has made clear its aim to destroy the ICC to shield US and Israeli officials from facing charges before the court,” said Philippe Bolopion, executive director of Human Rights Watch. “By attacking the court, the US government is threatening justice for victims of abuses from Palestine to Ukraine, Myanmar, and Sudan.” The ICC is a permanent international court created to try people, including senior officials, accused of war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide, and the crime of aggression. Following the genocides in the mid-1990s in Rwanda and in the former Yugoslavia, the international community created the ICC to prevent those most responsible for serious crimes from evading justice. Nearly two-thirds of UN member countries have joined the court. In addition to its Palestine investigation, the court has opened investigations into alleged crimes in 17 situations, including in Afghanistan, Darfur in Sudan, Bangladesh/Myanmar, Ukraine, and Venezuela. The US government’s decision to sanction the ICC was announced on the same day that the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge and renowned international lawyer, in recognition of her central role “in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.” In his October 9 announcement, Rubio stated the sanctions were aimed at shielding US nationals from investigation and prosecution at the ICC. The Trump administration has previously objected to the court’s investigation of Israeli nationals for their conduct in Palestine. The ICC has issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for serious crimes in Gaza. Palestine became an ICC member in 2015 and gave the court a mandate to address serious crimes committed on its territory or by its nationals since June 13, 2014. The Trump administration has already sanctioned ICC prosecutors, nine ICC judges, three prominent Palestinian human rights groups, and the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, and called on ICC member countries to leave the court. US sanctions have serious effects on those targeted, including frozen or closed bank accounts, rejected financial transactions, denied access to digital services, and US entry bans. US sanctions also have a chilling effect on non-US banks and other companies outside of US jurisdiction that could themselves lose access to the US banking system if they do not adhere to the sanctions. This means that the ICC could lose access to companies on which it relies for everyday functions, from banking to information, technology to travel. Human Rights Watch, together with three other human rights organizations, filed a lawsuit in US federal court on August 11, 2026, seeking to have the sanctions regime previously used to authorize court-wide sanctions struck down. A wide range of human rights organizations, other experts, and former US government officials have filed amicus (friend of the court) briefs in support of the suit. ICC member countries, including the Netherlands which hosts the ICC in The Hague, the leadership body of the court’s Assembly of States Parties, the European Union, UN human rights experts, the UN secretary-general, the UN high commissioner for human rights, civil society organizations, and the ICC itself have repeatedly spoken out against the sanctions. The ICC and its member countries have also taken important steps to insulate the court from the potential impact of sanctions, but more action is needed to protect the court’s ability to continue its critical work. The EU should immediately activate its blocking statute, which aims to shield European operators from the effects of extraterritorial sanctions. The Trump administration’s sanctions targeting international justice are part of a broader attack on the laws, institutions, and organizations created to protect human rights, Human Rights Watch said. The United States has also withdrawn from the Paris Climate Accords and the World Health Organization, while disengaging from the UN Human Rights Council. President Donald Trump and other senior US officials have also expressed contempt for international law, and threatened to commit war crimes. “The ICC was created to ensure that no one, no matter how powerful, can escape justice for the worst crimes,” Bolopion said. “Governments everywhere should take every available measure to counter the effects of the US sanctions and stand with the court and those relying on it to obtain justice.”

Gaza: Ceasefire Anniversary Marks Year of Failed Promises. Click to expand Image A Palestinian boy walks inside a destroyed building in Khan Yunis in the southern Gaza Strip, January 27, 2026. © 2026 Bashar Taleb/AFP via Getty Images (Beirut) – Israeli forces continue to kill and wound civilians and deny sufficient food, aid, and water to Palestinians in Gaza one year after a ceasefire agreement took effect on October 10, 2025, Human Rights Watch said today. Israel’s acts of genocide and crimes against humanity, including forced displacement and extermination, have persisted throughout the ceasefire. Other countries should take immediate measures to protect civilians and ensure that rights-based reconstruction begins. The Board of Peace, authorized under United Nations Security Council Resolution 2803, is tasked with assessing parties’ compliance with the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict. Promises of humanitarian relief and the restoration of essential civilian infrastructure are central to the plan. Yet, a year on, aid volumes remain far below required levels, critical humanitarian access routes have been repeatedly obstructed, and reconstruction has not yet begun. Continuing Israeli attacks have killed at least 1,400 Palestinians and wounded 4,881 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry, bringing the death toll since October 2023 to over 74,000, including over 21,000 children. “The outside world may be under a dangerous illusion that life in Gaza is returning to normal, but reality tells a very different story,” said Sarah Sanbar, acting Israel and Palestine researcher at Human Rights Watch. “There is nothing normal about living in a tent under bombardment, without enough food or drinking water for your family.” With winter approaching, families living in an Israel-engineered shelter crisis face preventable deaths and suffering affecting key human rights such as the rights to housing, health, and education. Ninety-four percent of Gaza’s population lacks adequate shelter, the Palestine Shelter Cluster reported based on a survey of nearly 2,000 households across Gaza. Nearly two-thirds of housing units have been destroyed, and many of those still standing are damaged and unsafe. The survey showed that over half of the nearly 2,000 households are living in tents. In September 2026, a damaged building housing about 100 people collapsed, killing 21, including 12 children. Gaza’s education and health sectors remain shattered. The new academic year began last month with 93 percent of schools destroyed or damaged. The World Health Organization (WHO) recorded 56 attacks on health care in Gaza between January and August 2026, with just 35 of Gaza’s 57 hospitals and field hospitals partially functional and not one fully operational. Meanwhile, humanitarian organizations report an increase in disease due to the living conditions in overcrowded camps and shelters, including poor waste management, sewage overflow, and rodent infestation. The risks of famine and acute food insecurity loom over Gaza, as the entry of humanitarian aid remains limited and inconsistent, and people in Gaza are unable to produce their own food due to Israeli forces’ widespread destruction of agricultural land and restrictions on fishing. In July, the Integrated Phase Classification (IPC), the world’s foremost experts on food security, reported that 67 percent of the population—over 1.4 million people—are “expected to face crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity in July-December 2026.” According to the European Union and UN, the recovery and reconstruction needs in Gaza are estimated at US$71.4 billion over the next decade. On September 23, the Board of Peace presented a “6-Month Gaza Recovery Program” ready to begin “the moment funding and access allow,” but one year on, no recovery efforts have begun. Israel continues to move the “Yellow Line,” the stated limit of the physical presence of Israeli ground forces under the ceasefire, westward beyond its agreed boundaries as Israeli officials call the line Israel’s “new border.” The area within the Yellow Line now amounts to about 64 percent of the Gaza Strip, and Israeli forces are displacing Palestinians as the line moves while preventing residents from returning to their homes beyond the line, corralling Gaza’s 2.1 million people into an ever-shrinking strip of land. In June, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) documented that 196 Palestinians had been killed near the Yellow Line and its westward movement is swallowing up water points and health facilities, further restricting Palestinians’ access to key services. Alongside these actions, Israeli officials continue to openly declare a goal of ethnically cleansing Gaza. For example, in September, Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir proposed the “710 Disengagement Plan,” aiming to depopulate Gaza in seven years, and establishing a ministry of “voluntary emigration” for that purpose. According to Palestinian civil defense authorities, over 630 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble since November 2025, and they estimate that over 8,000 remain buried under the rubble. The UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory warned in September 2026 that the large-scale removal of rubble in areas of Gaza under Israeli military control should not become a way to erase traces of atrocity crimes. Finding the remains of those lost under the rubble is essential so that families can know what happened to their loved ones, offer them dignified burial, and start a long process of recovery and remedy, Human Rights Watch said. As world leaders discuss the future of Gaza, it is essential for them to urgently address the rights of Palestinians to rebuild their lives in Gaza, categorically reject all Israeli propositions of forced displacement and ethnic cleansing, and support all measures of accountability to put an end to the catastrophic situation for rights in Gaza. “Palestinians deserve a better future where their rights are respected and they can live in dignity, but none of this is possible unless the atrocities stop and justice and redress become a reality,” Sanbar said.

UN: Burundi Set to Win Human Rights Council Seat Despite Abuses. Click to expand Image Burundi's President Evariste Ndayishimiye speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, in New York, New York, September 23, 2026. © 2026 AP Photo/Heather Khalifa (New York) – Burundi is set to win re-election to the United Nations Human Rights Council in a vote on October 13, 2026, with no competition, Human Rights Watch said today. Burundi is seeking to retain its seat even though the government of this Central African country has not improved its abusive human rights conditions. Burundi is one of the four African countries running for the same number of seats on the 47-nation council. The regional slates for the Western group, Latin America and the Caribbean, Central and Eastern Europe, and Asia also lack competition. This effectively guarantees all 15 candidates, fit or unfit, spots on the UN’s premier rights body for three years beginning on January 1, 2027. “This uncompetitive vote makes a mockery of the word ‘election,’” said Louis Charbonneau, UN director at Human Rights Watch. “UN member states should insist on competitive slates so they can reject candidates with poor human rights records. No one should have a seat on this crucial body handed to them on a silver platter.” Ghana, Nigeria, and Zambia are candidates for Africa’s other three available seats. In Asia, Japan, Jordan, Kuwait, and Nepal are running for the region’s four seats. In Latin America and the Caribbean, Brazil, the Dominican Republic, and Uruguay are set to take the region’s three spots. For the Western group, Germany and Ireland are on track to get the group’s two available seats, while Moldova and Ukraine will take Central and Eastern Europe’s two spots. Despite some positive government statements, Burundi has not carried out meaningful reform to address longstanding concerns related to governance, justice, or accountability. Grave abuses persist with impunity, including extrajudicial executions, enforced disappearances, arbitrary arrests, and detention. Freedom of expression, assembly, and association remain severely restricted. Burundi is in the third year of its current term and is allowed to run for another consecutive term. On October 6, the country’s delegation tried to use their membership to prevent UN scrutiny of Burundi’s poor human rights record, first by calling a vote to renew the mandate of the UN special rapporteur on Burundi and then by voting against it. The resolution was adopted, though, 22 to 7, with 17 abstentions. That resolution not only expressed concerns about ongoing rights violations but highlighted Burundi’s refusal to cooperate with the council and most of its mechanisms, including the special rapporteur. General Assembly Resolution 60/251, which created the Human Rights Council in 2006, says that countries voting for members should “take into account the contribution of candidates to the promotion and protection of human rights.” Council members are required to “uphold the highest standards in the promotion and protection of human rights” at home and abroad and to “fully cooperate with the Council.” Candidates only need a simple majority in the secret-ballot vote in the 193-nation General Assembly to secure a seat on the Human Rights Council. That makes it highly unlikely that any candidate will lose, no matter how unqualified. Nevertheless, UN member states should not cast votes for abusive governments that are demonstrably unqualified for council membership. Among the other candidates, Nigeria should ensure accountability for serious international crimes committed by all parties—including security forces—during the conflict with the armed group Boko Haram. Brazil should investigate and curb police abuse after law enforcement officers set a grim record in 2025 by killing more than 6,500 people, the vast majority of them Black. Ukraine has suffered countless atrocities committed by Russian forces on its territory since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. At the same time, Ukrainian authorities have unjustly prosecuted Ukrainian civilians living under Russian occupation, including teachers, medics, municipal workers, and volunteers for doing essential work that international humanitarian law permits civilians to perform under occupation. The Human Rights Council scrutinizes all UN member states’ rights records in the Universal Periodic Review process. In November 2025, the United States refused to participate in its review. If the US government does not participate in its rescheduled review in November, it will become the first member country not to complete its review. The Human Rights Council has played a crucial role in ensuring independent investigations of abuses in Syria, Myanmar, North Korea, Russia, Ukraine, Israel/Palestine, Afghanistan, Sudan, and elsewhere. Council members should press for investigations of abuses by other countries in need of scrutiny, including major powers. These should include China’s crimes against humanity against Uyghurs and others in Xinjiang, as well as the US military’s unlawful strikes targeting vessels the Caribbean and Pacific, amounting to extrajudicial killings. The council should also explore possible action to support global justice in the face of a US assault on international accountability mechanisms. The US on October 9 imposed unjustified sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC). The Trump administration has made clear its aim to destroy the ICC to shield US and Israeli officials from facing charges before the court. The US had previously sanctioned ICC officials, Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on human rights in the Palestinian Territory occupied since 1967, and several prominent Palestinian human rights groups. “The human rights movement is under increasing attack by powerful governments, including established democracies,” Charbonneau said. “The Human Rights Council has done victims of human rights abuses a huge service with investigations that often deter governments and armed groups from committing violations. We need the council now more than ever.”

Senegal: Brutal Crackdown Violates LGBT People’s Rights. Click to expand Image Renovated Dakar Railway station inaugurated, May 2026. © 2026 Human Rights Watch Senegal’s intensifying crackdown on LGBT people is violating their rights and causing increasing fear and stigma. Fear of arrest and stigma are causing people to go into hiding, to avoid HIV testing and treatment, and deterring lawyers from representing them. The crackdown on LGBT people calls into question Senegal’s compliance with its own laws and international law, as well as the Olympic charter, given it will host the Youth Olympics Games at the end of the month. (Dakar) Senegal’s growing crackdown on Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender (LGBT) people is violating their rights, causing increasing fear and stigma, and should be ended immediately, Human Rights Watch said today. Mass arrests forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation appear to be part of an increase in punitive government action against LGBT people in West Africa. On March 11, 2026, Senegal’s parliament amended article 319 of the penal code, doubling to 10 years the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex conduct and criminalizing “promotion” of or support to LGBT people and organizations. The amendment followed the detention by security forces of at least five men in Thiès region in December 2025 and 12 men in the capital, Dakar, in February 2026 on charges including “acts against nature” and “intentional transmission of HIV.” Police and gendarmerie then escalated arrests of suspected LGBT people in various other cities including Thiès, Rosso, Saint Louis, Yeumbeul, and Ziguinchor. “LGBT people are being forced to curb their normal activities and to keep from exercising their rights for fear of arrest and increased stigma,” said Larissa Kojoué, LGBT rights researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Senegal’s government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone’s rights.” Human Rights Watch interviewed 39 people in May in Senegal: 5 people who had been detained in late 2025 and early 2026, 2 journalists, 9 civil society representatives and human rights defenders, 2 national officials, 2 lawyers, 4 health professionals, and 15 members of the Senegalese queer community. Human Rights Watch also reviewed official statements, and media and nongovernmental group reports. On September 29, Human Rights Watch wrote to the Senegalese authorities, including the justice minister, the high commander of the National Gendarmerie and director of military justice, and the director general of the National Police detailing its findings and asking specific questions, but has received no response. Same-sex sexual conduct has been criminalized in Senegal since 1965, but hostility toward LGBT people has significantly intensified in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, President Diomaye Faye and former Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko pledged to strengthen laws criminalizing same-sex relations, framing the issue as a national priority and mobilizing broad political and public support. The March amendments have triggered new attacks against LGBT people, interviewees said. Mouhamadou Seck, secretary-general of the prominent Senegalese organization African Forum for the Defense of Human Rights (Rencontre Africaine pour la Défense des Droits de l’Homme, or RADDHO), said in May that “detentions, violence, and abuse against LGBT individuals have sharply increased across the country.” Human Rights Watch was not able to independently verify the total number of arrests linked to article 319. However, between February and July, at least 212 people have been arrested, according to data collected by RADDHO. HIV Justice Network reported that the number of arrests exceeded more than 300 during the same period. Of those arrested, 82 were also charged with “voluntary HIV transmission,” although a court dismissed these charges in August. These figures illustrate the scale of arrests and indicate a pattern in enforcement of article 319. Security force officials have stated that they have arrested people suspected of engaging in same-sex conduct based on information extracted from previously seized phones, third-party allegations, or raids on private premises. The March amendment to the penal code introduces broadly defined offenses criminalizing activities such as “promotion” and “glorification” of homosexuality, as well as financing and supporting LGBT individuals and organizations. Human rights defenders and lawyers said that the introduction of these offenses has led to fear and anxiety among legal professionals and contributed to an environment in which detainees struggle to secure legal representation. “In Senegal, lawyers are associated with the cause they represent,” a lawyer in Dakar told Human Rights Watch, adding that his colleagues and family members had urged him not to represent individuals arrested on charges of “acts against nature.” He said: “Everyone has the right to a fair trial. What matters to me is: were their rights respected or not?” Principle 18 of the United Nations Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers provides that “Lawyers shall not be identified with their clients or their clients’ causes as a result of discharging their functions.” People interviewed said that since February, the authorities have subjected detainees to HIV testing without informed consent and used detainees’ HIV status to justify additional criminal charges or prolonged detention. Health professionals expressed concern that the forced HIV testing and subsequent charges undermine medical confidentiality by allowing confidential test results to be used in criminal proceedings. They also discourage people from seeking HIV testing and treatment and jeopardize HIV-related public health efforts. “We have noticed that […] some people have fled while others are hiding,” a doctor in Dakar said. “One-third no longer come in for appointments to seek HIV treatment.” Security forces also appear to have violated the confidentiality of ongoing criminal investigations involving suspected LGBT people. News reporting on two cases involving public figures includes personal details that closely track details set forth in investigative records, suggesting authorities leaked confidential information to journalists. Local media also extensively reported personal and confidential data on the case of the 12 men arrested in February. This has exposed individuals to social stigma, family rejection, threats, and violence. The Senegalese Constitution and international human rights law applicable in Senegal guarantee fundamental rights, including equal protection before the law and non-discrimination; the right to effective legal representation and the presumption of innocence; the rights to privacy and to informed consent to medical treatment; freedom from torture and other ill-treatment, and the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time. Senegal’s Law No. 2010-03 of April 9, 2010, on HIV/AIDS establishes a legal framework to ensure access to treatment and support and protect the rights of people living with or affected by HIV. The law guarantees the rights to informed consent in medical testing and to privacy and confidentiality of health information, as well as protection against discrimination based on HIV status and protection of detainees from mandatory HIV testing. The African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, ratified by Senegal in 1982, guarantees, among other rights, the right to a fair trial, to equal protection before the law, and to nondiscrimination. The African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights, which will meet in Dakar from October 12–21, explicitly called on member states, including Senegal, to protect sexual minorities in accordance with the African charter, and has urged governments to protect people from violence based on their sexual orientation and gender identity. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), to which Senegal is a party, requires Senegal to ensure the protection of numerous rights including fair trial, equal protection, nondiscrimination, and the right to privacy. The UN Human Rights Committee, which oversees compliance with the ICCPR, has repeatedly held that the criminalization of consensual same-sex conduct between adults violates the covenant. From October 31 to November 13, Senegal will host the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, the first Olympic event on the African continent. The Olympic Charter prohibits discrimination on any grounds and commits host countries to respect human rights and human dignity. “The ongoing government crackdown on LGBT people raises serious concerns about Senegal’s compliance with international law, the Olympic charter, and Senegal’s own laws,” Kojoué said. “The government should call a halt to this crackdown.” Click to expand Image Interview with Sall (pseudonym), university student in Dakar, Senegal, who has barely left his room since February due to stigma and fear of arrest, May 2026. © 2026 Human Rights Watch Expanded Criminalization of Same-Sex Conduct On March 11, Senegal’s Parliament adopted amendments to article 319 of the penal code by a vote of 135 to 0, with three abstentions. The new law doubles, to 10 years, the maximum prison term for same-sex conduct and increases fines from 2 million to 10 million CFA francs (roughly US$3,000 to US$17,000). The law introduces penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5 million CFA ($850 to $8,500) for those accused of promoting homosexuality or supporting or financing LGBT persons and organizations. It also instructs judges not to suspend sentences or reduce prison terms below the minimum penalty recommended. Arbitrary Arrest, Detention According to data from July by the HIV Justice Network, since early February, authorities “have arrested over 300 individuals on allegations of acts against nature” in cities across Senegal. Data collected by RADDHO shows 212 people were arrested between February and July. RADDHO told Human Rights Watch that their data indicates that gendarmes from the Keur Massar unit carried out the majority of the arrests. Keur Massar is about 25 kilometers east of downtown Dakar. On June 25, Keur Massar district gendarmerie arrested the 101st suspect in connection with the arrest wave that began in February, according to media reports. Officers said the arrests followed their review of a mobile phone seized from one of the 12 men arrested in February. In July 30, international media reported that Keur Massar gendarmes arrested eight women who have been placed in pretrial detention. The gendarmes used phone data from two who were allegedly in a relationship to identify and arrest the six others. Beside “acts against nature,” investigators also cited allegations of pimping, corruption of minors, and drug-related offenses. Police in the Thiès region, about 70 km east of Dakar, arrested five men in December 2025 for smoking shisha, a tobacco product banned under local law, and held them for two days before presenting them to a judicial authority. The prosecutor ordered them held on charges of “acts against nature” but dropped the charges and released them a month later for lack of evidence. They said that they believe neighbors denounced them to the authorities because of their sexual orientation. One of the five, a 23-year-old man, said: We were arrested while preparing for a fashion show at my place. Around 9 p.m., three police officers arrived, took us to the station and confiscated our phones.… We were held for two days, then taken to the Thiès prosecutor’s office and charged with acts against nature, despite not being caught in the act.… I think our neighbors told the police we are gay because they were jealous of our successful fashion business. He said that, “we were beaten, whipped, and slapped, and called homosexuals.... I was injured on my thigh, causing lasting pain.” A social worker operating in Rebeuss, Senegal’s largest detention facility, located in Dakar, said he witnessed prison staff and detainees discriminate against those held on suspicion of homosexuality: “[LGBT detainees] are being excluded from communal activities, denied participation in collective prayer sessions, and required to access services, including the barber, separately from other prisoners. In some cases, they are even compelled to perform domestic labor.” Prolonged Pretrial Detention Since February, only one person arrested for “acts against nature” has been convicted according to local media. On April 10, the Pikine-Guédiawaye District Court, in a suburb of Dakar, sentenced a 24-year-old man, who had been arrested a week earlier, to six years in prison and imposed a fine of 2 million CFA franc (approximately $3,300) after convicting him of “acts against nature” and “public indecency.” He was not represented by legal counsel as it is often the case for people accused of “acts against nature” who may be denied access to legal representation or face difficulty finding lawyers willing to represent them. A lawyer in Dakar told Human Rights Watch that many of those arrested on homosexuality-related charges remain in pretrial detention because prosecutors have added supplementary charges, including criminal association, endangering the life of others, deliberate HIV transmission, and drug trafficking. The lawyer said that these additional charges often require longer investigations and are used to justify extending pretrial detention. Senegalese law generally limits pretrial detention to six months for minor offenses, with no limit for certain serious crimes such as murder, offenses against state security, and embezzlement of public funds. International human rights law requires that pretrial detention should be an exception, not the rule, and be justified on an individual basis in every case. Anyone held in pretrial detention is entitled to a trial within a reasonable time or release. Lengthy pretrial detention remains a significant concern in Senegal, as several civil society organizations and government officials interviewed said. On August 7, the Pikine-Guediawaye District Court officially closed the preliminary investigation into the case involving the 12 men arrested on February 9 and another 87 people arrested in connection with the same crackdown. The court dismissed cases for 28 and freed them, but 71 remain referred to trial on charges of criminal association and acts against nature. The district court also dismissed charges of “endangering other people’s lives” and “voluntary HIV transmission.” This decision raises questions regarding continued detention of the 12 accused as the investigative needs that are commonly invoked to justify prolonged pretrial detention may no longer apply. Barriers to Legal Representation Human Rights Watch found that that the newly introduced offense of “promotion of homosexuality” has had a chilling effect on access to legal representation. Lawyers and human rights defenders said they were concerned that representing people charged under article 319 could expose them to professional, social, or even legal repercussions. “How can we represent people arrested without being accused of promotion,” one lawyer said. “That’s why there is such strong reluctance.” The lawyer described serious obstacles to accessing legal representation, saying that detainees, including his own client, were pressured to waive their right to legal representation. He also said that authorities frequently questioned detainees and obtained statements in the absence of legal counsel. On February 9, the lawyer filed two complaints before the Dakar Court of Appeals, one on his own behalf and one on behalf of his client against a gendarmerie commander who pressured his client to waive his right to legal representation. He said in September that no progress had been made in either case. Another lawyer raised concern about gendarmes’ respect for due process. He suspected that authorities had obtained his clients “confessions” without their fully understanding of the proceedings and the implications of their statements. Forced HIV Testing; Disclosure of Medical Information RADDHO and HIV Justice Network told Human Rights Watch that the authorities have forced most detainees to undergo HIV testing and, when the results were positive, charged them with “deliberate HIV transmission” and “endangering the lives of others” in addition to offenses under article 319 of the amended penal code. Under article 36 of Senegal’s 2010 law on HIV/AIDS, anyone who is knowingly living with HIV and has unprotected sex may face 5 to 10 years in prison and a fine. The Keur Massar gendarmerie has officially stated that they required arrested people to undergo HIV tests. The national police also have conducted such tests and used the HIV status in criminal proceedings, as they mentioned in their June 13 statement. “We are aware about nonconsensual HIV testing by gendarmerie and disclosure of people’s HIV status,” a doctor told Human Rights Watch. The consequences of these practices have extended beyond individual detainees. Health professionals said that the use of HIV-related services has sharply declined and attribute it to fear of arrest, forced disclosure, and social stigma. “If, because of the law, people decide to stop coming to health clinics, it becomes a public health problem,” a doctor said. The Public Health Ministry and the National Council for the Fight Against AIDS (Conseil National de Lutte Contre le Sida, or CNLS), a government body leading and coordinating the HIV response in Senegal, released joint statements on Facebook on February 11 and February 23 stressing national efforts to treat and prevent HIV/AIDS and support people living with HIV/AIDS, as well as the need to keep medical and judicial records separate, and the difficulty of establishing intentional transmission. In a March 18 news statement, the Joint UN Program on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS), which advocates for global action against the HIV/AIDS pandemic, expressed concerns over the impact of the amended law, and called on Senegal to protect the confidentiality of medical information and the patient-provider relationship as non-negotiable foundations of a functioning health system. Breaches of Privacy and Confidentiality Numerous local media reports on the recent cases include highly detailed personal information about individuals arrested by the security forces. In at least four cases, the information closely tracks information in case records, nearly verbatim, suggesting that confidential information was being directly shared with journalists. “Our photos and items found [by Police] at my home, like lubricants and antiretroviral tablets, were published in newspapers and on social media,” the 23-year-old man said. In one prominent case, a rare instance in which the detainee had legal representation after his arrest, Keur Massar gendarmes detained a popular artist on charges of “acts against nature,” and his name, HIV status, and other confidential information appeared soon afterward in the media. As a Senegalese journalist put it: “Publishing ‘scandalous’ information, on such a taboo matter like homosexuality in Senegal, has increasingly become a means of driving audience engagement. This practice turns people’s suffering into spectacle, with little regard for the serious consequences for those whose privacy and dignity are violated.” Mental Health Consequences of the Crackdown The government crackdown has had serious social and psychological effects on LGBT people across the country. LGBT individuals interviewed said they experienced fear, anxiety, depression, and suicidal thoughts, and many have gone into hiding, restricted their movements, withdrawn from social and online life, relocated, or abandoned mobile phones to avoid detection by the security forces. A 22-year-old university student said he was forced to move after facing verbal threats and harassment: In the neighborhood where I was, people started insulting me. They would say things like ‘next time it is your turn,’ when I passed [by them]. Kids would even follow me singing ‘goor-jigeen’ [a Wolof word describing a man who appears and behaves like a woman] and adults would say nothing. I couldn’t even defend myself. I knew if I said something, they would all come after me. To come back home I had to wait until it is dark so no one would notice me. A 27-year-old community worker in Dakar, said constant fear has turned daily life “into a state resembling COVID confinement”: We have suspended all our activities, including online. Now nobody trusts anyone. There is a total lack of security. I know I have one foot in prison. I can be arrested anytime because I am a community leader. Even if I am not in prison right now, I live like I am in prison. Life has totally changed. Another 21-year-old man among those arrested in December 2025 said that, following his release in January 2026, he has been living in hiding in central Senegal, unable to return home out of fear his relatives would assault him: I received a call from my mother telling me not to come back home. Apparently, my [half] brothers and some of my cousins were waiting for me and [were] ready to teach me a lesson. I have been hiding since. I couldn’t even go back home to pick up some stuff. I have withdrawn from several online groups and deactivated my social media. Many of my friends left for Gambia, Mauritania, or Morrocco. I am staying because I am my mother’s only child. A 35-year-old man in Ziguinchor said his partner left with no prior notice for a neighboring country causing him psychological distress: My partner left the country at night on a motorbike when he heard that his close friends were arrested and the police raided his place. He threw away his phone. He lives in poor conditions on the other side of the border. He does not have his medication. I am scared for him. A psychologist at Cheikh Anta Diop University in Dakar said that her consultations on campus “have tripled” since March. “Many patients are young men experiencing severe anxiety, hypervigilance, withdrawal from social life, and obsessive behaviors driven by fear of being perceived and attacked as LGBT.” Recommendations To Senegal’s President Order the immediate release of everyone arbitrarily detained since February 2026 under article 319 of the penal code. Refer the amended law to the Constitutional Council for constitutional review of its compatibility with constitutional guarantees of the right to privacy, equality before the law, non-discrimination, and fair trial rights. Publicly commit, ahead of the Youth Olympic Games, to ensure that all participants, visitors, and residents alike, will be protected from discrimination and arbitrary arrests. To the National Assembly Repeal article 319 in its entirety, including the provisions of the amended penal code that criminalize the “promotion” or “glorification” of homosexuality, as well as the financing or support of LGBT individuals and organizations.Initiate a legislative review to remove HIV status as a criminal aggravating factor. To Senegal’s Government Open an investigation of abuses documented against LGBT people and hold those responsible accountable.Instruct judicial authorities to uphold national and international laws to guarantee access to legal representation for all detainees and ensure lawyers can represent clients without intimidation, harassment, or risk of prosecution.Ensure that pretrial detention is an exceptional measure, not a standard procedure, and that anyone in such detention is guaranteed a trial within a reasonable time or release.Prohibit forced HIV testing, ensure informed consent for all medical testing, prevent the use of confidential health information in criminal proceedings, and protect medical confidentiality, including by prohibiting the disclosure of detainees’ health information to the media.Open an independent investigation into the case concerning a gendarmerie commander who pressured a detainee to waive his right to legal representation before leaking the detainee’s HIV status to journalists.Respect and protect the rights to freedom of expression, association, and peaceful assembly, including for individuals and organizations advocating for the rights of LGBT people. To the National Medical Council Reaffirm that forced HIV testing violates medical ethics.

Türkiye: End Internet Censorship. Click to expand Image Tags, with “Access blocked” and the name of blocked accounts belonging to journalists and media outlets, LGBT and women’s rights groups, and other rights defenders, are tied to the gates of Turkey’s Constitutional Court, to protest the Turkish authorities’ blocking of hundreds of social media accounts and websites. Ankara, October 7, 2026. © 2026 Yıldız Yazıcıoğlu (Istanbul, October 12, 2026) – The Turkish authorities over the last month have substantially escalated internet censorship, Human Rights Watch said today, along with ARTICLE 19, the Freedom of Expression Association, and 18 other organizations. Social media platforms should take meaningful steps immediately to uphold their human rights responsibilities and avoid contributing to suppressing independent media and violating the right to freedom of expression. The Turkish authorities should stop issuing blocking orders to restrict content and accounts on social media and websites in violation of the right to freedom of expression. The following is the groups’ statement: ARTICLE 19, Freedom of Expression Association (İFÖD), Human Rights Watch, and the undersigned human rights and media freedom organisations are deeply concerned by the severe escalation of internet censorship in Türkiye in the past month. We urge social media platforms to take meaningful steps immediately to uphold their human rights responsibilities and avoid contributing to the suppression of independent media and violations of the right to freedom of expression. We call on the Turkish government immediately to cease the use of blocking orders and other restrictive measures that violate the right to freedom of expression, and to ensure that any restrictions on online content fully comply with Türkiye’s obligations under international human rights law. In the month of September 2026 alone, İFÖD documented Turkish authorities and courts ordering the blocking of access to at least 1,270 accounts on the social media platform X, which had a combined following of 35 million. X complied with at least 90 percent of the orders by geo-blocking them (withholding access to them in Türkiye only). In many cases, the accounts were blocked in the context of an ongoing and wide-ranging crackdown on associations and activists defending the rights of LGBTQ+ people. In other cases, the authorities cited unspecified “national security and public order” grounds. Accounts withheld include news outlets such as soL Haber and Mezopotamya Ajansı; rights organisations including Amnesty Türkiye and the Media and Law Studies Association (MLSA); LGBTQ+; and women’s rights organisations such as Kaos GL and the Federation of Women’s Associations, as well as those of numerous journalists and academics. X also withheld the accounts of İFÖD, its co-founder, Yaman Akdeniz, and its Engelliweb account, which monitors and documents internet censorship in Türkiye. This account plays a critical role in enabling civil society, journalists, and the public to monitor and track websites, social media accounts and content subjected to access restrictions. Blocking T24, one of Türkiye’s biggest and oldest remaining independent news outlets, is particularly troubling. On 29 September, access was blocked to the T24 website and X account with 1.9 million followers, with a court order citing 118 news articles published on the site. The order claimed that the content was “aimed at disrupting and weakening the Turkish family structure” and of a nature “that would adversely affect the developmental process of young and underage individuals concerning sexual orientation and gender identity.” The order cited preventing crime and protecting public order as grounds for the measure but provided no explanation about how the cited content posed a threat to either objective or why blocking an entire news website and social media account was necessary and proportionate. The website has been inaccessible in Türkiye since 30 September. T24 changed its X handle in an attempt to prevent the account from being withheld in Türkiye, then changed it again, after another order blocked access to its second handle. Bianet, another online news outlet which focuses on human rights, also changed its X handle to escape censorship after its account with 400,000 followers was blocked. The court order blocking access to T24 was taken in the context of the “my family is safe” criminal investigations – a crackdown on LGBTQ+ people which targets activists, associations and a journalist advocating for their rights. The websites and social media accounts of at least 96 organizations and individuals were blocked on the same grounds. While most of the cases concern X, Meta has also withheld access to the Instagram and Facebook accounts of several media and civil society organisations, including, Kısa Dalga, Kaos GL, and the Civic Space Studies Association as part of the same operation. Türkiye’s long-standing abuse of Article 8/A of its Internet Law Most of the blocking decisions in September and October invoked Article 8/A of Türkiye’s Internet Law. Article 8/A, used as a tool for internet censorship since its introduction in 2015, provides that online content deemed a threat to national security, public order or presenting a risk on other grounds listed in the article can be removed or blocked on orders of the executive in urgent cases, subject to review later by a Criminal Peace Judgeship, the court assigned such cases. Major examples include blocking access to Wikipedia for 2.5 years in 2017, and to Türkiye’s leading user-generated online discussion platform Ekşi Sözlük for a year in 2023. The Constitutional Court eventually restored both, finding that blocking the entire sites had violated freedom of expression. The use of Article 8/A intensified sharply from 2025, with few safeguards or independent oversight and limited redress for those affected. The Constitutional Court has not ruled on any restrictions under Article 8/A since 2023. Concerning developments aimed at expanding censorship There is no indication that this pressure will ease. On the contrary, the government is taking further measures to accelerate and centralise internet censorship. On 31 July, Law No. 7590 transferred the powers previously exercised by the Information and Communication Technologies Authority (ICTA) contained in the Internet Law, to the Cybersecurity Directorate. This includes the authority to block sites on the request of the presidency or relevant ministries based on Article 8/A. This transfer of authority is troubling. The Cybersecurity Directorate is directly attached to the presidency, consolidating executive control over information and serving as the command centre for Türkiye’s censorship regime. Separately, on 24 September, the justice minister announced the establishment of new “Digital Space Security and Countering Disinformation Bureaux,” where specialised public prosecutors will closely monitor “criminal content and activities encouraging crime on digital platforms” including ‘spreading disinformation.” They are tasked in particular with identifying suspects and initiating criminal proceedings to intervene “more swiftly.” Social media platforms should take urgent action to uphold their human rights responsibilities The conduct of social media platforms forms an essential part of internet censorship in Türkiye. In September and early October, account holders reported receiving only a notification from platforms stating that their account had been withheld in Türkiye under Article 8/A, without any reason or explanation why or how the article had been applied. Some were unable to access the underlying blocking orders even after repeatedly requesting them from the platforms. Without access to the orders, users cannot examine the legal basis for the restriction or even identify to which Criminal Judgeship of Peace to submit their objections. Even when users were able to obtain the orders, the orders often failed to identify the specific content allegedly justifying the blocking of the entire account. Neither X nor Meta have provided public explanations about their responses to the September-October censorship waves. Human Rights Watch wrote to the two platforms requesting comment on their compliance with Turkish courts’ recent blocking orders. Neither platform had responded by the time of publication. Under the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, companies have a responsibility to respect human rights by avoiding causing or contributing to adverse human rights impacts and by addressing impacts directly linked to their operations, products, or services. This responsibility should also inform social media platforms when they respond to government requests that violate international human rights law, and in particular freedom of expression. We therefore urge X, Meta, and any other platform faced with such orders by the Turkish government to also follow these recommendations: Resist complying with arbitrary 8/A requests Refuse to comply with account blocking requests under Article 8/A of the Internet Law unless Turkish authorities identify the specific content at issue and provide sufficient reasoning and evidence demonstrating that the content gives rise to a clear, serious and imminent danger to the right to life and property, national security and public order, public health or other ground listed in the provision. Where account blocking orders provide sufficient information to enable a meaningful assessment, assess them against international human rights law and resist complying with blocking orders that restrict access to protected expression. This includes but is not limited to legally challenging such orders. Where relevant, limit restrictions in scope and duration, for example by restricting access only to the specific content identified in the order rather than withholding the entire account. Ensure transparency Immediately notify users when their accounts are withheld in Türkiye and provide them with the orders on which the restriction is based. This allows account holders to take necessary steps to challenge the orders. Provide transparency concerning account blocking measures, at least by publicly sharing the number of orders received, the number of orders complied with, and publishing case studies. This information is essential for enabling public scrutiny of government censorship and platforms’ role in it. Engage with Turkish civil society Meaningfully engage with Turkish civil society to understand the human rights implications and broader impact of platforms complying with account blocking measures, including the significance of the accounts targeted and the potential consequences of withholding them in Türkiye. Urgently review appeals to restrictions Review user appeals to account restrictions imposed in Türkiye in September and October 2026 and immediately restore access to accounts if the underlying orders fail to meet the requirements of identifying the specific content at issue, establishing a link between that content and the alleged threat to national security, public order and other grounds listed in Article 8/A, and providing adequate reasoning demonstrating that blocking the entire account is necessary and proportionate. We call on Turkish authorities to take urgent steps to end internet censorship and uphold freedom of expression, including by Immediately halting new restrictions on online content that violate freedom of expression, media freedom, and access to information as protected under international law and Türkiye’s human rights obligations.Restoring access to content which has been restricted in violation of international law and Türkiye’s freedom of expression obligations Signatories: ARTICLE 19 Freedom of Expression Association (İFÖD)Human Rights WatchAmnesty International Association of European Journalists (AEJ)Balkan Investigative Reporting Network (BIRN)Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ)Çağdaş Gazeteciler Derneği (ÇGD, Progressive Journalists Association)Foreign Media Association (FMA Turkey)IFEXInternational Press Institute (IPI)Media and Law Studies Association (MLSA)Norwegian Helsinki Committee (NHC)Osservatorio Balcani Caucaso Transeuropa (OBCT)P24 Platform for Independent JournalismPEN AmericaPEN DenmarkPEN InternationalPEN NorwaySouth East Europe Media Organisation (SEEMO)Turkey Litigation Support Project (TLSP)

CALABRIA: SALVIAMO LO SCOGLIO DEL DELFINO. Ad Africo(prov. di Reggio Calabria) e dintorni tutta la popolazione si sta mobilitando per salvare il famosissimo "Scoglio del Delfino" sita nelle mitiche scogliere di Africo. L'iniziativa è stata promossa dalle varie associazioni nazionali e internazionali affinché l'erosione calcarea e la stupidità d alcuni turisti non rovini questa meravigliosa forma d'arte scultorea che Madre Natura ci ha regalato. A causa di alcuni turisti col vizio di staccare, armati d martelletto, pezzi di roccia da portare a casa come souvenir, la parte anteriore dello Scoglio del Delfino è profondamente lesionata.
